News.title: UK towns hit by earthquake as 2.2 magnitude tremor rocks homes and residents feel ‘shake’ and ‘rumble’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

QUAKE SHAKE UK towns hit by earthquake as 2.2 magnitude tremor rocks homes and residents feel ‘shake’ and ‘rumble’

AN EARTHQUAKE struck a UK town leaving homes “shaking and rumbling” as residents felt the ground suddenly jolt.

The 2.2-magnitude tremor hit just before 7.50pm yesterday, with people across Grimsby and nearby areas reporting a sudden bang.



Residents in Cleethorpes and surrounding areas also felt the earthquake, which struck at a depth of around 5km.

One resident described feeling a “really quick shake” inside their home.



They said: “I felt what felt like a really quick shake in my house, I thought something heavy had fallen down upstairs or in the loft.”

Another said they “felt a bang like the house being hit”.



A third resident wrote on Facebook: “Felt the house shake and rumble.”

Another said: “I heard a deep rumble, I thought it was thunder.”

The BGS said the epicentre was in the Scartho area of North East Lincolnshire.

A 2.2 magnitude earthquake is considered a minor tremor and would generally only be felt by people close to the epicentre.



BGS data shows around 200 to 300 earthquakes of this kind are recorded across the UK every year.

But the area has experienced much stronger quakes in the past.

A 3.9 magnitude earthquake struck Grimsby in June 2018, with reports of people feeling it up to 60 miles away.

That came ten years after the area’s most significant earthquake in decades struck shortly before 1am on February 27, 2008.

The huge tremor measured 5.2 on the Richter scale and was classed as a “moderate” earthquake.



Some damage to buildings was reported, while residents described substantial shaking lasting several seconds.

It remains the largest recent onshore earthquake recorded in the UK.

News.title: Mum-of-four, 37, died in devastating house fire as husband desperately tried to save her by scaling drainpipe
News.content:
TRAGIC RESCUE Mum-of-four, 37, died in devastating house fire as husband desperately tried to save her by scaling drainpipe

A MUM-of-four died in a “ferocious” house fire as her husband desperately tried to save her by scaling a drainpipe, an inquest heard.

Kate Mulcahy, 37, was found dead after the horror blaze broke out at a £1.2m property at Ramsden Farm in Middleton, Manchester, in November 2024.



Rochdale Coroners’ Court was told Mrs Mulcahy had attended a friend’s baby shower before returning home at around 1.30am on November 10.

Her husband, John Mulcahy, woke to the sound of a smoke alarm at 3.51am.



He safely evacuated their twin sons and two daughters to a neighbouring property before making frantic attempts to rescue his wife.

The court heard the couple had been experiencing relationship difficulties and the property had recently been placed on the market.



Mrs Mulcahy was sleeping alone in an attic room on the top floor – where the blaze is believed to have originated – while Mr Mulcahy and the children slept on the floor below.

After finding himself unable to force entry into the top-floor room from inside the house, Mr Mulcahy scaled a drainpipe onto the roof, the court heard.

The desperate dad smashed a skylight, and pulled away tiles in a frantic attempt to reach her, the inquest was told.

He was ultimately driven back by the intensity of the flames.



Neighbour Tim Ainsworth described hearing loud bangs and dog barking before Mr Mulcahy arrived at his door in “sheer terror,” dropping off the children while screaming in panic.

Mr Ainsworth, whose hair and forehead were later singed by the heat, attempted to enter the property but was turned back by a “wall of fire,” concluding that no one inside could have survived.

Firefighters tackled the blaze and discovered Mrs Mulcahy’s body inside the property.



A post mortem concluded Mrs Mulcahy died as the result of “burns and the inhalation of fire fumes”,

Forensic pathologist Dr Jamie Robinson said he found no evidence of an assault, injury or underlying disease.

Dr Robinson said Mrs Mulcahy likely to have been rendered unconscious quickly and that there was no evidence of “a prolonged period of survival”.

Forensic scientist Martin Crookes said he believed the loud bangs would have been the result of “roof windows failing”.

He said the fact the front door and attic bedroom door were open would likely have created a “chimney effect”, with oxygen sucked in, fuelling the blaze.



He said he believed the “seat of the fire” was in the attic room but that he was unable to reliably determine the precise cause.

The entire room was engulfed in flames, he added, which made the investigation “very difficult”.

Detective Inspector Kim Tallis-Hines said she was satisfied there was no evidence of any suspicious circumstances or third-party involvement.

Coroner Mr Salt, concluding Mrs Mulcahy’s death was accidental, said: “These are circumstances that have been thoroughly investigated.

“Sadly, for various reasons, we don’t know 100 percent what took place.”



A number of flowers and tributes were placed on the front lawn in honour of the mum-of-four at the time.

News.title: TikTok star, 39, dies after ‘courageous’ cancer battle as heartbreaking final message revealed
News.content:
A BELOVED mum and TikTok star has died after a long battle with cancer as her final heartbreaking message is revealed.

Andree Greig Baudoin, 39, pre-recorded a final video to be shared in the event of her death.



The mum and influencer passed away on August 22 at Calcutta House by Hospice of Acadiana in Lafayette, Louisiana.

In Andree’s last video, released after her death, she said: “Hi, my TikTok family. If you’re seeing this video, it just means that my time has come and I’ve crossed over.



“This TikTok account has become my diary. It has become my way to let things out. It has become something I turned to first.”

She initially created her TikTok account so that her children would have video clips of her after she died.

READ MORE TRAGIC STAR TikTok star mom dies of cancer aged just 30 after amassing 237k fans

Andree said: “I started it because I wanted my kids to be able to follow my journey. And for it to be able to be accessed at any time and all times if they wanted to see me or see a video of me.”

Under the name “Andreethegirl”, the TikToker posted content about her battle against metastatic cancer to her thousands of followers.

Treatments, diets and different medications formed part of her struggle to beat back the cancer – all of which she posted about online.

But tragically Andree revealed that her illness had deteriorated rapidly to the point where there was “just nothing we can do about it”.



Her greatest fear was leaving behind her children and her husband.

In a heartbreaking admission, she said: “I’m 39. I’ll never be able to see my son get married, my daughter get married.

“I’ll never be able to meet my grandchildren. I’ll never be able to grow old with my husband, who I love dearly.”



Her final plea to fans is to be grateful for the everyday.

“My biggest, biggest wish is that you don’t take your health and what’s in front of you for granted,” she said, adding: “Enjoy the day in front of you.”

News.title: ‘Sporty’ girl, 14, who collapsed and died at cricket club is pictured as tributes flood in for ‘deeply loved twin’
News.content:
unimaginable void ‘Sporty’ girl, 14, who collapsed and died at cricket club is pictured as tributes flood in for ‘deeply loved twin’

A TEENAGE girl who sadly died after collapsing at a cricket club has been pictured as tributes pour in.

Emergency services rushed to the scene after 14-year-old Amélia Jones collapsed at the club in Cornwall.



The sporty teen, who loved netball and cricket, collapsed at Grampound Road Cricket Club on August 20.

She died after being rushed to hospital in a medical incident.



Her family has paid tribute to the “deeply loved daughter, sister, friend, and cherished twin”.

A fundraiser set up by her uncle read: “There are no words that can truly express the heartbreak of losing a child.



“She had the most beautiful smile and brought so much happiness to the people around her.

“She had so many interests and little things that made her wonderfully and uniquely Amélia.

“Her love of sport was a huge part of her life. Just last week, Amélia captained the Cornwall Girls Under-14s against Glamorgan — an achievement that reflected her talent, confidence and determination.

“She was also exceptionally talented and academically gifted.



“Her passing has left an unimaginable void in the lives of everyone who knew and loved her.

“We are raising funds to help with Amélia’s funeral expenses and to ease some of the family’s immediate financial burden in the weeks and months ahead.”

A cricket club spokesperson said: “It is with profound sadness that Grampound Road Cricket Club can confirm a tragic incident took place on Thursday evening.

“A teenage girl collapsed and was taken to hospital, but has now sadly died. This is believed to be a medical incident not connected to cricket.”

The Club Chair Lewis Sanders said: “Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with her family, friends and everyone who knew and loved her at this unimaginably difficult time.



“We would also like to thank all those who responded on Thursday evening, particularly those who provided immediate first aid and the emergency services including the Cornwall Air Ambulance.”

News.title: Birmingham to become England’s first 20mph city with speed limit on nearly ALL roads in ‘anti-motorist’ plan
News.content:
BIRMINGHAM is set to become England’s first 20mph city under controversial plans to cut speed limits across almost all of its roads.

The city’s council, led by a coalition of Liberal Democrats, Greens and independents, has pushed for every route except major A-roads to cap speeds despite critics blasting the plans as “anti-motorist”.



Birmingham town hall leaders insisted the move would ensure private vehicles “no longer dominate street life”, while actively encouraging residents to walk or cycle instead.

The controversial plan also promises to reallocate space on the tarmac to build a public transport network they believe is more fitting for a major city.



But critics have branded the initiative an “anti-motorist policy” that will hamper travel and snarl up transit across the West Midlands.

Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, said that left-wing councils had turned 20mph into the “national speed of bureaucracy”.

Meanwhile, Reform UK’s Jex Parkin, the leader of Birmingham’s opposition, said of the latest proposal: “This is another anti-motorist policy from a council that seems determined to make getting around Birmingham harder.

“People already have enough congestion, restrictions and disruption to deal with without another blanket measure being imposed on them.”

The shift marks a stark turning point for a city once celebrated as Britain’s motoring capital due to its heritage of mass vehicle manufacturing and pioneering road engineering.

In its plan, which was put out for public consultation last week, Birmingham City Council said: “A limit of 20mph will be standard on all local roads.



“Residential neighbourhoods and local centres will be places where people are put first.

“Cars will no longer dominate street life around homes and schools.”

The authority has been discussing the measure for several years, after it declared a road safety emergency in July 2024, but plans would need to go through consultation before being adopted.

The move echoes a contentious nationwide scheme introduced in Wales by the Labour government in 2023.

That default 20mph limit sparked immediate backlash, forcing ministers to water down the rules a year later as local councils began restoring 30mph zones.



The debate comes as Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham pushes for further regional devolution.

Greater local control could soon grant authorities across the country the powers to enforce similar measures on their own road networks.

England has had a 30mph speed limit in residential areas since 1935, but almost a third of roads now have a 20mph restriction.

The number of drivers caught breaking 20mph speed limits has increased dramatically, from 37,219 drivers in 2023 to 125,133 in 2025.

Bristol currently holds the highest proportion of reduced-speed routes in England, with 86 per cent of its roads set to 20mph.



However, unlike Birmingham, officials in Bristol have stopped short of adopting a total blanket approach.

The Department for Transport said in June that 20mph limits “should only be used where they are appropriate and supported by evidence”.

A Birmingham City Council spokesman said: “Evidence from around the world on slower speed limits is very clear: it reduces collisions, saves lives and reduces injuries – so our message is simple: slower is safer.

“Slower speeds are less intimidating towards those who walk or cycle, activities that we need to encourage more of if we are to reduce the number of harmful emissions and traffic levels in the city.”

The spokesman added that the city’s 20mph rollout had so far been done on a “targeted basis in response to local road safety concerns or near to schools”.

TRAIN ATTACK Manhunt as woman sexually assaulted on train during rush hour by man sitting behind her as cops release CCTV

COPS have released a CCTV image of a man they would like to speak to after a woman was allegedly sexually assaulted on a train during rush hour.

The alleged attack took place on a morning train service from Leeds to Skipton on Friday July 24, said British Transport Police.

The woman reported being sexually assaulted by a man sitting behind her at around 8.40am, said the force.

News.title: At least 14 newborn babies killed as fire engulfs hospital’s maternity ward after ‘air conditioning unit explosion’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BABY TRAGEDY At least 14 newborn babies killed as fire engulfs hospital’s maternity ward after ‘air conditioning unit explosion’

AT LEAST 14 newborn babies have been killed after a horror fire tore through a hospital’s maternity ward.

An air conditioning unit reportedly exploded sparking the deadly blaze and trapping several people inside with just one baby being rescued alive.



Nineteen people were saved in total from inside the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital after the fire broke out.

These included the newborn tot, six other children, 10 women and two men.



All survivors were reportedly rushed to intensive care units for further treatment.

Pakistani officials believe the fire broke out on the hospital’s third floor at around 6.45am this morning.





Six fire trucks, four ambulances and dozens of emergency responders rushed to the scene to carry out rescue operation around PIMS.

The compressor of an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the gynaecology unit of the nursery, according to local reports.

Pictures from the scene show glass windows close to where the fire broke out shattered under the intense heat.

Health Minister Mustafa Kamal told Geo News: “The fire spread very quickly, and the hospital’s electricity also went out immediately with the explosion.”



The infants in the ward were in incubators or connected to oxygen equipment at the time of the fire, Kamal added.

Newborns who died will have to be identified using DNA tests, local police said.

Heartbroken parents have been unable to say their goodbyes as the bodies of the babies remain with medical examiners.

Rescuers said no doctors, ward boys or other staff were in the incubation centre when the fire broke out.



Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an “immediate investigation” into the cause of the fire.

He said in a statement that he has “deep sorrow and heartfelt regret” over the hospital tragedy.

Sharif added: “Such a situation with children is irreparable.”

An eight-member inquiry committee has been set up to investigate the fire.

News.title: Moment police officer borrows bike from passerby then races after ‘thief’ and tackles him to ground
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment a police officer borrows a bike from a cyclist and uses it to chase down a suspected thief.

After commandeering the bicycle, bodycam footage shows the cop tackling the man to the ground and shouting: “You’re f****** nicked!”.



The chase began with the officer driving through the streets of Twickenham, south-west London in pursuit of an alleged thief.

Realising he needs to carry on the chase on foot, the Metropolitan Police officer exits his car and starts running.



But he soon passes a member of the public with a bike – who says: “Do you guys want to chase him on this?”.

The grateful officer replies “would you mind?” and tells the cyclist he only needs it for “five minutes”.



He races off, eventually reaching the suspect on a towpath near to the Twickenham Stoop stadium.

He then tackles the man to the ground and shouts: “Get over, get on the ground”.



“You’re f****** nicked!” he adds.

The officer then contacts his team, saying: “Additional officers coming to join me.

“I’m going to have to repatriate this bike to my hero member of the public.”

Insp Jon McLoughlin said of the incident: “The video below shows a recent arrest after a bike was stolen on Whitton High Street and is a great example of the public and police working together.

“In this case, a quick-thinking cyclist lent an officer their bike so they could continue their pursuit of a suspect.



“It’s a brilliant example of how a small act can make a big difference.”

This isn’t the first time an officer has used a member of the public to help catch a suspect.

In June, one armed police officer was helped by a van driver in the middle of a police chase before they catch the suspect fleeing on foot.



The officer clutching a firearm can be seen approaching a mini-roundabout after the suspect evaded attempts to arrest him.

Standing in the middle of the road, he then turns to a passing motorist in a van who stops and urges the officer to “get in the back, get in the back”.

The officer climbs in shouting “go, go, go” and tells the driver to follow the other officers.

In another amusing clip an out of breath bobby is picked up by a driver as he is chasing down two thieving boys.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The woman who filmed the incident said she and her friend were driving home when they saw the chase unfold.



“He opened the door and told us to follow the suspect,” she said.

News.title: Dolly Parton dies after brief battle with cancer as final sighting revealed
News.content:
Dolly Parton's life in her own songs

Many of Dolly Parton's songs reveal details of her life, whether that's through the lyrics themselves or the hidden true story behind them.

Coat of Many Colours (1971)

Dolly's single 'Coat of Many Colours' is an autobiographical song, about how her mother had made her a coat out of rags when she was younger. In the lyrics, Dolly recounted how her family struggled to afford clothes and her mother's ingenuity with a needle and thread left her daughter at the mercy of classmates' ridicule.

She sang: “I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be, in my coat of many colors my mama made for me.”

My Tennessee Mountain Home (1973)

Dolly really did grow up in a Tennessee Mountain Home. She spent her childhood in a two-room log cabin in Locust Ridge, with her parents and all her siblings.

Though they didn't have electricity or running water, the lyrics point towards everything Dolly loved about her childhood home, including: "Sittin' on the front porch on a summer afternoon, in a straight back chair on two legs leaned against the wall, as I watch the kids a-playin' with their June bugs on a string and chase the glowin' fireflies when evenin' shadows fall."

Jolene (1973)

Jolene was a red-headed bank clerk who had flirted with Dolly's husband, Carl Dean, early in their marriage. Though Carl was deeply devoted to Dolly, she had feared losing him to the glamourous clerk and penned the song to get through her jealousy.

I Will Always Love You (1974)

Dolly's career kicked off when she formed a partnership with Porter Wagoner. But there came a point where she felt the need to move on and the only way she could explain it was through song.

Thus, I Will Always Love You was born. The song, which is one of the most loved break-up tracks ever, was origianlly written to tell Porter that though Dolly would always love him, their time together was over.

News.title: £150 cost of living discounts for millions on 4 benefits after bill rise - but some miss out
News.content:
£150 cost of living discounts for millions on 4 benefits after bill rise - but some miss out

In blow today Ofgem said average power bills to rise to £1,723 - but if people on 4 DWP benefits failed to take action they will miss out on boost

View Image People on some benefits can get a boost to help with energy bills this winter (Image: Getty)

Households this morning were given a blow when regulator Ofgem raised its price cap to a three-year high. This means the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the average household using both electricity and gas if this level was sustained for a year.

‌



But there is help available - to millions who are on some of the biggest benefits in the UK. Energy customers have been told that 24 companies have signed up to a scheme which will give millions a £150 boost straight into their accounts.

‌



Every household where the billpayer is on means-tested benefits is in line for the rebate. In England and Wales, households in receipt of Housing Benefit, Income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and Universal Credit will be eligible – the same cohort as last winter.

‌



However some will miss out - there was a key deadline this month - August 23 - for people to make sure the person in the household who is on benefits is named on the power bill. If a household has failed to do this, then they will miss out on the £150 rebate.

The following suppliers will be part of the winter 2026 to 2027 scheme:

100Green (formerly Green Energy UK or GEUK)

Boost

British Gas

E - also known as E (Gas and Electricity)

Ecotricity

EDF

EnergyCoop – see Octopus Energy

E.ON Next

Fuse Energy

Good Energy

Home Energy

London Power

Octopus Energy

Outfox Energy

OVO

Sainsbury’s Energy

Scottish Gas – see British Gas

ScottishPower

So Energy

Square 1 Energy Ltd

TruEnergy

Tulo Energy

Utilita

Utility Warehouse

‌



On today’s bill rise Ofgem said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas prices as a result of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with volatile global markets remaining the dominant driver of price changes. Neil Kenward, Ofgem’s director general for markets, said: “High international gas prices are continuing to drive energy costs in the UK.

“We welcome the Government’s intervention to remove VAT from electricity bills, without which customers would have faced even higher costs this winter. Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap, and many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for electricity consumed out of peak times.

Millions on 4 benefits must act by Sunday to secure £150 boost READ MORE :

Energy bills rise to three-year high as winter Ofgem price cap announced READ MORE :

“It’s also worth considering different payment methods, with prepayment customers paying the lowest price cap rates, and could save consumers an average of about £45 compared to direct debit.”

‌



The latest price cap is based on Ofgem’s updated definition of a typical consumer, which came into effect from July to reflect falling household energy use. It would be the equivalent of £1,941 per year based on its previous calculations, up from £1,862 currently.

The increased October cap, which will remain in place for three months, will come into force as households start to increase their energy usage further by using their heating more regularly, adding to bills.

In a further blow for households, analysts Cornwall Insight released their latest forecast on Wednesday for a further 9% increase to the price cap in the New Year.

‌



This would put an average January bill up to £1,872 a year, £149 higher than October’s £1,723.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: “Families will be understandably concerned about the cost of energy bills this winter, which is being driven up by the Iran war. “Energy is an everyday essential and it needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills from October, to give families some breathing space.

“This has limited the rise in the price cap and follows the £150 in costs we removed from bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills.”

‌



Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said: “Labour promised to cut energy bills by £300, but they have gone up by nearly £400 instead.

“Our cheap power plan would cut energy bills for households and businesses by scrapping Government taxes and levies on bills, and it wouldn’t cost the taxpayer a penny. We have to put cheap energy first.”

Ned Hammond, Energy UK’s deputy director for customers, said: “This latest increase is in line with the predictions and any such rise is always more worrying over the winter months when customers naturally use more energy.

‌



“Coming off the back of a significant hike over summer, this further intensifies the challenges faced by customers struggling to afford their bills.

“As well as measures to improve targeted support, the Government needs to assess how to bring bills down over the longer term.

“The impact the conflict in the Middle East has had on gas prices underlines why we need to move to using more of our own sources of clean energy.

Article continues below

“But it’s equally true that we need to look at a fairer way of funding the policy and system costs that are also driving bills higher.”

News.title: Sisters both diagnosed with breast cancer just six weeks apart after spotting same symptom
News.content:
Sisters both diagnosed with breast cancer just six weeks apart after spotting same symptom

Aisling Muckian and Áine Mallie were both diagnosed with advanced breast cancer just weeks apart and the Irish sisters have now spoken about their difficult experiences in the last year

View 4 Images Áine Mallie and Aisling Muckian (Image: The Silverbridge Sisters Instagram/BELFAST LIVE)

Two brave sisters have opened up about being diagnosed with breast cancer just six weeks apart. Aisling Muckian and Áine Mallie were completely shocked after getting the cruel disease so young — but the siblings supported one another as they both went through chemotherapy, radiation and surgery.

‌



Their nightmare began when Aisling, who was just 31 at the time, found a lump in April 2025. Speaking on Ireland AM, she said: “Just obviously a massive shock. It’s not something I thought would be part of my life. Obviously, I’m sure everybody feels that way, but certainly not at my age.

‌



“I was perfectly fit. I was exercising. I was eating healthily. I was working nine to five. I have two little kids. You know, everything was kind of normal, I suppose.”

‌



After initially finding the lump, the mum, who was feeling tired but put it down to having a one and a three-year-old, didn’t think much of it, and presumed it was either a small cyst or muscle related. As a precaution she got it checked before eventually being diagnosed with stage three grade three ER-positive breast cancer.

View 4 Images Cancer advocate Aisling Muckian (Image: Ireland AM/YOUTUBE)

“Even when I was told, it didn’t really sink in,” she said. “Even now when I look back, obviously we’re kind of one year on now, it still doesn’t feel real, you know.”

‌



The sisters, both mothers from Silverbridge, County Armagh in Northern Ireland, were hit by another shock just weeks later. Áine, 34 at the time, was horrified to then find a lump on her own breast, and she instinctively knew it was cancer.

She remembered: “Aisling maybe spent a couple of weeks thinking that everything was all right. When I found my lump, it was literally two weeks after Aisling’s diagnosis. So, I did automatically think, ‘Oh my goodness, this could be the same.’”

Áine asked her younger sister if she could inspect her lump, and although it appeared different to hers, she added: “I knew in my heart when I felt hers that mine was the same, to be honest.”

‌



View 4 Images Áine Mallie (Image: Ireland AM/YOUTUBE)

After being diagnosed with a grade three, oestrogen and progesterone receptor positive breast cancer, it was also revealed that Áine’s had already spread to her lymph nodes, and the sisters then faced challenging treatments together.

Áine, who had a single mastectomy, said she “benefited slightly more” because her chemotherapy and operation was six weeks behind Aisling’s — meaning she was able to get her advice on both.

‌



Aisling meanwhile, who had a single mastectomy with reconstruction, revealed: “I think a cancer diagnosis can be very lonely. And one silver lining was that we went through it together, you know, and it I supposed reduced that loneliness side of it.”

She also said it helped her being able to reassure her sister, who like her has since been diagnosed with the BRCA2 gene, that she would be able to get through the chemotherapy by explaining how she felt throughout each stage.

Dr Sonja Bobart also joined in on the discussion and she said that men and women of all ages should be checking their bodies every single month.

‌



View 4 Images GP Dr Sonja Bobart (right) also joined the sisters on Ireland AM (Image: Ireland AM/YOUTUBE)

And as regards to symptoms of breast cancer specifically and what to look out for, she added: “So it’s not always a lump and as Aisling and Áine did, they checked themselves.

“But also look at your skin changes. So, are there any changes in terms of a rash, any redness, any heat that could be in either breast? Look at the breast in terms of the size.

Article continues below

“Compare one breast from the next. Are they the same? Look at the nipple. Is there any discharge retraction? Any eczema type sensation within the nipple? So anything that looks abnormal, get checked.

“And sometimes, people who do have a slight discomfort, not necessarily pain, but if you’ve got slight discomfort, always get that checked because lumps aren’t as Aisling said, they weren’t painful. They were painless. And that’s sometimes a suspicious sign.”

News.title: Tourists trade punches and swing chairs at shopkeepers in Italian resort brawl
News.content:
Tourists trade punches and swing chairs at shopkeepers in Italian resort brawl

Shocking footage shows tourists and shop owners brawling in the upmarket Italian resort of Capri, with the local mayor now issuing a statement

Tourists and shop owners brawl in Italy tourist hotspot

Tourists and souvenir shop owners were seen trading punches, kicks and even swinging chairs after furious brawl erupted in Capri.

‌



The broad daylight fight broke out in the Marina Grande port area of the upmarket Italian holiday destination.

‌



It reportedly flared up after shopkeepers asked a group of tourists to move their children away from the entrance to a souvenir shop.

‌



Shocking footage shows several people embroiled in the chaotic scenes as stunned tourists and locals look on. People could be seen throwing punches and kicks, while chairs were also swung during the melee.

The confrontation lasted for several minutes, with mobile phone footage showing the fight already in full swing before it eventually came to an end.

View 3 Images The shocking footage has been shared online (Image: Jam Press)

‌

Footage of the ugly scenes was sent to Capri mayor Paolo Falco.

He said: “The reasons were trivial, but it was an extremely unpleasant incident. It is not, however, a security emergency.

“When two million people arrive, unfortunately, a dispute can happen.

‌



“We have mobilised all available forces, together with the municipal police, to patrol the busiest areas.”

View 3 Images The confrontation lasted for several minutes (Image: Jam Press)

The video was also shared online by Francesco Emilio Borrelli, an MP for the Greens and Left Alliance (AVS), who called for greater security on the popular holiday island.

‌



He said: “This is yet another brawl. Greater security is urgently needed. At night, a single patrol covers the island, and that is not good enough.

“Seeing people fighting with chairs, kicks and punches is unacceptable. Capri is one of Campania’s main tourist destinations and deserves a level of security appropriate to its importance.”

View 3 Images It reportedly flared up after shopkeepers asked a group of tourists to move their children (Image: Jam Press)

Mayor Falco said the island is also monitored by around 80 high-resolution CCTV cameras.

It is unclear exactly where the tourists were from.

News.title: Grimsby rocked by earthquake as Lincolnshire locals fear houses 'have been hit'
News.content:
Grimsby rocked by earthquake as Lincolnshire locals fear houses 'have been hit'

The tremor was recorded in Grimsby, Lincolnshire, just before 7.50pm yesterday, with nearby Cleethorpes and surrounding areas also feeling the earthquake

View Image Grimsby and the surrounding areas have been hit by an earthquake (file) (Image: Andy Commins / Daily Mirror)

Residents in a UK town felt their homes "shake and rumble" as an earthquake hit yesterday.

‌



The 2.2-magnitude tremor was recorded in Grimsby, Lincolnshire, just before 7.50pm, according to the British Geological Survey (BGS) website.

‌



Residents in nearby Cleethorpes and surrounding areas also felt the earthquake, which took place at a depth of 5km.

‌



Taking to social media to write about their experience, one said: "I felt what felt like a really quick shake in my house, I thought something heavy had fallen down upstairs or in the loft."

Manchester Evening News reports another commented: "Felt a bang like the house being hit." One person wrote on Facebook: "Felt the house shake and rumble."

Another resident said: "I heard a deep rumble, I thought it was thunder."

‌



BGS explained the epicentre of the earthquake was in the Scartho area in North East Lincolnshire.

A 2.2 earthquake only represents a minor tremor that would have only been felt by those close to the epicentre.

BGS data shows between 200 and 300 earthquakes of this kind take place around the UK each year.

Article continues below

Grimbsy Live reports a 3.9 magnitude earthquake previously had its epicentre in Grimsby in June 2018, with people as far as 60 miles away feeling it. This was 10 years after the area's most significant earthquake in decades, which occurred at 12.56am on February 27, 2008.

The tremor measured 5.2 on the Richter scale, making it a "moderate" event. Some damage to buildings was reported and people said they experienced substantial "shaking" for a few seconds.

The tremor is the largest recent onshore earthquake in the UK.

News.title: 404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group
News.content:
404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group

Siân Robinson would sometimes eat McDonald's twice a day and then have pizza for dinner

404lb woman on three takeaways a day loses 12st after comment at slimming group

A woman who says she was addicted to food and regularly ate three takeaways a day has shed more than 13 stone. At her heaviest, Siân Robinson weighed 28st 12lbs and wore a size 32.

‌



The 33-year-old would start her day with a McDonald’s breakfast before having Greggs or another McDonald’s for lunch. Dinner could be a large half-and-half Domino’s pizza with wedges, with chocolate, crisps and cookies eaten in between meals.

‌



After years of failed diets, Siân’s weight began taking a devastating toll on her everyday life. She became breathless walking upstairs, avoided public transport because she worried about taking up too much space and needed a mobility scooter to get around Disney World in March 2024.

‌



View 7 Images Siân needed a mobility scooter to get around

“I was scared of flying and fitting in the seat,” said Siân, from Worcester, Worcestershire. “I didn’t like public transport in case I had to sit by someone and make them uncomfortable due to my size. Most physical activity was so hard for me.

‌



“It was affecting my day-to-day life. I had no confidence. I felt I’d lost my spark and was hiding away. I didn’t want to attend any events or meet friends, etc., as I was worried people would look at me because of my size.”

Siân said one cruel comment at a slimming group particularly stuck with her. She said: “People very rarely made comments. They just didn’t want to speak about it. However, something that has stuck with me is that at a local slimming group.

View 7 Images Siân before her weight loss

‌



“I attended for the first time in a while, and the lady weighing there said, ‘Oh my God, Siân, I didn’t recognise you; you’ve got so big’.

“That really upset me I was so upset when I realised I’d need a mobility scooter to get round Disney. It cost $60 a day but was essential because I just couldn’t do it. I was only 30 and already needed a scooter. I wondered how many years I had left with the way it was going.”

‌



Siân says her struggles with her weight began in childhood and food eventually came to dominate her life. She said: “I was always the biggest in my class at school. I noticed this from early years, and looking back in photos, I was always a bigger child.

View 7 Images Siân Robinson weighed 28st 12lbs and wore a size 32

‌



“I went on my first diet at a slimming club at the age of 10, and would always lose a bit, then put more back on. It became more of an addiction for me. All I would think about was food, and my life would revolve around it.”

But after getting engaged to her partner of 13 years, Matt, 32, in August 2024, Siân decided she wanted to transform her health before walking down the aisle. The aesthetics nurse prescriber began taking the weight-loss jab Mounjaro in November 2024 as a final attempt before considering surgery.

She has since lost 13st 10lbs, dropping from a size 32 to a size 16. Siân said: “I wanted to feel amazing on my wedding day and fit into my dream dress. I wanted something that actually worked, as one last try before I would make the decision to have surgery.

‌



View 7 Images Siân after her weight loss

“I followed a lot of people who were on Mounjaro and decided I wanted to give it a go. I chose a company that was CQC registered, and I felt safe with. I ordered the pen whilst I was on a Disney cruise, and it was waiting for me when I got home.

‌



“I felt terrified. I was scared that it wouldn’t work and the only thing left would be surgery. I was also scared I’d have horrific side effects, but I haven’t.”

Siân has also overhauled her diet, ditching her regular takeaways in favour of high-protein, balanced meals. She now starts her day with a protein shake and has salads, sandwiches or eggs with avocado on toast for lunch.

View 7 Images Siân has been using jabs

‌



Dinner might be chicken skewers with a jacket potato and salad. Siân said: “I now focus on the nutrition and fuelling my body rather than just food. I haven’t had Domino’s since December 2024. My likes and dislikes have completely changed.”

Now weighing 15st 2.3lbs and wearing a size 16, Siân says she has regained the confidence she thought she had lost. She hopes to shed another three stone before her wedding next July. She added: “My life is completely different. I have confidence, and I feel like I’ve got my spark back.

‌



View 7 Images Siân used to be addicted to food

“I want to go out, buy new clothes and enjoy myself. I go to the gym regularly; I’m not out of breath, feel physically fitter, and I’m making plans like going on holiday and enjoying life. I could have cried the first time I went clothes shopping for a size 16.

‌



“It was finally working, and I felt good in myself. I’m now wearing clothes I like rather than clothes that just hide me People can’t believe it; sometimes they don’t recognise me.

View 7 Images Siân hasn't had a Domino's in two years

Article continues below

“Everyone is so proud. Matt is so proud and happy for me. I’m going back to Disney next month, and I can’t wait to be able to walk around. It feels amazing, life-changing. To anyone else who is struggling with their weight and doesn’t know where to start, don’t be scared to give it another try.

“I’m so glad I made the decision to try. I feel free.”

News.title: Grandmother, 101, in bitter neighbour row as she's slapped with £1,500 bill
News.content:
Grandmother, 101, in bitter neighbour row as she's slapped with £1,500 bill

The grandmother claims that she "might be 101" but she knows the boundary for her fence that has caused high tensions between herself and her neighbours who made the replacement "in good faith"

View 3 Images The great-great-great-great-grandmother says she never agreed to how the new fence was put up and won’t take it lying down. (Image: A Current Affair )

A 101-year-old grandmother has been slapped with a £1,500 bill after a bitter neighbour row.

‌



Nala Lipp, a woman who lives in the Gold Coast of Australia has lived at her home for nearly 60 years, and agreed to a new fence being put up for privacy and security.

‌



However, the location of the fence has caused high tension between the elderly woman and her neighbours.

‌



View 3 Images “I might be 101, but I know what side of the fence I’m on,” Nala told A Current Affair. (Image: A Current Affair )

The partition has been placed in her neighbour's garden rather than on the boundary line.

She told A Current Affair: "I might be 101, but I know what side of the fence I’m on."

‌



Although it may appear the grandmother has gained space from this, the positioning leaves a leftover patch which she claims was not part of the deal.

Nala said she was happy to agree when her neighbour offered to replace the old fence at his own cost, describing it as a practical fix to improve privacy and security between the two homes.

The original low-rise fence was built by her husband in 1966 and despite signs of wear and tear still served its purpose.

‌



“It was old, but it was still standing up. It’s done a good job all these years,” she said.

However, the simple changing of the fence has now turned into a drawn out feud.

At the time the work was being carried out, Nala was unable to go and inspect it due to mobility issues.

‌



View 3 Images The fence had led to a bitter row between the neighbours

“It was to put it on the fence line. I gave him permission, not in his own yard,” she said.

Central to the dispute is the exposed concrete line from the original fence, which Nala says has been left visible because the replacement was built away from the boundary.

‌



She added: “Don’t I have any right to say I don’t want your yard in mine?

“It is not mine, it is still his. That’s why he has to maintain it, and it will never be mine, it’s his. And I don’t want it.”

To properly challenge the position of the fence, Nala said she would need to pay for a surveyor. The dispute has now gone far beyond a disagreement over appearances.

‌



“If I want to do anything about it, I have to get a surveyor, which will cost anywhere between $1000 and $3000 (around £1500). I just can’t afford to do it,” she said.

The neighbours provided a statement to A Current Affair, saying the previous fence was “significantly aged and deteriorated” and that the replacement fence was paid for in full by them in good faith.

“The new fence was deliberately constructed slightly within our property, rather than directly on the existing concrete edging, to avoid any potential encroachment onto … the property,” the statement said.

Article continues below

They added that during the building process it was clear of the location of the new fence and no concerns were raised at that time.

They rejected claims that the remaining concrete was a “mess” or that it had been left in place to save time or money.

Instead, they urged that it was existing garden edging that formed part of the established landscaping and garden border, and was not touched because it was not considered necessary or appropriate to remove it.

News.title: Homeowners urged to check their gardens before Monday for 1 invasive plant
News.content:
Homeowners urged to check their gardens before Monday for 1 invasive plant

One invasive plant could be silently destroying your property's value right now and August is the critical window to catch it

View 2 Images Homeowners urged to check their gardens before Monday for 1 invasive plant (Image: ands456 via Getty Images)

It looks deceptively ordinary. Tall, slightly bamboo-like stems, a zigzag of leaves, clusters of creamy white flowers catching the late summer sun. But if you spot this plant growing in your garden right now, the consequences could be far more serious than you might think – and the clock is ticking to do something about it.

‌



Japanese knotweed has a well-earned reputation as one of the most destructive invasive plants in Britain, capable of slashing a property's value and even blocking prospective buyers from securing a mortgage. Now, with August presenting the best window of the year to identify it, the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) is calling on homeowners to inspect their gardens before September, while the plant is still easy to spot.

‌



Why August matters

Japanese knotweed is at its most visible during late summer, when its towering, bamboo-like stems and distinctive creamy white flowers make established growth far easier to identify. Once identified, however, it must be treated with extreme care – because this is a plant that plays by its own rules.

‌



Notorious for its ability to regenerate from even the tiniest fragments of its underground rhizomes, Japanese knotweed can swiftly take over large sections of a garden. Worse still, rhizomes can lie dormant in the soil for years, meaning the problem can return long after gardeners believe they have dealt with it.

Attempts to dig it out without expert guidance can make things worse, spreading plant fragments to new areas and potentially extending the infestation. The RHS warns that even the smallest piece of rhizome or stem is enough to spark a new growth.

The damage it causes

While many people associate Japanese knotweed primarily with overgrown borders, the real threat extends well beyond the flower beds.

‌



The plant is classified as an invasive non-native species and listed under Schedule 9 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981, reflecting the serious risk it poses to the wider environment.

According to the RHS, its aggressive rhizomes allow it to form dense patches that choke out native plants by competing for space, light, moisture and nutrients. It can also push through and exacerbate existing cracks and weaknesses in paving, paths and other hard surfaces – causing structural damage that is both costly and difficult to reverse.

For homeowners, the financial stakes are significant. The presence of Japanese knotweed on or near a property can reduce its value and, in some cases, make it very difficult to sell or remortgage until the problem has been professionally treated and certified.

‌



View 2 Images Japanese knotweed can spread fast (Image: Photosbypatrik via Getty Images)

How to identify the plant

Japanese knotweed can be recognised by its bamboo-like hollow stems, which feature leaves arranged in a distinctive zigzag pattern along the length of the stalk. In late summer, clusters of small creamy white flowers appear, making the plant particularly conspicuous right now.

The RHS, however, stresses that correct identification is absolutely crucial, as several other plants have a similar appearance. If in doubt, seek expert guidance before taking any action.

Article continues below

So what should you do?

The RHS is clear: if you suspect Japanese knotweed, do not attempt to deal with it yourself. The simplest and most effective course of action is to contact a professional company that specialises in Japanese knotweed removal.

Under no circumstances should the plant – or any part of it – be disposed of in home compost, council green-waste collections or household waste bins. Doing so risks spreading the plant further and could even carry legal implications, as Japanese knotweed is classified as controlled waste under UK law.

Gardeners are urged to inspect their borders, boundaries, and the areas surrounding sheds, fences and garden paths before September. Catching the problem early is by far the best way to prevent it from developing into something far more serious – and far more expensive.

News.title: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the removal of VAT on energy bills for six months from October was a "down payment" on helping households with energy costs.

She said bills would be Â£45 less than they would have been and the warm homes discount would take Â£150 off bills for six million households this winter.

"We know people are under huge amounts of pressure due to the cost of living, and I know that people are really worried about their energy bills, and we are absolutely alongside them and trying to do everything we can," she told BBC's Today programme.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households at the coldest time of the year.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government had to "put cheap energy first".

"Labour promised to cut energy bills by Â£300, but they have gone up by nearly Â£400 instead," she said.

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said: "The prime minister must wake up to the scale of the challenge and accept that bold change is needed to bring bills down."

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed into the issue, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use the proceeds to help those struggling with energy bills.

Longer term, he said the government should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting", he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

"So we are now seeing for the second price cap in a row a bit of a gap open up between gas bills and electricity bills, and that in a sense is positive because it means the transition for example to heat pumps becomes cheaper for households," he told BBC's Today programme.

News.title: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
News.content:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

News.title: Yellow warnings in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: Ex-England footballer Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crashing Lamborghini
News.content:
Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May.

The former England winger, who most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, crashed his Lamborghini into barriers on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of Thursday, 28 May.

The 31-year-old was arrested and then released on bail pending further enquiries.

A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: "A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

"Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

"The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange [Hampshire], on 28 May, 2026.

"No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September."

Police suspected Sterling of "driving a vehicle whilst unfit through drugs," but that has not been included in the charges.

In May a source close to Sterling told BBC Sport there was "no proof" of drugs in his system.

The source added the player had faced "an extremely tough couple of years" and had been made to "feel worthless" and "forgotten about".

Sterling has been without a club since leaving Dutch side Feyenoord at the end of last season.

He joined Feyenoord in February on a short-term contract after leaving Chelsea by mutual consent.

Chelsea paid Â£47.5m to sign Sterling from Manchester City in 2022, where he had won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup in seven years.

In 2024 the former Liverpool winger joined Arsenal on loan, but upon returning to Chelsea in 2025 was exiled from the first-team squad and made to train separately.

Sterling earned 82 England caps between 2012 and 2022, and appeared at three World Cups and two European Championships.

News.title: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims in adulthood, say psychiatrists
News.content:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discreet episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support â many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

News.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
News.content:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (Â£14,500) and $50,000 (Â£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: Major gangland figure Steven Daniel arrested in organised crime raid
News.content:
One of Scotland's most high-profile gangland figures has been arrested during an early morning police raid.

Steven 'Bonzo' Daniel, 46 was taken into custody at around 06:00 from his home in Robroyston in the north of Glasgow.

Daniel is understood to be the head of the notorious Daniel crime family which has been engaged in a violent feud with the rival Lyons family for 25 years.

He was arrested in connection with serious and organised crime, firearms and drugs offences as part of Operation Ventetic, a major UK-wide operation which has dismantled several gangs.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Libyan who was cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
News.content:
A Libyan who was cleared after standing trial over the Lockerbie bombing has died aged 70.

Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was accused of murdering 270 people in the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in December 1988.

He was found not guilty but a second Libyan, Abdulbasset Al Megrahi, was convicted of playing a key role in the bombing of the American airliner.

A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced Fhimah's death and expressed the company's condolences to his family.

Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

His funeral is set to take place on Wednesday in Tripoli, the capital of Libya.

News.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
News.content:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost Â£6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) â with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says, external the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

News.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder
News.content:
The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail, external on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

Baby food pouches sold in UK supermarkets are effectively "equivalent to fruit smoothies" and should not be given to children under a year old, experts have warned.

Researchers found that very few pouch products "meet the desired characteristics for complementary foods", leading to calls for regulators to review how they are classified and sold.

The study, conducted by academics from the University of Glasgow’s College of Medical Veterinary and Life Sciences and the First Steps Nutrition Trust, examined every wet commercial baby food (CBF) item available at six major UK supermarkets.

Their analysis evaluated sugar, protein, and energy contents across 298 products, comparing them to breast milk.

Six out of 10 products evaluated (60%) were sold in "spouted pouches" or sPouches.

open image in gallery Experts say baby food pouches are effectively ‘equivalent to fruit smoothies’ ( Getty/iStock )

Of these pouches, 70% were targeted at infants under six months of age, despite health guidelines recommending that weaning begin from around six months.

Compared to breast milk and alternative products, pouches were found to carry lower levels of protein, reduced energy, and higher concentrations of sugar.

Researchers stated that many of these products are "similar to sweet fruit smoothies", which are not recommended for infants or pre-school aged children.

According to NHS guidelines, infants under 12 months "do not need fruit juice or smoothies".

Writing in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood, the authors noted: "Many wet CBF delivered in sPouches have the texture and composition of sweet drinks, while very few meet the desired characteristics for complementary foods,"

They added: "These CBFs, which in texture and content are equivalent to fruit smoothies, should not really be given at all before 12 months and their intake limited after."

The team said parents regularly select these options due to "misperceptions of suitability and healthfulness", pointing out that "CBF packaging often displays the misleading claim no added sugar despite containing high amounts of free sugars due to pureed fruit content".

The authors urged regulators to "review whether labelling spouted-pouch, baby food products as complementary foods is appropriate and consider whether these delivery systems are inappropriate for complementary feeding."

open image in gallery NHS guidelines state infants under 12 months ‘do not need fruit juice or smoothies’ ( Getty/iStock )

Dr Vicky Sibson, co-author of the study and director at the First Steps Nutrition Trust, said: "The NHS advises parents not to give babies fruit drinks and smoothies because their high sugar and acid content can cause tooth decay.

"And yet, right now, supermarkets and pharmacies are full of fruit-based baby ‘food’ pouches marketed for use from four months and six months of age as ‘first foods’, when our research shows they are actually often more like fruit drinks or smoothies.

"Parents are being misled in to believing that these are healthy and appropriate choices for their babies.

"The Government have given the baby food industry until February 2027 to comply with new voluntary baby food guidelines.

"A quick glance at the shelves and online suggests slow progress and undoubtedly a mandatory approach would be preferable.

"Stronger regulations on the composition, marketing and labelling of commercial baby and toddler foods and drinks should be based on the latest evidence, to ensure maximum protection for infant and young child health."

The government will tell households to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to prepare for extreme weather or cyber attacks on the country, according to reports.

The Financial Times reports Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia and this summer’s heatwaves.

Russia said there would be “consequences” for Britain providing Ukraine with blueprints for British components used in the French-produced Scalp missile as Paris looks at setting up assembly lines for the weapon in Ukraine.

The country’s foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said his country had a right to regard the “direct involvement of British missile forces” as “participation in the war, with all the ensuing consequences”.

Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia and this summer’s heatwaves ( AFP/Getty )

But in a speech outside Kyiv’s St Sophia cathedral on Monday, Mr Burnham vowed he would not be deterred from providing aid to Ukraine.

According to the FT, the government is accelerating work on its “war book” – a manual for the defence of the nation against external threats – as well as a social media campaign with advice to help people to deal with the impacts of extreme weather, such as the heat waves which have hit the country this summer.

A source told the newspaper: “There will be practical advice on things you can do to improve domestic resilience, like having some bottled water and tinned food. It will be common sense, not scaremongering.”

The Independent has approached the Cabinet Office for comment.

Earlier this month, The Independent reported analysts warned extreme heat and ongoing droughts are putting Britain at risk of its “worst food security crisis in decades”.

The knock-on impact of five heatwaves and prolonged dry conditions could destroy farmers’ harvests, leading to food shortages later this year and increasing reliance on foreign imports, according to analysts from the investment bank Shore Capital.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) warned the situation is “increasingly concerning” and that dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing.

Speaking to The Telegraph at the time, Shore Capital’s Akhil Patel and Clive Black said the recent extreme weather could ruin homegrown supplies and potentially drive up animal feed costs, leading to greater costs for consumers.

“The UK has not been so close to a food security challenge for many decades,” they said.
