Sports.title: Wilson scores on full debut as Brentford hit Birmingham for six
Sports.content:
Callum Wilson scored just six minutes into his full debut and captain Nathan Collins converted two headers as Brentford routed Championship side Birmingham 6-1.

The 34-year-old Wilson, who joined on a free transfer from relegated West Ham, seized his first opportunity with a crisp finish which took a deflection off defender Dael Fry, who had a debut to forget.

Brentford's Premier League quality was evident throughout and although Blues equalised through Demarai Gray just before the half-hour they were level for just seven minutes.

Image: Callum Wilson scored six minutes into his full Brentford debut

Lax defending saw Aaron Hickey and Collins score in quick succession to effectively seal the tie before half-time, with Mikkel Damsgaard getting on the end of a counter-attack to add the fourth.

Igor Thiago's smart close-range finish sent fans streaming for the exit, missing Collins' second header.

The Bees, quarter-finalists last season, had not beaten Birmingham in six previous meetings, the last a goalless draw more than five years ago in the Championship before they went on to bigger and better things which their ambitious hosts now hope to emulate.

Birmingham's priority remains promotion so, after opening with two league draws, boss Chris Davies made six changes, including goalkeeper Ryan Allsop, Fry and Argentinian striker Luis Vazquez.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Callum Wilson produced a composed finish to put Brentford ahead just six minutes into his first competitive start for the club.

However, the gulf to a Premier League squad was evident as Keith Andrews retained only three of the team which demolished Tottenham and saw three of his newcomers score and another, Yehor Yarmoliuk, run the midfield before he was forced off with injury.

Davies wants to meet the club's aspirations by playing their way out of the Championship but it proved their undoing before they had even had chance to get a foothold in the game as they fell foul of Brentford's high press at a short goal-kick.

Paik Seung-ho was slow to react to the loose ball and Yarmoliuk played in Wilson to fire home first-time from the edge of the area with the aid of a deflection.

But a miscontrol by Jannik Schuster saw the centre-back booked for bringing down Vazquez and from Paik's short free-kick Gray drilled a deflected shot through a crowd of players.

It was a brief moment of joy in an otherwise chastening night as a failure to deal with Vitaly Janelt's chip and Wilson's strength allowed Hickey to fire home an angled shot.

Collins jumped in front of Fry to nod in a simple header from Jaidon Anthony's cross but a ruthless Brentford went for the kill and, after bringing on the likes of Igor Thiago, Kevin Schade and Mamadou Sangare, scored three more after the break.

The managers...

Birmingham's Chris Davies:

"My message to supporters tonight is 'sorry'. It's not very pleasant and I can understand how frustrating it is for them.

"It was a very tough evening for us, a painful evening, and incredibly disappointing to lose a game 6-1 at home.

"There were many situations where we were just not good enough to compete and I take ultimate responsibility for it - and the players will have to do it in their own minds.

"We were beaten by a team a long way ahead of us in every aspect. Was 6-1 a fair reflection? Probably."

Brentford's Keith Andrews:

"I didn't really blink an eyelid making so many changes.

"There is a huge narrative around cup games with coaches making changes but with the squad we have, there are fine margins between who plays and doesn't play.

"We needed to compete really hard to play the game we wanted. I thought overall we produced a really good performance."

Sports.title: Celtic throw away four-goal aggregate lead to crash out of Champions League against Lask
Sports.content:
Celtic threw away a four-goal lead in Austria as they missed out on the Champions League for the second year running. The Scottish champions looked to be cruising into the league stage when Callum McGregor put them 4-0 up on aggregate against Lask with a 21st-minute deflected strike.

However, they went on to endure one of their all-time European lows with a 5-1 defeat in Linz delivering a £20m-plus blow.

The Hoops had other chances in the first half but the Austrians gave themselves a lifeline when Moses Usor pounced on a loose pass from Benjamin Nygren to level on the night in the 32nd minute.

The tie began to spiral out of Celtic’s control early in the second half as Robert Ljubicic and Samuel Adeniran netted from outside the box. Martin O’Neill’s side looked like they would cling on but Florian Flecker nodded home from close range in stoppage-time to spark an additional 30 minutes.

Celtic had disappeared as an attacking force at half-time and Adeniran delivered the knockout blow that sends them into the Europa League.

The Hoops exited on penalties at the playoff stage last season after failing to sign a proven striker before drawing a blank against Kairat Almaty. Fans will this year question the decision to sell Arne Engels just ahead of the first leg after they lost control in midfield in Austria.

The quality of Celtic’s finishing had been the difference in Glasgow but Lask created chances throughout and the second leg started in similar fashion.

Celtic looked to extend their lead. Mika Baur stabbed an early chance just wide and Kasper Høgh forced a couple of first-half saves from decent opportunities. McGregor opened the scoring in between those chances when he drilled a first-time shot in off a defender after Yang Hyun-jun had played a one-two with Kieran Tierney.

The home side had exerted some pressure just before McGregor’s goal and they levelled following careless play from Nygren. The Austrian champions pulled a goal back three minutes after the restart when Usor outmuscled Auston Trusty and worked the ball inside for Ljubicic to drive home from 20 yards.

View image in fullscreen Dismayed Celtic players react to their capitulation against Lask. Photograph: Severin Aichbauer/SPP/Shutterstock

Celtic endured some nervy moments before they conceded again in the 58th minute when Adeniran curled a wonderful first-time strike into the top corner from 25 yards.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Celtic were on the ropes. Several shots flew past Viljami Sinisalo’s goal before the Finn pulled off a great stop from Sascha Horvath. João Victor Tornich headed inches wide from the resulting corner.

Adeniran fired off the underside of the bar and Celtic defended with four centre-backs as Liam Scales and Dane Murray came on to join Trusty and Cameron Carter-Vickers.

With Luke McCowan, Reo Hatate and Sebastian Tounekti also off the bench, Carter-Vickers had to struggle on with cramp and Celtic could not hold out. Sinisalo made a great stop from a Tornich header but Flecker converted the rebound.

Anthony Ralston replaced Carter-Vickers as extra-time allowed O’Neill to make a further change and Celtic appeared to stem the tide. However, Adeniran fired home from 25 yards with five minutes left after dispossessing McCowan and Celtic could not threaten after Sinisalo’s penalty save denied the striker his hat-trick.

Sports.title: After Dom Ballard’s backheel, what is the earliest goal of the season? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“After watching Dom Ballard’s backheel volley for Bristol City against Birmingham in game week two of the Championship, it begs the question: what’s the earliest in a season a goal has gone on to win goal of the season?” asks Ricardio Sentulio.

There is no doubting Dom Ballard’s outrageous flick for Bristol City at Birmingham City should be a Puskás contender, especially with his finish kissing the crossbar on its way in, and has a very good chance of being the best goal scored in the 2026-27 Championship season, even though there is a long way to go.

Ballard’s wondergoal was scored on 22 August, on gameweek two. Eleven years ago to that day, Marco Matias notched this ridiculous effort for Sheffield Wednesday at Leeds United, although it should be said that Yorkshire derby was gameweek four, so technically later in the 2015-16 season than Ballard’s. Matias was given the goal of the season gong in April 2016.

The earliest Championship goal of the season we could find was the 2022-23 effort from Ismaïla Sarr for Watford. The Senegalese, now at Palace, scored from the halfway line to stun West Brom on the opening day (8 August). It doesn’t get much earlier, especially as Sarr’s strike was just 12 minutes into the match.

David Beckham’s famous goal for Manchester United against Wimbledon in 1996-97, lobbing Neil Sullivan from the halfway line – later voted the best of that Premier League campaign – was also on the opening day of the league season but came later in the year (11 days after Sarr) and also in the 87th minute (so 75 minutes later than Sarr in the match).

View image in fullscreen A 21-year-old David Beckham, there, on his way to superstardom. Photograph: Tony O’Brien/Action Images/Reuters

In Scotland, the 2017-18 SPFA goal of the season was given to Kieran Tierney for Celtic versus Kilmarnock, also on 8 August (2017) in the League Cup. Even though that is the same date as Sarr’s strike, the cup tie actually came three days after Celtic’s opening league game, a 4-1 win over Hearts on 5 August 2017. We could also mention that Celtic’s Jota once scored a goal of the month (for August even though the goal was in July) for Celtic against Aberdeen (31 July 2022, game one).

We finish with a goal that probably doesn’t quite fit into this category but is too good to ignore or forget. Schalke’s goal of the year (not season, it should be stated) in 2013 came as early as on 27 July but comes with three caveats: a) it was in a pre-season friendly; b) it was by a player that wasn’t even on Schalke’s books at the time of scoring; and c) it was a tap-in.

After two successful years at Schalke, Raúl had joined Al-Sadd, with a pre-season friendly arranged as part of the deal. So when Al-Sadd travelled to Gelsenkirchen on 27 July 2013, Raúl agreed to play the first half for his new side and the second half for Schalke. The Spaniard scored twice for the latter, the first of which was a textbook right-place-right-time finish from two yards out. To understand why it was voted Schalke’s goal of the year, you are going to have to check out the assist from a teenage Julian Draxler.

Have you any earlier examples from further afield? Mail us with your questions and answers.

Spinning plates

“Has a club’s player-manager ever been called up for an international cap, or travelled to play during an international break in the club season?” asks Frederick Sondheimer-Acosta.

Let’s start with a couple of famous examples from the Scotland team of the mid-1980s. “Kenny Dalglish became Liverpool player-manager in the summer of 1985 and subsequently played a few games for Scotland, including the first leg of their World Cup playoff win against Australia,” writes Dom Miller. “He won his 100th cap against Romania in March 1986 and was initially selected for the World Cup squad but withdrew due to a knee injury picked up in the FA Cup final (there has always been a suspicion he didn’t go because his mate Alan Hansen wasn’t picked). Dalglish won his last two caps in the autumn of 1986.”

View image in fullscreen Player-manager Kenny Dalglish (top right) and Liverpool celebrate winning the 1985-86 First Division at Stamford Bridge. Dalglish scored the winning goal to beat Chelsea and clinch the title. Photograph: David Cannon/Getty Images

Scotland, with Alex Ferguson in temporary charge after the tragic death of Jock Stein, did have a player-manager in their squad for the World Cup. Graeme Souness was appointed by Rangers in April and played the first two games at Mexico 86, when Scotland were a little unfortunate to lose to Denmark and West Germany. But Souness struggled with the altitude, saying he never felt worse on a football field than during the West Germany game, and Ferguson left him out of their final group match against Uruguay.

Another mighty, all-purpose midfielder, Johnny Giles, went one better than Souness. “Perhaps uniquely, Giles held player-manager positions for club and country simultaneously,” writes Bruce Mair. “He was player-manager of the Republic of Ireland, a part-time post, from May 1973 until March 1980 while playing for Leeds United (1973-75) and serving as player-manager of both West Bromwich Albion (1975-77) and Shamrock Rovers (1977-80). Giles selected himself for 24 of his 59 international appearances.”

Those are the most high-profile examples in Britain and Ireland, but there are dozens more cases – thanks to Bruce Mair, in particular, for doing so much work on this. We’ve picked some of the more interesting examples:

Andy Aitken “The earliest player-manager I can find,” writes Bruce. “Won three caps for Scotland while player-manager of Middlesbrough, 1907-08, and three more when player-manager/secretary at Leicester Fosse (now Leicester City), 1910-11.

Orvar Bergmark “Played 41 internationals for Sweden, including their run to the 1958 World Cup final, while player‑manager of Örebro between 1958 and 1961.”

Gunnar Gren “Seventeen caps for Sweden while player-manager of Örgryte IS, 1957-58. A teammate of Orvar Bergmark in the Swedish side that reached the 1958 World Cup final.”

Stuart Pearce “Capped twice for England in 1997 during his stint as caretaker player-manager at Nottingham Forest.”

Fanny Vágó “Hungary’s most‑capped women’s international made 19 appearances for her country while player‑manager of Ferencvárosi TC between 2021 and 2023.”

Elisha Scott “Liverpool legend won four caps for Northern Ireland while player-manager of Belfast Celtic at the tail end of his career, 1934-36.”

John Toshack “Six appearances for Wales as Swansea City player-manager in 1979.”

Jim Platt “Played twice for Northern Ireland in 1984 as player-manager of Ballymena United and made one further appearance as player-manager of Coleraine in 1986. Member of Northern Ireland’s 1986 World Cup squad.”

Knowledge archive

“Has there ever been an occasion where a major team has been disrupted by jury service, with either a manager or a player being called up during the season?” James Schofield asked back in May 2018.

“Plymouth’s Welsh international Carl Fletcher once tried to argue he couldn’t sit on a jury as he was too well known,” answered Andy Carswell. “According to reports in 2010, Judge Francis Gilbert told the midfielder that being Plymouth captain was not sufficient reason to excuse him, and that he had enough time to travel to Cheltenham for a Johnstone’s Paint Trophy tie after completing his duties. Fletcher argued that his position meant he was in a position of potentially being threatened, saying: ‘I don’t want anything to come back on me for sitting on a jury.’ His protests fell on deaf ears, with Judge Gilbert adding: ‘Lots of well-known people, some more famous than you, have been required to sit on juries.’”

James Perch had just helped Newcastle United to fifth place in 2012 but was also forced to cut short a holiday to Dubai after learning of his higher calling. “I’ve got jury service, unless I can be excused,” he told the club website. “It’s killed my holiday a bit, but at the minute I’m set to be in court at the end of May.”

Can you help?

“As someone who occasionally has to search for football stadiums to find directions and the like, I always enjoy that people take the time to rate their experience of visiting a football ground,” begins our own Will Unwin. “Hull City, for example, have 4.3 stars from 3,655 reviews. I therefore ponder … which ground has the highest and lowest Google rating?”

“I was surprised, staggered in fact, to see Nottingham Forest as the 18th team in the Guardian season previews,” writes Ross Connett. “I associate 18th place with the likes of Tottenham or West Ham, never a team beginning with N, just scraping over halfway into the alphabet. Has there ever been a more ‘early alphabet team’-dominated Premier League?”

“During Fulham v Chelsea, the previous jobs of both the opposing managers was coincidentally at the same club, Real Madrid,” notes Sarang Satish. “Are there other times this has happened?”

“Who has scored the highest percentage of their professional goals in hat-tricks?” asks Michael D.

“Last weekend every match in the Gibraltar league was a draw,” mails Stephen Hogg. “There are very few teams in the league, however. What’s the biggest league where this has happened?”

“This season Istanbul has six clubs in the Turkish top flight,” starts Vasco Wackrill. “What is the record number of top-flight clubs supplied in a season by a non-capital city?”

“Three of Kevin Lisbie’s sons are playing professionally; in the Championship (Kyrell, Millwall), in League One (Kyreece, Reading) and League Two (Kaion, Colchester United),” writes Stuart Willsher. “Have we ever had four brothers playing in all four top English divisions?”

Sports.title: De Zerbi hopes Sávio’s fresh start will help Spurs’ much-needed rebrand
Sports.content:
What’s in a name? Quite a bit, judging by the discussion at Roberto De Zerbi’s Tottenham press conference on Tuesday, shortly after the club had completed the £75m signing of Savinho from Manchester City and the Brazil winger had let everybody know that he wanted to be called Sávio from now on. He will have that name on his Spurs shirt above his No 17, which he has taken over from Cristian Romero, the former captain who has moved to Atlético Madrid.

The 22-year-old went by Sávio at various times before his two seasons at City but there was nonetheless speculation about the reasons for the reversion. Savinho translates roughly from the Portuguese as “little Sávio”. Was it him saying that he was now an older and more mature player?

On the subject of theories, there is one about the fee, which could rise to £85m in add-ons. Even at £75m, it represents a record sale for City, who paid £30.8m to take Sávio from Troyes. Spurs are pushing to sign another attacker from City – Omar Marmoush, whose previous club Eintracht Frankfurt have a sell-on clause. Are Spurs paying more for Sávio in order to pay potentially less to City for Marmoush, which could reduce the liabilities to Eintracht?

De Zerbi has plenty on his plate after Spurs’ dismal 3-0 defeat at Brentford on Saturday in their Premier League opener and before the Carabao Cup tie at home against Charlton on Wednesday night.

“Listen, I lost 3-0 in the first game in the Premier League … do you think for me it’s a problem if Savinho becomes Sávio?” he said, turning to face his interpreter. “If Enrico [the interpreter] becomes Savinho, it’s a problem. If Savinho stays Sávio, nothing changes for me.”

De Zerbi said the talks for Sávio had started three days after the end of last season. It has been a mini‑epic to get the deal over the line but well worth it, according to the Spurs manager, who rates Sávio as one of the best in the world for being able to get past his marker when one‑against‑one. The challenge for Sávio will be to improve his end product, particularly in terms of goals. He scored only seven for City in all competitions and only two in 53 Premier League appearances. Sávio is available for selection against Charlton, his paperwork having been completed in time.

De Zerbi did get around to accepting that Sávio’s rebrand was part of a fresh start for the player. What is not in doubt is Spurs’ need for one after Brentford, when all the excitement around a summer of heavy spending turned to frustration; a very familiar sinking feeling.

View image in fullscreen New Tottenham signings Jan Paul van Hecke (left) and Sandro Tonali (right) after Spurs conceded their second goal during their 3-0 defeat at Brentford. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

It is possible to explain away the shambles against Brentford, who were not only much more joined-up but appeared to want it more in the duels. De Zerbi has attempted to do so in that way beloved of managers, emphasising he is not making excuses, you understand, just stating facts.

He had a completely new back four compared with his preferred unit from the end of last season; a new midfield pair, too. Up front from right to left, Mikey Moore, Richarlison and Mathys Tel were nobody’s idea of a trio to drive the push for Champions League football. De Zerbi was missing a host of players because of fitness issues, including Pedro Porro, Micky van de Ven, Mateus Fernandes and Dominic Solanke. Some of the issues can be traced to the slog of a pre-season tour to New Zealand and Australia, which De Zerbi continues to reference in irritated tones.

These facts do not really wash. The performance against Brentford was unacceptable. There is the sense that it will work out for Spurs, mainly because they have De Zerbi and a collection of Premier League‑ready new signings. They have certainly put themselves under pressure for the visit of Charlton. A relevant statistic: Spurs have won one domestic home game in 2026 – against Everton on the final day of last season which enabled them to avoid relegation.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

De Zerbi made the point that he and the squad had “started the project right now, not last season”. Which was when he was parachuted in with seven games to go; he picked up 11 points to dodge the unthinkable. “Last season, we fought to stay up,” he said. The inference was that it would take rather more to become a proper team.

On the other hand, the experiences of the previous campaign do offer reassurance. “Maybe last season was a tougher challenge to stay up than this season,” De Zerbi said. “I said to the players: last season, in a worse situation, we showed character, we showed balls. We showed pride and quality. Now we have to stay calm and to analyse better the situation – not to have an emotional reaction. We have to be intelligent.”

What De Zerbi craves is consistency, which he defined as being five wins in a row. It seems a distant goal after Brentford but De Zerbi has faith. What it will take is a change to the collective mentality. “We have to get used to winning games and games and games – we have to change habits from the last two seasons,” he said.

“For me, the Carabao Cup is like the Premier League. We are not in the condition to make differences [between the competitions]. We have to play well and get used to winning – and winning matches, not a match. We have to change the mood. And we can.”

De Zerbi said that Porro and Van de Ven will return as substitutes against Charlton and Solanke may start. James Maddison is out for two weeks with a shoulder injury suffered against Brentford. De Zerbi has a decision to make on Sávio. Victory is non-negotiable.

Sports.title: Victor Torp seals Coventry’s Carabao Cup win at Plymouth in six-goal thriller
Sports.content:
A midweek jaunt to Devon always had the makings of a tricky trip for a Coventry team focused on Premier League survival. Such feelings quickly evaporated when Frank Lampard’s side raced into a two-goal lead with just four minutes and six seconds on the clock, Taiwo Awoniyi opening his account for his new club before Jack Rudoni doubled Coventry’s advantage. But, ultimately, Coventry were made to toil before chalking up a welcome first victory of the season.

Plymouth have form for a cup upset and another was brewing when Xavier Amaechi pulled Tom Cleverley’s side level nine minutes into the second half. Coventry, to their credit, roused once more, the substitute Ephron Mason-Clark regaining the lead before Victor Torp sealed progress to the Carabao Cup third round from the penalty spot. “You’ve got to enjoy a win, always,” Lampard said. “A win is a big deal because it’s a nice feeling to take back on the bus for four hours.”

The 2,244 Coventry supporters, many of whom made the 444-mile round trip, cycled through the catalogue of songs after crisp finishes by Awoniyi and Rudoni. Then Lampard obliged when they craved a wave from a manager who led them back to the top flight after 25 years away. But the game did not turn into the non-event most would have envisaged. “It’s very easy to go: ‘Why don’t you just go 2-0 up and then beat Plymouth 5-0, 6-0?’” Lampard said. “I’ve played in these games many times with different teams and they can become awkward, especially when the flow of the game goes against you: the crowd turns, emotions catch up and all of a sudden the game feels very different. I thought we dealt OK with that, in the end.”

Plymouth were suddenly liberated at 2-0 down. The Danish centre-back Mathias Ross sent a header wide from a free-kick and a couple of minutes later Oliver Irow read Harvey White’s flighted pass and the Tottenham loanee, 24 hours after signing, drove inside Joel Latibeaudiere and drilled past the Coventry goalkeeper Dan Bentley, another debutant. From there, aside from Awoniyi heading wide unmarked, Coventry had to withstand Plymouth pressure. After fumbling White’s shot from distance, Bentley diverted Will Evans’s rebound on to his left post.

Cleverley knew the value of recording an upset, Lampard the damage of defeat. It must have crossed his mind when Amaechi levelled on 54 minutes. Amaechi swarmed Liam Kitching and pinched the ball after the Coventry defender got in a tangle and fired in. Plymouth introduced the homegrown academy graduates Tegan Finn and Caleb Roberts, joining the 17-year-old full-back Joe Mwaro, this his full debut, on the pitch. “I couldn’t be happier with the reaction and the quality we showed to make sure it was still a competitive game,” Cleverley said.

View image in fullscreen Jack Rudoni doubles Coventry’s lead from close range in the fifth minute. Photograph: Dan Mullan/Getty Images

Mason-Clark arrived for his first appearance of the season after a hamstring issue and added the fifth goal of an entertaining game. It was a galling goal from a Plymouth perspective. Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s cross from the right caused problems, Mason-Clark at first failing to divert the ball goalwards. But Torp was alert to the ball dropping at the back post and squared to provide Mason-Clark the simplest of finishes, the forward poking in from inside the six-yard box.

Lampard made a triple sub, Sidiki Cherif replacing Awoniyi for his debut, while Josh Eccles and Brandon Thomas-Asante also entered. Joe Edwards, the Plymouth midfielder, arrived from the bench but his first notable action was to inadvertently swipe at Thomas-Asante in the box when trying to clear the leftovers of a Coventry corner, giving the referee, Elliott Swallow, no choice but to award a penalty. Torp capped the scoring, thrashing the spot-kick into the top corner.

For Cleverley, this also represented a touchline duel with a friend and a former England teammate and he had spoken on the eve of the game of wanting English coaches like Lampard and Michael Carrick, another former teammate, to succeed. “If you do well in it, you’re great for a moment, if you don’t do so well, then you’re not,” Lampard said after. “If you have the English tag, I do think we’ve got a bit of a bracket of saying: ‘There’s another one [struggling].’ Hopefully we’re not idiots and we can show that over a period of time and do our jobs well.”

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 5: Charlton Athletic
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 14th (NB: this is not necessarily Sophie Downey’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 3rd (WSL2)

Prospects

Just under 20 years since Charlton’s successful women’s team were disbanded after the men’s team’s relegation from the Premier League, they are finally back in the limelight and ready to make a name for themselves again.

Karen Hills’s side impressed for much of last season, going on a 27-game unbeaten streak and possessing the meanest defence in WSL 2. A mid-season blip harmed their race for the title, however, and they lost out to Birmingham City on the final day of the season, ultimately going through a playoff to achieve their goal of promotion. Beating Leicester in that game will have given Hills and her players confidence that they can compete. There will be no complacency, however, having seen how newly promoted sides have fared in recent history.

Six players have departed since last season, including the influential Katie Bradley But they have been replaced with a blend of knowhow and exciting young talent. The arrival of Ashleigh Neville and Emily van Egmond will bring experience to Hills’s dressing room. Leah Davidson’s and Grace Johnston’s arrivals from Australia are intriguing moves. Meanwhile, Sophie Whitehouse was the hero of the previous campaign and Charlton will be looking to the goalkeeper to again lead from the back. It is the attacking side of the game that perhaps causes the most concern. Charlton managed only 31 goals last season, the lowest of the WSL2’s top six.

Preparations got under way with a pre-season trip to Cádiz, a chance for a new-look side to come together. There is no doubt that the task to stay up is a challenging one, but a club that have defied the odds on more than one occasion will believe they can do it again.

Off-field picture

A record-breaking partnership has seen haircare brand Sofnfree become the women’s team’s official sleeve partner. The branding will feature on all playing and replica shirts this season, while content creation will be a focus as Charlton hope to access new and existing audiences. The club have also launched their first women’s-centric TikTok channel. The news, however, that ownership group Global Football Partners have put the club up for sale could cause a bit of instability in the short term.

The manager

Reaching the Women’s Super League was part of the five-year plan Hills had when she was appointed in 2021, bringing a club close to her heart back into the limelight. The 51-year-old represented Chartlon for six years as a player, winning the FA Cup in 2005. This is the second time in Hills’s coaching career she has guided a team to the top flight, having previously done so with Tottenham in 2019, and watching Charlton walk out at the Valley against Liverpool on 6 September will inevitably be an emotional moment for her.

View image in fullscreen Karen Hills has guided a club into the top flight for the second time after have done so with Spurs in 2019. Photograph: Tiego Grenho/Alamy

Star signing

Only three months ago, Neville was lining up against Charlton in the promotion playoff. Now she is a fully fledged Addick, joining from Leicester on a two-year deal. The full-back brings with her a wealth of experience having made more than a century of appearances in the WSL. The majority of those were under Hills at Tottenham after arriving there from Coventry United. A tough-tackling, intuitive defender, Neville never shirks a challenge and has the ability to push forward. She will also be a strong leader in the dressing room.

Stat attack

Despite finishing third in WSL2, Charlton kept the joint-most clean sheets and conceded the fewest goals in the division. No club saved as high a percentage of their shots on target faced, with Whitehouse playing every minute. She saved four penalties in the playoff shootout, too.

Set for a breakthrough

Johnston was named Charlton’s first signing of the summer during a transfer window that has seen many A-League players depart for Europe. The versatile young full-back arrives at the Valley hoping to make her mark on English football after three seasons with Perth Glory. She impressed during her time with her home town club, played every minute of last season, winning the club’s 2026 best young player award. Johnston’s form led to her being called up to the Young Matildas in 2023, representing the under-20s and now the under-23s. She was an integral member of the squad that won the Asean Women’s Championship last year.

What they say …

“I know what Karen’s about and vice versa; she knows what I bring. I’m really looking forward to working with her again” – Ashleigh Neville

Where are they playing their home games?

Charlton will play their home games at the Valley for a third consecutive season. Season-ticket sales started almost immediately after their successful promotion push. Alcohol will also still be allowed in the stadium, with an alcohol-free section established. Other fan activations include giving supporters the opportunity to sponsor a player.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes and Khadija Shaw land PFA Player of the Year awards
Sports.content:
Manchester United’s captain Bruno Fernandes has been crowned Professional Footballers’ Association Player of the Year as Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw won the women’s award for the second time.

Playmaker Fernandes broke the record for Premier League assists during an outstanding 2025-26 campaign, setting up 21 goals as he surpassed Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne.

The 31-year-old also scored nine times as United overcome a shaky first half of the campaign to finish third in the Premier League under Michael Carrick to earn a Champions League return.

Fernandes was pleased to have been voted the winner by his fellow professionals. He said: “It is obviously a very proud moment. They are the ones you go on the pitch against and it’s probably not easy to vote for someone you play against, so it is a very good moment.”

The Portugal international is the club’s first winner since Wayne Rooney took home the trophy in 2009-10, and adds to his Football Writers’ Association Footballer of the Year award from May.

Shaw, who was also recognised by the FWA, scooped the PFA Women’s Player of the Year award for the second time. The 29-year-old claimed the trophy in 2023-24 and won it again having scored 21 goals on the way to a third consecutive Golden Boot and her maiden Women’s Super League title.

Arsenal’s Olivia Smith picked up the women’s PFA Young Player of the Year title for the second campaign running, having won the 2025 crown for her exploits at Liverpool before continuing her form in the capital.

Manchester City’s Nico O’Reilly was named men’s PFA Young Player of the Year following an outstanding campaign that ended with the versatile talent helping England to win World Cup bronze. The 21-year-old was part of the PFA Premier League Team of the Year along with City teammates Erling Haaland, Rayan Cherki and Antoine Semenyo.

O’Reilly said: “I had a great season. I’m very proud of the season I had. I won two trophies with my club and managed to play at the World Cup with my country. I’m over the moon how it turned out.”

Champions Arsenal had five representatives in David Raya, Gabriel, William Saliba, Jurriën Timber and Declan Rice, with Player of the Year Fernandes of United and Brentford’s Igor Thiago completing the team.

The PFA WSL Team of the Year featured three players from triumphant City, with Shaw joined by teammates Kerstin Casparij and Yui Hasegawa.

Mariona Caldentey, last year’s PFA Women’s Player of the Year, was joined in the XI by fellow Arsenal players Emily Fox and Alessia Russo. Tottenham defender Toko Koga and Manchester United’s Jess Park were also included in the team, as were the Chelsea trio of Hannah Hampton, Ellie Carpenter and Lauren James.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Hayden Hackney, now of Everton, was named Championship PFA Players’ Player of the Year for his performances for defeated play-off finalists Middlesbrough.

Dom Ballard, who scored a jaw-dropping effort for new club Bristol City at the weekend, collected the League One award for a goal-laden season at Leyton Orient.

Swindon striker Aaron Drinan’s performances saw him collect the League Two award, while Lily Crosthwaite of Birmingham took the WSL2 player accolade.

Sir Kenny Dalglish and Karen Carney received the PFA merit awards in recognition of their contribution to football. Dalglish enjoyed a success-laden career as a player with Celtic and Liverpool, and is Scotland’s most capped performer having represented his country on 102 occasions. The 75-year-old, who confirmed in June he was undergoing treatment for cancer, went on to enjoy a successful managerial career, leading Liverpool to three league titles before masterminding Blackburn’s Premier League triumph.

Carney played 144 times for England, including being part of the Lionesses squad which finished third at the 2015 World Cup. Having come through the ranks at Birmingham, Carney won the quadruple with Arsenal in 2007 as well as a league and FA Cup double with Chelsea in 2018.

Sports.title: Delap heads to Forest for £50m as Chelsea open talks to sell Jackson to Aston Villa
Sports.content:
Nottingham Forest have agreed a deal worth £50m to sign Liam Delap from Chelsea, who have also opened talks over selling Nicolas Jackson to Aston Villa.

Xabi Alonso has made João Pedro and Danny Welbeck his main strikers this season, leaving his other frontmen to seek opportunities elsewhere.

Forest were one of several clubs interested in Delap, who has struggled since joining Chelsea from Ipswich for £30m last summer, and will pay a club record of £45m plus £5m in add-ons for the 23-year-old.

Delap managed only one league goal last season and was hindered by injuries after leaving Ipswich. But the former Manchester City striker was a key target for Forest’s manager, Oliver Glasner, and has a chance to revive his career at the City Ground.

Chelsea are focused on outgoings before the transfer window shuts next Tuesday and are also hoping to sell Jackson, who was on loan at Bayern Munich last season. The Senegal international is valued at £65m and has been earmarked by Villa as a potential replacement for Ollie Watkins, who is expected to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.

Chelsea are not willing to agree to another loan for Jackson and want his valuation met but Villa are likely to press for a favourable payment schedule to ensure they can afford a permanent deal. Atlético Madrid are also interested in the 25-year-old, who joined Chelsea from Villarreal in 2023. Unai Emery, Villa’s manager, worked with Jackson at Villarreal.

West Ham’s clear out after relegation from the Premier League is expected to continue with El Hadji Malick Diouf joining Brentford for about £35m. The clubs are in discussions over a deal for the left-back and an agreement is likely soon.

Diouf wants to leave and was left out of the squad when Nuno Espírito Santo’s side continued their disappointing start to the Championship season by losing 2-1 at home against Charlton last Saturday.

West Ham signed the Senegal international for £19m from Slavia Prague last year. Brentford have made four signings and are plan to strengthen further.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Nuno, who is understood to be under growing pressure after West Ham’s flat start, has had his hand weakened by a host of players hoping to force their way out. The Mexico midfielder Edson Álvarez has not been involved in the first two league games and is the subject of interest from Olympiakos and Real Sociedad.

Torino have had a bid rejected for the midfielder Soungoutou Magassa, who is on Crystal Palace’s shortlist. Marseille could sign the French centre-back Jean-Clair Todibo. West Ham have raised funds through the sales of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville and Freddie Potts, and have loaned Aaron Wan-Bissaka to Aston Villa and Niclas Füllkrug to Werder Bremen.

Sports.title: Xavi hopes time at the ‘university of football’ will end with Dutch success
Sports.content:
“My feeling today is that I’m going to the university of football.” Those were Xavi Hernández’s opening words at his presentation as the Netherlands coach on Tuesday. “I learned a lot from this university of football during my career as a player and as a coach. I have many connections with this country.”

Those connections date back to when Xavi was drafted as a youngster into La Masia, the famed Barcelona academy whose fundamentals are rooted in Dutch total football, inspired by Rinus Michels and Johan Cruyff. Xavi’s first-team debut came under Louis van Gaal, and he spent many years under Frank Rijkaard before becoming one of the main pillars of the dream team under Pep Guardiola, who was hugely inspired by Cruyff.

Xavi opened a Cruyff court – a multifunctional sport space for children – with Cruyff in his home town of Terrassa in 2014, and on Tuesday shared special memories of his time with Cruyff, who died in 2016. “With Johan in the last period of his life I had some meetings,” he said. “And he was always positive. Even when he was sick, he was positive. This is what I learned: always smiling. This is what I want to show here to the players. My first goal is to help them, and then enjoy the process. And we will be in a process to win.”

Xavi says he wants to “dominate the game, to take the initiative with the ball and at the same time our goal is to show everybody a team with passion, with desire and ambition. And this is very important for me as a coach.”

In the Netherlands, there has always been a strong emphasis on attacking football, which is why Xavi fitted the bill. The Catalan was asked whether he would use five defenders, as Van Gaal and Ronald Koeman did at times in recent years. “That this is not my idea,” he said. “We want to play in another system [like] 4-3-3, 4-2-3-1, 3-4-3. In those systems we can dominate the game more.”

Xavi said he had spoken to Frenkie de Jong – whom he coached at Barcelona – and Virgil van Dijk. He added that he would speak again to Van Dijk, the captain, in the near future to hear his ambitions with the team.

The 46-year-old was also clear he is willing to select players from the Saudi Pro League, something more relevant after Tijjani Reijnders moved from Manchester City to Al-Qadsiah last week. Two years ago, Koeman was clear when Steven Bergwijn moved to Al-Ittihad that the forward would no longer be selected because the league did not match the level he expected from his players.

View image in fullscreen Xavi Hernández said he wants to play attacking systems with the Netherlands to ‘dominate the game more’. Photograph: Stefan Koops/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

“It’s a good league as well,” Xavi said. “Maybe we choose some players from Saudi, from Eredivisie, Premier League, La Liga. I don’t care about the leagues, I care about the performances and the players.”

Nigel de Jong, the director of elite football at the Dutch football federation (KNVB), had earlier been open about the process that led to Xavi’s appointment. He said he had first tested the waters with Guardiola, who indicated he did not want to take a job in the near future, before holding two meetings with Arne Slot, who eventually chose to remain a club coach.

De Jong then invited Xavi to Amsterdam for a meeting also attended by Clarence Seedorf, a member of the KNVB’s supervisory board. The following day De Jong and Seedorf spoke at length with Michael Reiziger, the Netherlands’ under-21s coach, who played alongside Xavi at Barcelona for several years.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They were considering promoting Reiziger in a way similar to Luis de la Fuente’s journey with Spain, his knowledge of the country’s upcoming talents regarded as a major plus. When the meeting with Reiziger became known in the Dutch media, there was an assumption the former full-back would become the national team coach. But then, on 12 August, the KNVB announced Xavi, a decision that seemingly came out of the blue.

Xavi said drily that he was fine with the process. “Well, it’s not a bad position, after Guardiola and after Slot, no? At least you are at the podium. I don’t care if I’m the third [choice] or I’m the 10th. It’s a big honour to be here. He [De Jong] explained to me, very honestly: ‘We need your philosophy, we need to change with ambition, with passion.’ And we will work in this way.”

First up for Xavi is a Nations League game against Germany in Amsterdam on 24 September, when he will face Jürgen Klopp, who is also starting a new job. “I feel excited, I feel motivated,” Xavi said, “because we are playing against Germany, one of the best teams in Europe, one of the best coaches in recent years.”

Xavi, speaking in front of his staff, including Ruud van Nistelrooy, wants his team to adopt the Dutch style he saw as a young boy. “I remember when I was a kid, watching the Netherlands and watching good football,” he said, “and this is my way, this is my target.”
