A patrol car located the bus in southern Morón. An officer from the fourth precinct of Gervasio Pavón went to a stop a few metres from the station, raised his arm as though he were a passenger and, when the vehicle stopped, boarded, identified himself and told the driver he was under arrest.

The case is being handled by Prosecutor's Office No. 2 in Morón, headed by Fernando Capello, which ordered a psychiatric evaluation of the detainee to determine whether he is fit to face charges. On being detained, the man said: “I wanted to fulfil my dream of being a bus driver.” According to the newspaper Perfil, officers seized a knife from him. No injuries have been reported.

The bus sustained bodywork damage as a result of the collision and was handed to the company for repairs before returning to service. The detainee has not been publicly identified and has not been convicted.

Urban bus lines, known locally as colectivos, are the main form of transport in greater Buenos Aires, a metropolitan area of around ten million people surrounding the Argentine capital. The route the man covered extended for more than eleven kilometres, according to some local reports.

World.title: Colombia orders deportation of irregular migrants after a decade as the main host country
World.content:
Colombia orders deportation of irregular migrants after a decade as the main host country

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:37 UTC Full article

“The order to Migration is clear: first those committing crimes, second those who have not regularised their status, who in due course will have to be deported,” he said

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has ordered coordinated operations between the migration authority and the police to begin this week to identify and deport foreigners without regular migration status, marking a shift from the policy the country has maintained for more than a decade as the main destination for Venezuelan migration.

“The order to Migration is clear: first those committing crimes, second those who have not regularised their status, who in due course will have to be deported,” he said during a security council meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the alternate seat of his government. The remarks became known through a leaked video of that meeting. “I will not accept illegal migration. First Colombians, second Colombians and third Colombians,” he added.

Figures on the scope of the measure differ. The Venezuela Observatory at Universidad del Rosario puts the number of Venezuelans without regular status at 848,000, of whom 193,000 would be minors. Migración Colombia data as of January 2026, cited by the outlet La Silla Vacía, indicate that around 82% of Venezuelan migrants hold regular status and close to 500,000 do not. The United Nations refugee agency estimated three million Venezuelans living in Colombia in 2025.

The announcement calls into question the Temporary Protection Statute for Venezuelan Migrants, created by decree in March 2021, which provides a free temporary protection permit and made the country an international reference point on migration regularisation. Colombia took in almost a third of the 7.8 million people who have left Venezuela since 2015, under governments of differing political persuasions.

“A person in irregular status is not a criminal,” said Ronal Rodríguez, a researcher at the observatory, warning against linking irregularity with crime. Congresswoman María Fernanda Carrascal, of the Pacto Histórico, called the measure “an affront to human rights” and said it lacked evidence. Academic Andrés Sampayo estimated the Venezuelan population's contribution to the Colombian economy at around 3 billion dollars a year in consumption, taxes and entrepreneurship.

Implementation faces practical obstacles. Colombia shares a 2,219-kilometre land border with Venezuela, and any mass deportation would require cooperation from the government of acting president Delcy Rodríguez, in a country undergoing a US-backed negotiated transition.

At the same security council meeting, De la Espriella ordered the activation of a rewards system, the strengthening of the informants network and prison transfers to prevent jails from operating as bases for extortion.

World.title: Milei links Lula to the case of the Argentine former adviser detained in Bolivia
World.content:
Milei links Lula to the case of the Argentine former adviser detained in Bolivia

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:26 UTC Full article

The remarks come during the worst diplomatic crisis between the two countries since the return to democracy

Argentine President Javier Milei has attributed the criminal case against his former adviser Fernando Cerimedo, detained in Bolivia over an attempted femicide, to a regional plot in which he included Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, former Bolivian president Evo Morales and Argentine lawmaker Marcela Pagano. He offered no evidence to support the claim.

“Let's not rule out that behind this is the whole rabble,” he said on Saturday in an interview with Radio Mitre, before listing those names and referring to “castrochavismo,” a term used in the region to describe governments seen as aligned with Cuba and Venezuela. He said it was “a band of castrochavista criminals operating in the region.” In previous days he had accused Lula of running an “anti-Argentine campaign” and of “interfering in electoral processes across the region.”

The remarks come during the worst diplomatic crisis between the two countries since the return to democracy. Brasília recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations on July 26 and on August 4 downgraded relations to chargé d'affaires level, after Milei took part in a campaign event for Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro at which he referred to Lula in terms the Brazilian government deemed offensive.

In the same interview, Milei distanced himself from Cerimedo. “He is someone who is not part of our movement, who has no link of any kind with us, and with whom we stopped having contact in 2023,” he said. Casa Rosada visitor records examined by the newspaper La Nación show at least thirteen entries by the consultant to the seat of government between December 2023 and June 5, 2024. The logs record who enters and who authorises access, but do not establish meetings with the president. Then interior minister Lisandro Catalán appears as the official who most often approved the visits.

Cerimedo co-founded the digital outlet La Derecha Diario, took part in the communications strategy of Milei's 2023 campaign and advised the campaign of Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz. A judge in Santa Cruz de la Sierra on Friday ordered 180 days of pre-trial detention on a charge of attempted femicide. He denies the accusations and has not been convicted. His business partner in the outlet, Spaniard Javier Negre, told the newspaper Clarín that Cerimedo had agreed to give up his stake before the arrest.

Last week Milei reposted messages on social media questioning the severity of the injuries suffered by Nadia Beller, Cerimedo's former partner. The medical report from the clinic where she was treated records an open, comminuted fracture of the right humerus with metal fragments, requiring emergency surgery.

World.title: Some 25,000 people are seeking housing in Cali two weeks after Colombia's earthquake
World.content:
Some 25,000 people are seeking housing in Cali two weeks after Colombia's earthquake

24th Monday, August 2026 - 21:08 UTC Full article

Among those seeking accommodation, the prevailing perception is of a generalised rise in prices

The municipal survey in Cali, Colombia's third city with more than two million inhabitants, now covers 10,000 families affected by the magnitude 7.4 earthquake of August 10 and estimates around 25,000 people have been left without adequate housing. Many have spent recent days in shelters or with relatives while searching for a rental, in a market strained by the sudden loss of supply.

The city government has carried out detailed assessments of 920 buildings, of which 56 collapsed. Technical analyses place the greatest concentration of damage in commune 19, where close to 200 properties may end up being demolished.

Among those seeking accommodation, the prevailing perception is of a generalised rise in prices. “Rents have gone up in every neighbourhood,” says Laura del Mar Villada, 29, who left her flat in the El Limonar district on the day of the quake and has not yet been able to retrieve her belongings. Manuel Alejandro Molina, 40, who lived with his wife and three-month-old son in the south of the city, says properties that previously cost 2.8 million pesos a month are now being advertised at up to 3.8 million.

Available data, however, point to a localised effect. Economist Sebastián Súlez, a former finance secretary of Jamundí, compiled listings from sixteen portals and estate agencies across 63 neighbourhoods up to August 19 and compared them with a partial snapshot from August 9, the day before the earthquake. Of the eleven comparable neighbourhoods, six recorded falls, one held steady and four rose. In Bellavista, in the affluent western area, the median went from 4.1 to 4.8 million pesos, a rise of 17.1%; in Ciudad Meléndez, in the harder-hit south, prices fell 6.3%. These are asking prices set by landlords, not amounts finally agreed.

Property adviser Harold Andrés Millán observes that owners managing their own properties are asking between 25% and 30% more, while rents on company-managed stock have not changed. Along the corridor where buildings collapsed, he adds, supply and demand have fallen alike.

Mayor Alejandro Eder said days after the earthquake that rents in some areas had doubled and asked the national government for a temporary rent freeze. He also acknowledged a gap in support programmes aimed at middle-income households.

The Colombian Federation of Real Estate Boards clarified that the earthquake does not automatically terminate leases or exempt tenants from payment, though the Civil Code allows termination to be sought if a property becomes uninhabitable. According to the national statistics institute, four in ten Colombian households were renting in 2025, the highest share since at least 2019.

World.title: México Canta and Spotify partner up to amplify young talent across Mexico-US border
World.content:
México Canta is turning up the volume for its second season, tapping the music streaming service Spotify to give the cross-border contest’s top singers even more exposure.

The partnership will give the 14 semifinalists from Mexico and the United States an official Spotify playlist and offer them a career-development master class, and the three winners will be invited to a Spotify flagship event for emerging artists, the Mexican government said in a press release.

México Canta (Mexico Sings) is a federal initiative led by the Culture Ministry in collaboration with the Mexican Music Council.

Open to Mexican and Mexican American artists ages 18 to 29, it is akin to “American Idol” with one overriding rule: It seeks songs promoting themes such as love, tradition and culture rather than glorifying violence, drugs, discrimination or misogyny.

Unlike last year’s inaugural contest — which staged semifinals in Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, Tijuana, Oaxaca and Mexico City that blossomed into must-see TV — this year’s whittling-down process was left in the hands of the Mexican Music Council. It reviewed online auditions to determine the best of more than 16,000 entries (about 1,200 more than last year).

Of the 5,760 U.S.-based registrants, seven were chosen for the first semifinal, which was Sunday at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles. It produced three finalists.

The second semifinal is scheduled for Sunday at the Ángela Peralta Theater in Mazatlán, where three more finalists will be selected, plus a wild-card from either semifinal. The contest drew 10,528 registrants from Mexico.

The finals are set for Sept. 13 at the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City, where winners will be selected in three as-yet-unnamed categories. Last year’s titles were for best performer and best song, alongside a wild-card pick.

The agreement with Spotify comes during a boom in regional Mexican music.

Global listening to the genre on Spotify has risen 450% over the last five years, while consumption in Mexico increased 560%, the Ministry of Culture noted. Moreover, more than 70% of Spotify Mexico’s daily Top 50 is made up of Mexican artists compared to 10% a decade ago, the ministry added.

Also, for the first time, Mexico has entered the world’s 10 largest recorded-music markets, noted Spotify representative Karen Duque.

“A decade ago, it was quite difficult to imagine that Mexico would become one of the most important powers in the world of the music industry,” she said.

Following the finals in Mexico City, the three winners will be scheduled to perform during Mexican Independence Day celebrations on Sept. 15.

With reports from La Jornada and Informador

World.title: Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant coming to Jalisco
World.content:
The western state of Jalisco will soon boast Mexico’s very first solar panel recycling plant, an installation with the capacity to recover up to 95% of the materials from equipment that reaches the end of its useful life.

The project evolved in response to the growth of photovoltaic generation in Jalisco, which has approximately 1.6 million installed solar panels, equivalent to about 50,000 tonnes of equipment.

Rafiqui — a non-profit civil organization dedicated to recycling and repurposing — is building the plant in Ciudad Guzmán, about 125 kilometers south of the state capital, Guadalajara.

In its initial phase, the recycling plant is expected to process up to 1,000 tonnes of “retired” solar panels annually, recovering core materials like silicon, aluminum and silver to be used in other production chains.

Rafiqui director Ximena Cantú said her company’s model “goes beyond recycling because we believe in the circular economy.”

Before sending any materials to the recycling plant, the decommissioned equipment will be evaluated to determine if it is still functional. Those that remain in suitable condition may be reused or donated to communities and non-profit organizations.

Manuel Gómez-Herrera Lasso, executive director of the Mexican Photovoltaic Industry Association, praised Jalisco as a pioneer in the adoption of solar energy. The first photovoltaic system interconnected to the national energy grid was installed in Jalisco in 2007.

The growth of the technology, however, presents a challenge for managing the waste generated by the replaced equipment.

The International Renewable Energy Agency estimates that 30,000 tonnes of solar panels in Mexico will be retired due to premature failure by 2030, while at the same time 6,500 tonnes will reach the end of their life cycle naturally.

As part of the strategy to address this, Rafiqui has established a collection center in a southern Guadalajara neighborhood to receive small volumes. It has also developed a collection scheme for larger quantities in different regions of the country.

Additionally, Rafiqui is holding discussions with municipalities and industrial associations to expand the alternatives for collecting solar panels in Jalisco.

With reports from Mexico Industry, Jalisco TV and El Financiero

World.title: Schneider Electric plans major Querétaro expansion to meet growing power demand
World.content:
Schneider Electric, a France-based multinational, plans to expand its manufacturing capacity in Querétaro state with 115,000 square meters of new industrial facilities that will support the creation of 4,000 direct jobs by the end of 2027, the company has announced.

The expansion includes two completed facilities and a third planned for a later growth phase, where the firm will manufacture solutions for electrical distribution, equipment for critical energy infrastructure, and specialized projects under custom “engineer-to-order” (ETO) models.

Schneider Senior Vice President of Power Systems and ETO Guillaume Le Gouic said that Querétaro, in Mexico’s Bajío region, provides the talent, industrial capacity, and strategic location required to advance the region’s electrification and digitalization processes.

“We are very pleased to continue growing in Querétaro, and very grateful for the support of the state government,” Schneider Mexico and Central America President Luis D’Acosta Anezin said. “The truth is, we feel right at home here, and this is the first of many investments to come, and we’re very happy and excited.”

According to the announcement, Schneider is now hiring between 200 and 250 workers a month and training engineers, technicians, and specialists in advanced manufacturing and energy infrastructure to support its operations.

Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri González met with Schneider Electric executives last Wednesday to discuss the project. While the company did not share an investment figure, Kuri González said he expects the total job creation from new facilities to reach 7,000 or 8,000 by 2028.

Schneider currently has production plants in Querétaro, Nuevo León, and Tlaxcala, supporting industrial demand in North America and Central America.

The firm aims to strengthen production for sectors with a higher demand for electrical infrastructure, such as data centers, industry and the digital economy.

In a 2025 interview with MND, the president and managing director of Schneider Electric Mexico & Central America, Jesús Carmona Colina, said that President Claudia Sheinbaum had “correctly recognized that more energy is needed in Mexico” to meet demand, including from the country’s growing industrial sector.

He noted an energy imbalance in Mexico, with sufficient electricity in some regions and a shortfall in others.

As part of its overarching economic strategy, Plan México, the government aims to increase electricity generation by 22,000 megawatts by 2030, investing US $12.3 billion over the next six years to build new power plants, $7.5 billion to strengthen transmission networks and $3.6 billion to improve distribution networks.

With reports from Mexico Industry, Mexico Now and TYT

World.title: Despite a Q2 dip, first-semester Foreign Direct Investment was Mexico’s highest ever
World.content:
Mexico attracted US $34.968 billion in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) between January and June 2026, marking the highest amount ever recorded for a first semester, the Economy Ministry (SE) reported.

The figure represents a 2.1% year-on-year increase compared to the same period last year and confirms Mexico’s continued appeal as a destination for established international companies.

Going back further, foreign investment practically doubled, with an accumulated growth of 89.7%, compared to the first half of 2021, when Mexico attracted US$18.433 billion,

The 2026 advance lost momentum, however, during the second quarter, when revenues reached $10.464 billion, 3.5% less than the $10.848 billion originally recorded during the same period in 2025.

The SE attributed the contraction to last year’s high base of comparison and indicated that it does not represent a change in trend. Despite the year-on-year decline, the result for the second quarter of 2026 was the second highest in the last 16 years.

Who received the foreign investment?

The manufacturing industry was the primary recipient of the arriving resources, receiving $13.482 billion, equivalent to 38.6% of total FDI. The figure represents a 9.3% year-over-year increase for manufacturing.

Financial and insurance services ranked second, with $10.15 billion, followed by the transportation, postal, and warehousing sectors, which registered the strongest growth, attracting $2.65 billion.

Mexico City came in as the top destination for foreign investment, receiving $16.862 billion, or 48.2% of the national total. It was followed by Nuevo León, with $3.712 billion; México state, with $2.114 billion; Baja California, with $1.743 billion; and Jalisco, with $1.406 billion.

Together, these five states accounted for 73.9% of all FDI received during the first half of the year.

Where did the first semester FDI come from?

In the first half of 2026, the United States remained the leading source of FDI in Mexico, with a flow of $16.871 billion, equivalent to 48.2% of the total.

Spain ranked second with $4.954 billion, followed by Canada ($1.741 billion), Australia ($1.698 billion) and Germany ($1.647 billion).

According to the SE, the positive FDI numbers are attributed to the country’s macroeconomic and institutional fundamentals and the guidelines of Plan México, the government’s flagship economic and policy strategy.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local: Is the tourism outlook in Los Cabos improving?
World.content:
Spring was a poor season for tourism in Mexico. International air arrivals — the driver of 80% of all tourism revenue in the country, with two out of every three passengers hailing from the U.S. — were down nationwide in March, April and May.

That trend continued in June, as spring turned to summer, despite Mexico’s role as a host for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But outside of the host cities, which received a boost from the event — albeit not to the extent expected — high-value tourism to traditional beach tourism destinations in Mexico like Los Cabos continued to plummet. International air arrivals fell 7.1% in Los Cabos in March, 9.7% in April, 10.5% in May and 14.2% in June, relative to the same months in 2025.

July was even worse, with international air arrivals falling by 16.6%. That means that in the first seven months of the year, international tourism fell by 7.2% in Los Cabos, with overall tourism declining by 5.4%. Unfortunately, things don’t look much better for the second half of the year, with U.S. air bookings for the next six months down 13% from 2025.

That said, there are some signs of a brightening outlook for Los Cabos.

Domestic tourism is beginning to improve

After seeing falling numbers for 10 straight months — from July 2025 to April 2026 — the domestic travel market has recently shown signs of life in Los Cabos. Domestic arrivals nosed into positive numbers in May and were up 7% in July, with nearly 20,000 more Mexican nationals visiting the destination relative to the same month in 2025.

Low season rates are part of the appeal. High season prices typically peak in April (US $470 per night for hotels in 2026), with summer seeing lower average hotel room rates in Cabo San Lucas (US $336 as of the most recent numbers from May) and San José del Cabo (US $339), as well as for the destination as a whole (US $414).

But since airline bookings for the next six months are up 5.4% domestically, with a better than 9% increase in passengers from Mexico City expected through the end of the year, it appears that this isn’t just a seasonal spike, but rather a welcome return to form for what has traditionally been an important market, accounting for over one-third of overall tourists to Los Cabos.

Tourism from Canada is on the uptick

The Canadian tourism market is not as robust as the U.S., at least not in Los Cabos. Last year, for example, over two million tourists from the U.S. visited Los Cabos, versus 215,000 from Canada. So even though tourism from Canada is up 8.8% in 2026, that doesn’t make up for U.S. tourism being down by more than 7%.

Still, it’s significant that numbers are up this year for visitors from Canada, as well as for visitors from Europe, the Caribbean, and Central and South America. This diversification is important to the local economy, especially if U.S. tourism to Mexico continues to slump.

Cruise tourism continues to boom

The reason international arrivals are considered “high-value” is because these tourists, on average, spend more than US $1,300 each. Cruise ship tourists, by contrast, traditionally spend less than US $100 per person. Every little bit helps, however, especially when it comes to keeping businesses alive in downtown Cabo San Lucas.

Last year, the Land’s End city set a record, surpassing one million cruise ship tourists for the first time. This year, that record will almost certainly be broken, as through June, cruise ship arrivals were up by 64.5% through June; 789,919 through the first six months of 2026, compared to 480,198 during the same timeframe in 2025.

If this pace continues, Cabo San Lucas will top 1.5 million cruise ship passengers for the year, cementing its position as the nation’s fourth largest cruise ship destination, behind only Cozumel, Mahahual and Ensenada.

New air routes added to replace those that have been lost

Airline capacity cuts due to rising jet fuel costs, combined with a declining demand for seats to Mexican beach destinations, have led to the cancelation of several Los Cabos-bound routes this year, including the loss of Southwest flights from Baltimore, Chicago and Indianapolis, and a Delta flight from Seattle.

Fortunately, though, new flights have been added this summer to make up for, or at least mitigate, previous tourist losses. Southwest added its first nonstop flight from Las Vegas to Los Cabos during the first week of June, the same week a new domestic route was added by Volaris connecting Puebla to Los Cabos.

Once high season returns this fall, expanded service to Los Cabos will also be offered by several airlines, including Volaris in Mexico; American, Southwest and United in the U.S.; and Air Transat, Porter and WestJet in Canada.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Former Sinaloa state official arrested in Utah with more than 100,000 fentanyl pills
World.content:
A former Sinaloa state official was arrested this month in a Utah hotel room with more than 100,000 fentanyl pills in his possession, U.S. authorities said.

Ricardo Verduzco Bernal, former head of the high-performance program at the Sinaloa Institute of Physical Culture and Sport, was detained in Salt Lake County on Aug. 12, according to an Aug. 20 statement released by the U.S. Attorney’s Office in the District of Utah. He is currently in preventive detention awaiting trial.

Over 200,000 Fentanyl Pills Taken Off Utah Streets During Two Separate Unrelated Seizures PRESS RELEASE: 🔗https://t.co/J4P7GFf1GC pic.twitter.com/m9luPFOsax — US Attorney Utah (@USAO_UT) August 20, 2026

In its statement, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said that “according to allegations contained in court documents, in August 2026, the FBI Wasatch Metro Drug Task Force initiated a criminal investigation on Bernal and co-conspirators, both known and unknown, associated with a drug trafficking organization believed to be distributing large quantities of fentanyl and other narcotics in the District of Utah.”

The suspect is referred to as Bernal throughout the statement, although his first surname is Verduzco.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office said that in August 2026, FBI agents “conducted a controlled purchase of fentanyl from Bernal.”

“As a result of the controlled purchase, agents obtained and executed a search warrant on a hotel room in Salt Lake County, Utah. On August 12, 2026, agents executed the search warrant, and Bernal was alone inside the room where agents located and seized approximately 11,160.65 grams of field-tested positive fentanyl,” the Attorney’s Office said.

“Agents estimated the fentanyl evidence to be approximately 111,000 fentanyl pills. According to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Bernal is in the United States on a visitor visa.”

At the start of its statement, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said that Bernal and another Mexican national “were indicted by a federal grand jury after they were arrested and charged in two separate and unrelated cases that led to the seizure of approximately 204,000 fentanyl pills in one week.”

“Jesus Alexis Cecena Cota, 22, of Mexico, residing illegally in West Jordan, Utah; and Ricardo Verduzco Bernal, 54, of West Valley City, Utah, were charged in two separate complaints August 13, 2026,” the statement said.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office said that “Bernal is scheduled for a jury trial on August 26, 2026, before a U.S. Magistrate Court Judge at the Orrin G. Hatch United States Courthouse in downtown Salt Lake City.” He is accused of “possession of fentanyl with intent to distribute.”

During a court appearance last Wednesday, the suspect maintained his innocence despite the discovery of the fentanyl in the hotel room where he was arrested.

Verduzco’s civil service career

Verduzco served as head of the high-performance program at the Sinaloa Institute of Physical Culture and Sport, a state government institute, during the governorship of Rubén Rocha Moya, who is also accused of drug trafficking by U.S. prosecutors. He left that position on July 31, according to the newspaper Milenio.

Verduzco previously served as the director of the Municipal Institute of Sport in Guasave, a city in Sinaloa around 150 kilometers northwest of the state capital, Culiacán. He occupied that position between 2022 and 2024. Before taking up that role, Verduzco was a manager with the Guasave water authority.

With reports from Milenio and Reforma

World.title: US issues security alert concerning area of Mexicali
World.content:
U.S. officials have expressed concern that a recent drug bust in the northern border city of Mexicali could result in retaliatory violence by the “Los Rusos” crime gang.

In a tersely worded alert issued on Monday, the U.S. Embassy in Mexico urged U.S. citizens to be aware of the potential threat, adding that all “U.S. government activities in, and travel to, Mexicali have been suspended on August 25.”

The statement encouraged U.S. citizens to be aware of their surroundings at all times, to avoid local government buildings in Mexicali and to “notify friends and family of your safety in the event of an incident.”

The U.S. Consulate in Tijuana — about 180 kilometers (112 miles) east of Mexicali — shared the warning, but did not provide any details about the supposed threat.

On Tuesday morning, President Claudia Sheinbaum said the alert was issued due to the possibility that a criminal group could pose a danger, though she said “there is no specific issue.”

The Baja California state government said it has reinforced security in the entire municipality of Mexicali with the cooperation of federal agents and members of the armed forces.

“Prevention, patrol and surveillance efforts continue on a permanent basis to protect the peace of mind of Mexicali families,” Baja California Governor Marina del Pilar said on social media.

She urged members of the public to call 911 in case of emergency, or to make an anonymous report by calling 089.

State Security Minister General Laureano Carrillo said that “rigorous, continuous and coordinated work” is being carried out by state and federal authorities “to prevent and contain any type of contingency in Mexicali.” Mexico’s federal security cabinet released a statement saying it had not identified evidence confirming “a specific or imminent risk to the public” at midday on Tuesday.

El Gabinete de Seguridad informa: pic.twitter.com/43Qwwxr7O1 — Gabinete de Seguridad de México (@GabSeguridadMX) August 25, 2026

Last week, Mexican authorities — with the help of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) — seized 120 kilograms of fentanyl pills in a joint operation carried out in Mexicali by federal and state agents.

The raid occurred at a property linked to “Los Rusos” — a cell operating as part of the Los Mayos faction of the Sinaloa Cartel — and resulted in the seizure of approximately 4 million opioid doses.

According to reporting by Luis Chaparro, U.S. authorities decided to issue the security alert after the DEA intercepted at least one call in which alleged members of Los Rusos appeared to be planning an attack on the Municipal Police and the offices of the Federal Attorney General’s Office in Mexicali.

With reports from El Financiero, El País and La Jornada

World.title: Sheinbaum puts out more fires in the Morena party: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

⚖️ Rocha’s fate hinges on evidence : Sheinbaum reiterated that no one can be arrested or extradited from Mexico without evidence proving they committed a crime. Her remarks came after Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya requested leave again amid U.S. drug trafficking accusations.

: Sheinbaum reiterated that no one can be arrested or extradited from Mexico without evidence proving they committed a crime. Her remarks came after Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya requested leave again amid U.S. drug trafficking accusations. 🚪 Other accused officials should follow suit : Asked whether Senator Enrique Inzunza — named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha — should also step aside, Sheinbaum said she believes other accused officials still in office should go on leave as investigations continue. However, she stressed that “everyone has to make their own decisions.”

: Asked whether Senator Enrique Inzunza — named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha — should also step aside, Sheinbaum said she believes other accused officials still in office should go on leave as investigations continue. However, she stressed that “everyone has to make their own decisions.” 🤝 New interim governor praised as “honest” : Sheinbaum said she doesn’t know Graciela Domínguez well but called her “an honest woman” who has long fought for social justice. The Morena deputy and former Sinaloa education minister was designated interim governor by the state Congress on Tuesday.

: Sheinbaum said she doesn’t know Graciela Domínguez well but called her “an honest woman” who has long fought for social justice. The Morena deputy and former Sinaloa education minister was designated interim governor by the state Congress on Tuesday. ✈️ Lezama pressed on private jet travel: Responding to a Reforma report alleging Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama took 97 private plane flights while in office, Sheinbaum said it’s up to Lezama to clarify the details. Lezama denied the figures and said she never used public funds for the flights.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The case of Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — who U.S. prosecutors accuse of drug trafficking and weapons offenses — continues to be a hot topic in Mexico.

Rocha went on leave in early May, but returned to the governorship last Friday. However, under pressure from President Claudia Sheinbaum and Morena governors and lawmakers, he requested leave again on Saturday and the Sinaloa Congress approved his request on Sunday.

Another return to the governorship of Sinaloa appears highly unlikely for Rocha, a 77-year-old Morena politician who has essentially been disowned by his own party. Whether he can ultimately avoid extradition to the United States remains unclear. His fate appears to largely depend on U.S. authorities’ ability to submit evidence to Mexican authorities that convinces them that there is probable cause to believe the governor committed the crimes he is accused of.

At her Tuesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum stressed, once again, that no one can be arrested in Mexico or extradited from Mexico without evidence supporting an accusation that they committed a crime.

Her remarks came in response to a question about whether a Morena senator named in the same U.S. indictment as Rocha should also go on leave. The U.S. accusations against Rocha and other officials affiliated with Morena are a major headache for Sheinbaum, the leader of the “fourth transformation” political movement, of which Morena is a central part.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about Sinaloa’s new interim governor, who is slated to govern the state until a new elected governor takes office in late 2027.

In addition, the president briefly commented on Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama’s reportedly extensive travel on private planes, revealed by the newspaper Reforma on Monday.

Should Enrique Inzunza go on leave?

A reporter asked the president whether Senator Enrique Inzunza should go on leave ahead of the Senate’s legislative period in September.

Inzunza, a senator for Sinaloa, is one of 10 current and former officials accused by U.S. prosecutors of drug trafficking in league with the Sinaloa Cartel.

Sheinbaum noted that she offered an opinion on the case of Governor Rocha on Monday, before declaring that she believed that other accused officials who are currently in office and under investigation in Mexico should also go on leave.

“But everyone has to make their own decisions,” she said.

Sheinbaum subsequently reiterated that “in Mexico Mexicans decide” whether a person accused of wrongdoing by U.S. authorities has a case to answer.

“When there is an investigation by the U.S. Department of Justice and it is asking for an extradition or an arrest, there has to proof,” she said.

“We’re always going to defend that [position],” Sheinbaum said.

“… It’s a matter of the law, of the constitution,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Interim governor of Sinaloa is an ‘honest woman’

A reporter noted that Graciela Domínguez, a federal Morena deputy, appeared likely to be appointed as interim governor of Sinaloa. Domínguez, who previously served as education minister in Sinaloa during Rocha’s government, was proposed for the job by the Sinaloa Congress and designated as interim governor on Tuesday morning during the president’s mañanera.

Sheinbaum said that she doesn’t know Domínguez well, but added: “I do know she is an honest woman.”

“… She’s a woman who has been fighting for social justice and people’s well-being for many years,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that the federal government would support Domínguez as interim governor. Her task, she said, will be to “work for the peace, security and well-being of the people of Sinaloa,” a violence-plagued state where rival factions of the Sinaloa Cartel are engaged in a long-running and very bloody war.

After a reporter noted that there were calls for a person not linked to Rocha to be appointed as interim governor, Sheinbaum highlighted that the decision corresponded exclusively to the Sinaloa Congress.

“It’s not a decision for the president, it’s a decision for the state Congress,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Lezama has to explain her extensive travel

A reporter asked the president about Lezama’s reported travel on private planes to Mexican and international destinations, including Orlando and Vail in the United States.

According to Reforma, Lezama — a Morena governor who took office in Quintana Roo in September 2022 — has taken 97 flights on private planes while serving as a public official. Her husband and children accompanied her on many of those flights.

Sheinbaum said that it’s up to the governor to explain her travel.

“That’s the first thing,” she said. “It comes out in the media, but we don’t know how true it is,” Sheinbaum said.

“… [Lezama] has to clarify whether she used these planes and under what conditions,” she said.

In a social media post on Tuesday morning, the Quintana Roo governor said that she had taken flights on private planes, but asserted that she never paid for them with public money.

Lezama rejected Reforma’s reporting regarding the number of flights she has allegedly taken on private planes.

“It would mean being on vacation a whole year, it would be impossible,” she wrote.

“My commitment is to work 24/7, without rest, without neglecting my responsibility at any time,” Lezama said.

World.title: Caiado Asks Supreme Court to Lift Secrecy on Master, INSS Probes
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · POLITICS

Key Facts — Candidate Ronaldo Caiado, former governor of Goiás, is running for president for the PSD

— Appeal lift STF secrecy over the INSS pension-fraud, Banco Master and Operação Carbono Oculto cases

— Amnesty repeats vow to pardon all those convicted over the 8 January coup attempt, including Bolsonaro

— Other pledges a Latin American transnational police force and tighter control of public spending

— Calendar the first round of the election is scheduled for Sunday 4 October 2026

The PSD candidate told voters they risk being deceived unless the court opens the files on Brazil’s biggest fraud scandals before the October election.

Ronaldo Caiado, the Social Democratic Party (PSD) candidate for president of Brazil, used a prime-time television interview on Tuesday 25 August 2026 to appeal to the Supreme Federal Court (STF) to lift the secrecy that shields the country’s biggest fraud investigations, and to restate the Caiado amnesty plan covering everyone convicted over the January 2023 coup attempt, including former president Jair Bolsonaro.

Caiado asked the Supreme Court in Brasília to open the Master and INSS fraud files before the election.

What Caiado asked the Supreme Court to do

Speaking to journalists Renata Vasconcellos and César Tralli in the second of a Globo series with the six best-placed candidates, Caiado closed the interview with a direct appeal to the justices in his final-minute statement. Alongside the Caiado amnesty plan, it was the clearest political message of the night. He asked the court to lift the secrecy covering the INSS, the Master case and the Carbono Oculto operation, so that voters “would not be deceived by people involved in serious crimes who could be elected tomorrow”, in remarks broadcast by Globo.

The appeal, made without naming names, politically wears on two of his rivals: Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), whose circle has been touched by the Banco Master fallout, and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT), whose administration has been battered by the pension-deduction scandal at the National Social Security Institute (INSS). The Supreme Court has kept layers of confidentiality over the Master investigation since late 2025, when the case reached the tribunal under then-rapporteur Dias Toffoli; the rapporteurship passed to André Mendonça in February. Secrecy decisions since then, including orders sealing seized material and restricting access to case files, have turned the court itself into a campaign issue, with opposition figures accusing it of shielding powerful names and the justices insisting that confidentiality protects ongoing police work.

The Caiado amnesty plan returns to the campaign

Caiado reaffirmed that, if elected, he will grant amnesty to all those convicted over the 8 January 2023 invasion of Congress, the Supreme Court and the Planalto Palace, and over the wider coup plot, explicitly including Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving his sentence under house arrest. He has described the proposal since 2025 as “broad, general and unrestricted”, and the Caiado amnesty plan would be sent to Congress as one of his first acts in office.

The candidate again compared his position to the release of Lula and the restoration of the president’s political rights in 2021, after the annulment of his Car Wash convictions. Critics across the legal and political spectrum argue that an amnesty for coup convicts would weaken accountability for attacks on democracy, while supporters frame it as a way to pacify a polarized country. Caiado insists the country must close that chapter to discuss growth and public services, and he has said he would follow the example of Juscelino Kubitschek, the president remembered for governing through amnesty and national reconciliation in the 1950s.

Security and economic pledges

On public security, Caiado defended the creation of a transnational police force for South America, involving Brazil and its ten neighbouring countries, with shared intelligence and officers able to operate across borders. He compared the idea to European police cooperation and said he would tour the ten bordering countries as president to build it.

On the economy, he promised to rein in public spending and criticised the growth of the public debt, but declined to detail where he would cut. Pressed repeatedly on the fiscal adjustment, the minimum wage and pensions, he answered that he had already defined the macro framework and would prioritise fighting corruption, extortionate salaries and the diversion of budget funds. “I will manage,” he said.

The fraud cases behind the appeal

The Banco Master scandal centres on banker Daniel Vorcaro, arrested in the Federal Police’s Operation Compliance Zero, which investigates an alleged R$12 billion fraud involving credit portfolios traded with the Banco de Brasília; the bank is now in extrajudicial liquidation, and the INSS has withheld about R$2 billion in payroll-loan transfers over irregularities in some 254,000 contracts. The Rio Times reported this week on Operation Saturno and the Campo Grande pension probe linked to the same web of investigations.

The INSS scandal, examined by a joint parliamentary inquiry in Brasília, involves billions of reais in unauthorized deductions from retirees’ and pensioners’ benefits. Operação Carbono Oculto, the third case named by Caiado, is a Federal Police investigation that the candidate argued should be made public alongside the others. The court has not indicated whether it will respond to the appeal, which Caiado framed as a defence of the voter rather than an attack on the judiciary.

Six candidates and a fixed calendar

The Globo series, based on a 14 August Quaest voting-intention poll, opened on Monday with Romeu Zema (Novo) and continues with Renan Santos (Missão) on Wednesday, Lula on Thursday, Flávio Bolsonaro on Friday and Augusto Cury (Avante) on Saturday. It is the first time the network’s candidate interviews air after the Jornal Nacional flagship newscast rather than inside it, and the first round is set for Sunday 4 October. The order of the interviews was drawn by lot, in the presence of party representatives.

Analysts read the secrecy appeal as a way for Caiado to press the vulnerabilities of both front-runners while presenting himself as the candidate of transparency. At the same time, the Caiado amnesty plan courts the conservative electorate that Flávio Bolsonaro also needs, setting up a direct contest for the right-of-centre vote in the five weeks before the ballot.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ronaldo Caiado ask Brazil’s Supreme Court? In a Globo interview on Tuesday 25 August 2026, he asked the court to lift the secrecy covering the INSS pension-fraud investigation, the Banco Master case and Operação Carbono Oculto, arguing that voters should know before the election whether any candidate is implicated in serious crimes. Who would the Caiado amnesty plan cover? The Caiado amnesty plan would cover everyone convicted over the 8 January 2023 attacks and the attempted coup, including former president Jair Bolsonaro. Caiado compares the idea to the release of Lula and the restoration of his political rights in 2021. When is Brazil’s 2026 presidential election? The first round is scheduled for Sunday 4 October 2026. If no candidate wins more than half of the valid votes, a runoff between the two best-placed candidates is held later in October.

World.title: Quaest Polls Show Clear Frontrunners in Five Brazilian States
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · POLITICS

Key Facts — São Paulo Tarcísio de Freitas 40%, Fernando Haddad 27%

— Rio de Janeiro Eduardo Paes 37%, Douglas Ruas 14%

— Minas Gerais Cleitinho Azevedo 29%, Patrus Ananias 11%

— Pernambuco Raquel Lyra 44%, João Campos 36%

— Federal District Celina Leão 34%, Arruda 20%

Less than six weeks before Brazil votes, the Quaest state polls show incumbents and favorites pulling ahead in five key governor races.

A new round of Quaest state polls released on Tuesday 25 August 2026 shows frontrunners consolidating their leads in five of Brazil’s most important gubernatorial races, less than six weeks before the first round of voting on 4 October. The surveys, commissioned by Globo and conducted in person between 21 and 24 August, put Governor Tarcísio de Freitas ahead in São Paulo, former mayor Eduardo Paes in Rio de Janeiro, Senator Cleitinho Azevedo in Minas Gerais, Governor Raquel Lyra in Pernambuco and Celina Leão in the Federal District.

A voter confirms her choice on a Brazilian electronic voting machine ahead of the 4 October election.

São Paulo: Tarcísio opens a 13-point gap

In the country’s largest electorate, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas of the Republicans party leads the race for re-election with 40% of voting intentions, against 27% for former finance minister Fernando Haddad of the Workers’ Party. Police officer Edjane of the Agir party has 2%, and four left-wing candidates have 1% each, while blank and null votes plus declared non-voters total 14% and 13% remain undecided. In a simulated runoff, Tarcísio beats Haddad by 47% to 30%. Quaest interviewed 1,800 voters in São Paulo, with a margin of error of two percentage points.

The numbers reflect a well-evaluated incumbent. The governor’s administration is approved by 56% of those polled, and 57% say he deserves re-election. Violence tops the list of voter concerns in the state, cited by 34%, followed by health at 22%. Haddad faces a steep wall of rejection: 59% of voters say they know him and would not vote for him, against 37% rejection for Tarcísio. Two-thirds of São Paulo voters say their choice is already definitive, which narrows the room for a late shift in the race.

Rio de Janeiro: Paes leads a fragmented field

In Rio de Janeiro, former capital mayor Eduardo Paes of the PSD leads with 37% of voting intentions, 23 points ahead of state deputy Douglas Ruas of the PL, who has 14%. Former governor Anthony Garotinho registers 7%, and no other candidate reaches 4%. Undecided voters are a sizable 20%, the largest share among the five states surveyed. Paes also dominates the runoff simulations, beating Ruas by 50% to 20% and Garotinho by 53% to 12%. The poll heard 1,302 voters with a margin of error of three points.

Paes leads in 20 of the 21 demographic and political breakdowns analyzed by the Quaest state polls, losing only among voters who identify as bolsonaristas, where Ruas beats him by 39% to 22%. The race is marked by a strong appetite for change: 54% of Rio voters want the next governor to change everything, and only 11% want continuity. Garotinho carries the heaviest baggage, with 68% of voters saying they know him and would never vote for him, against 41% rejection for Paes.

Minas Gerais: Cleitinho ahead in a wide-open race

Minas Gerais has the most fragmented contest of the five. Senator Cleitinho Azevedo of the Republicans leads with 29%, followed by veteran Workers’ Party figure Patrus Ananias with 11%, former Belo Horizonte mayor Alexandre Kalil of the PDT with 10%, Vice Governor Mateus Simões of the PSD with 7% and Gabriel Azevedo of the MDB with 5%. Nearly one in five voters, 19%, is undecided, and in the spontaneous question, where no names are offered, 80% cannot name a preferred candidate. Quaest interviewed 1,506 voters, with a three-point margin of error.

Cleitinho wins all six runoff scenarios tested, defeating Kalil by 48% to 27% and Patrus by 51% to 26%. The outgoing governor, Romeu Zema, has a 37% approval rating, and 47% of voters say he does not deserve to elect a successor, a warning sign for Simões, the candidate identified with his administration. Health is the top voter concern in the state, cited by 28%, followed by violence at 13%. Cleitinho also posts the lowest rejection among the leading names, at 20%, while Kalil and Patrus are rejected by 41% and 40% respectively.

Pernambuco and the Federal District

In Pernambuco, Governor Raquel Lyra of the PSD leads Recife mayor João Campos of the PSB by 44% to 36%, an eight-point advantage that widens to ten in the runoff simulation, where she wins by 47% to 37%. The result marks a turnaround from polls taken earlier in the race, when Campos held the lead. Lyra’s administration is approved by 68% of voters, the best mark among the governments surveyed, and 61% say she deserves re-election. Quaest director Felipe Nunes said the numbers show the governor converting her positive evaluation into electoral advantage. The poll heard 1,302 voters, with a three-point margin of error.

In the Federal District, Celina Leão of the PP leads with 34%, against 20% for Arruda of the PSD and 13% for Leandro Grass of the Workers’ Party. She wins the runoff simulations against both rivals, beating Arruda by 42% to 32% and Grass by 52% to 24%. Brasília voters are the least decided of the five races: only 47% say their vote is definitive, and 53% admit they may still change. Health dominates local concerns, cited by 58%, far ahead of corruption at 14%. The survey interviewed 1,104 voters, with a three-point margin of error.

What the Quaest state polls mean for October

All five surveys were conducted in person between 21 and 24 August among voters aged 16 and over, with a 95% confidence level, and are registered with the Superior Electoral Court. The samples ranged from 1,800 interviews in São Paulo to 1,104 in the Federal District, with margins of error of two points in São Paulo and three points elsewhere. The Quaest state polls also tested the weight of national alliances, asking whether voters prefer a governor aligned with President Lula, with Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, or independent of both.

The answers point to different national dynamics in each state. Pernambuco recorded the strongest preference for an ally of Lula, at 50%, while São Paulo showed the largest share preferring an ally of Flávio Bolsonaro, at 33%, and the Federal District the biggest vote for independence, at 42%. With less than six weeks to go, the Quaest state polls suggest that incumbency and approval ratings are doing much of the work in these races. Whether the presidential coattails can move state contests will be the central question as the campaigns enter the final stretch.

Frequently Asked Questions

When were the Quaest state polls conducted? The Quaest state polls were conducted in person between 21 and 24 August 2026 and released on Tuesday 25 August. They were commissioned by Globo and registered with the Superior Electoral Court. Who leads the races for governor in São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro? In São Paulo, Governor Tarcísio de Freitas leads Fernando Haddad by 40% to 27%. In Rio de Janeiro, former mayor Eduardo Paes leads with 37%, against 14% for state deputy Douglas Ruas. What are the margins of error in the five polls? The margin of error is two percentage points in São Paulo, where 1,800 voters were interviewed, and three points in Rio de Janeiro, Minas Gerais, Pernambuco and the Federal District, all with 95% confidence.

World.title: Brazil Opens US$1.36 Billion Credit for Tariff-Hit Exporters
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Measure provisional measure MP 1387/26, published on Tuesday 25 August 2026

— Amount R$7 billion (about US$1.36 billion) in extraordinary budget credit

— Mechanism financing operations backed by the Export Guarantee Fund, not direct transfers

— Beneficiaries exporters of goods and services and their suppliers under the Brasil Soberano plan

— Next step review by Congress’s joint budget committee, then floor votes in both chambers

Brasília tops up the Brasil Soberano plan with fresh budget credit as new US tariffs squeeze Brazilian exporters.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a provisional measure on Tuesday 25 August 2026 opening R$7 billion (about US$1.36 billion) in extraordinary budget credit to finance Brazilian exporters hit by United States tariffs. The text, published in the Official Gazette as MP 1387/26, directs the money to companies covered by the Brasil Soberano plan, the umbrella program the government created last year in response to the trade measures imposed by Washington. It takes effect immediately but must be approved by Congress to become permanent law.

Container ships at the Port of Santos, the main gateway for Brazilian exporters covered by the credit measure.

What the measure does

The measure opens an extraordinary credit in the 2026 federal budget earmarked for export financing. The money is not transferred directly to companies. Instead, it funds financing operations under the responsibility of the Export Guarantee Fund, known by its Portuguese initials FGE, which is supervised by the Finance Ministry. According to the annex attached to the measure, the credit is calibrated to support 1,966 financing operations. The beneficiaries are Brazilian exporters of goods and services, as well as their suppliers, provided they fall within the scope of the Brasil Soberano plan.

In the message sent to Congress, the Executive argues that the United States has announced a 25% import tariff on a relevant share of Brazil’s export basket, on top of an additional 12.5% charge linked to the so-called Section 301 process. The government says it has identified potential demand for credit because the program’s deadlines and coverage have been extended, new sectors have become eligible, and exporters and suppliers remain exposed to tariff measures already in force or being implemented. Economic uncertainty tied to higher oil prices is also cited as a justification.

Who can access the credit

Eligibility follows the architecture built over the past year. The program targets companies with proven exposure to the US market, their suppliers, and sectors considered strategic for the trade balance. Earlier rounds covered agriculture, livestock, fishing and aquaculture, planted forests, mining, chemical and pharmaceutical industries, fertilizers, textiles, machinery and equipment, and the automotive sector, 22 segments in total under the third round announced in July. Priority criteria, such as the share of revenue dependent on US sales and company size, are set by joint acts of the Finance Ministry and the Industry and Trade Ministry.

The credit can be used for working capital, the purchase of machinery and equipment, productive investment, technological innovation and the adaptation of products and processes, as well as the opening and prospecting of new markets. Under the program’s rules, companies that take the subsidized financing must commit to maintaining or expanding their payrolls, and can lose the benefit of lower interest rates if the employment commitments are not met. The conditions, rates and terms of each line are regulated by the National Monetary Council and operated through accredited banks.

How the Brasil Soberano plan got here

The Brasil Soberano plan was launched in August 2025, after Washington raised tariffs on Brazilian products to as much as 50%, citing among other issues the Pix payment system, digital trade, ethanol market access and deforestation. The original measure authorized up to R$30 billion (about US$5.84 billion) in credit lines backed by the surplus of the Export Guarantee Fund, alongside government purchases of unsold foodstuffs and changes to export credit insurance. That first measure lapsed in December without a congressional vote, though the development bank BNDES had approved R$19.6 billion in operations under it.

The government rebuilt the program in stages this year. A second round, signed into law as Law 15.473 in July, authorized up to R$15 billion (about US$2.92 billion) in credit for exporters and agribusiness. A third round followed weeks later with R$18.5 billion (about US$3.6 billion), combining R$13.5 billion from the Treasury and R$5 billion from the BNDES, and broadened coverage to exporters hurt by international conflicts as well as tariffs. The new R$7 billion measure is, in effect, a budget top-up to keep those financing lines funded as demand grows.

A companion measure on tax suspensions

Published on the same day, a second provisional measure, MP 1386/26, extends by one more year the deadlines for tax suspensions granted under the drawback customs regime, which exempts or discounts taxes on inputs used in goods destined for export. The extension applies only to suspensions whose original end dates fall between 22 July 2026 and 31 December 2026, and only for companies that can document that their export commitments to the United States were hurt by the tariff measures.

To qualify, exporters must show that a previous extension was already granted and present documents proving a pre-existing commercial intention to sell to the US market. Data from the Industry and Trade Ministry indicate that US$1.2 billion in sales to the United States in 2025 involved products covered by drawback that are potentially affected by the tariffs. Together, the two measures show the government leaning on both sides of the export balance sheet: cheaper credit on one flank, tax relief on the other.

Congressional timeline and next steps

Although the measure is already in force, it must clear Congress to survive. Because it opens a budget credit, it will first be examined by the joint budget committee, made up of deputies and senators, before going to the floor of the Chamber of Deputies and then the Senate. Under Brazil’s constitutional rules, a provisional measure is valid for 60 days and can be extended once for the same period; if it is not approved within that window, it lapses. From the 46th day onward, it begins to block the voting agenda of each chamber, a mechanism designed to force a decision.

The political weather favors fast action. Previous measures in the same package moved through Congress with broad support, and lawmakers from exporting states have pressed the government to keep the credit lines funded ahead of the October elections. The government, for its part, argues that the new credit meets the constitutional requirements of urgency and relevance because it answers an external shock beyond Brazil’s control. If approved, the measure will give the Brasil Soberano plan fresh ammunition at a moment when the trade dispute with Washington shows no sign of cooling.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Brasil Soberano plan? It is the federal program created in August 2025 to shield Brazilian exporters from US tariffs. The Brasil Soberano plan combines subsidized credit lines, export guarantees, tax relief and government purchases of goods that lost their US market. How will the R$7 billion reach companies? Not through direct transfers. The extraordinary credit funds financing operations backed by the Export Guarantee Fund, supervised by the Finance Ministry, and the annex to the measure provides for 1,966 operations for exporters and their suppliers. Does the measure need congressional approval? Yes. It takes effect immediately, but must pass the joint budget committee and both chambers of Congress within 60 days, extendable once for the same period, or it lapses.

World.title: Brazil’s CVM Orders Oncoclínicas Tender Offer for Minorities
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · MARKETS

Key Facts — Decision CVM board voted 3-0 to require the tender offer

— Voters president Otto Lobo and directors João Accioly and Igor Muniz; Marina Copola recused

— Estimated value around R$6.5 billion (about US$1.26 billion), not yet fixed

— Trigger 2024 fund reorganization took the Centaurus-linked stake past a 15% bylaw threshold

— Next step written vote expected on Wednesday 26 August 2026

A 3-0 vote by Brazil’s securities regulator forces the Oncoclínicas tender offer long demanded by minority investors, but the final price tag is still to be defined.

Brazil’s securities regulator, the CVM, voted on Tuesday 25 August 2026 to require a tender offer for the shares of Oncoclínicas, the country’s largest private cancer-care chain, settling a dispute that had gripped the stock market for months. The board ruled by three votes to zero that asset manager Centaurus must launch an Oncoclínicas tender offer to buy out minority shareholders, reversing the regulator’s own technical staff, which had concluded in June that no offer was owed. The written vote is expected to be published on Wednesday.

The B3 stock exchange in São Paulo, where Oncoclínicas shares have risen more than 170% in August.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

A unanimous board reverses the technical staff

The three voting members of the CVM board, president Otto Lobo and directors João Accioly and Igor Muniz, sided with the minority investors who had appealed against the regulator’s technical area. Director Marina Copola had declared herself recused and did not take part, and one of the board’s five seats is vacant. The ruling overturns a June opinion by the CVM’s registration superintendency, known as the SRE, which had accepted Centaurus’s argument that it fell under an exception written into the company’s bylaws. Asset manager Latache, which leads the minority camp, and an association of investors in listed companies brought the appeal that was judged on Tuesday.

At the heart of the case is a poison-pill clause in the Oncoclínicas bylaws. It obliges any shareholder who comes to hold 15% or more of the capital after the company’s 2021 initial public offering to make an offer for the remaining shares at a premium. Minority investors argue the trigger was pulled in November 2024, when a reorganization of the Josephina funds, long managed by Goldman Sachs, transferred 104.6 million shares, about 16% of the company at the time, to the Josephina III fund linked to Centaurus. The manager contends it was the economic owner of the stake since 2018, before the IPO, and that the operation merely changed the form in which the position was held.

Price, scope and value remain open

Tuesday’s decision establishes the obligation, not the final bill. Market estimates cited by Brazilian media put a potential Oncoclínicas tender offer at around R$6.5 billion (about US$1.26 billion), assuming a price close to R$16 (about US$3.11) per share, but the CVM has not set any figure. The bylaws lay out several pricing criteria, including 120% of the highest quotation recorded by the stock over a defined 12-month window and an independent economic valuation. Some shareholders have argued for a price between R$16 and R$17 per share, a level that could still be contested in further proceedings.

The written vote, expected on Wednesday, should specify which group of shareholders will be eligible to sell into the offer. Lawyers following the case say the reference date matters as much as the price: if the obligation arose in late 2024, the offer should arguably have been made by January 2025, when the stock traded far above current levels. Oncoclínicas shares changed hands at R$1.57 (about US$0.31) as recently as Friday 21 August, after falling around 70% between January and July, which explains why the gap between the market price and any tender price is so wide.

What the Oncoclínicas tender offer means for minority shareholders

The clearest beneficiary is Latache, which became the largest individual shareholder with about 14.6% of the capital after building its position in the wake of the Banco Master collapse. Estimates suggest the manager could raise around R$1.5 billion (about US$292 million) if it tenders its full position. For smaller investors who bought shares after the stock collapsed, the Oncoclínicas tender offer represents a rare chance to exit at a premium to recent prices rather than wait for an operational turnaround at a company carrying heavy debts.

That turnaround is far from guaranteed. Oncoclínicas filed for extrajudicial recovery in July, seeking to renegotiate debts of about R$5.1 billion (about US$992 million). The company also booked a loss of R$433 million (about US$84 million) on bank certificates issued by Banco Master, the lender liquidated by the central bank last year. State lender Banco de Brasília, which received Oncoclínicas shares as part of credit recovery operations, has said it does not take part in the tender offer discussions and has no role in the company’s governance.

Arbitration and investigations run in parallel

The ruling does not end the legal fight. On Saturday 22 August, three days before the vote, Centaurus filed an arbitration claim against Latache at the Market Arbitration Chamber of B3, the São Paulo stock exchange. After the decision, the Josephina III fund said it disagreed with the board, arguing that the arbitration chamber holds exclusive jurisdiction over what it called a commercial dispute between partners of a listed company. The arbitration is confidential and, in principle, does not suspend the effects of the CVM ruling, but it could shape how and when any offer is carried out.

The dispute has also spilled beyond the regulator. In early August, the São Paulo civil police indicted two Goldman Sachs representatives on suspicion of fraud in an investigation related to the company’s shareholder structure and the failure to carry out the offer; the bank has denied any wrongdoing. Separately, the federal audit court opened an inquiry into potential conflicts of interest involving former CVM directors who later worked for parties linked to the case, and minority investors have filed complaints with the government’s comptroller and the CVM’s own internal affairs office.

Market reaction and what comes next

The decision landed after a week of frenzied trading. As reported by The Rio Times on Monday, Oncoclínicas shares soared 34% ahead of the ruling, and they jumped a further 12.5% on Tuesday morning before the board met. The stock has now risen more than 170% in August, a rally built almost entirely on expectations of the Oncoclínicas tender offer rather than on the company’s results. Analysts caution that once the tender terms are fixed, the shares should converge toward the offer price, leaving limited upside and meaningful downside if the operation stalls.

Attention now turns to the publication of the written vote and to three open questions: the price, the reference date and the universe of shares eligible to participate. Any of these could return to the CVM or end up in arbitration. Centaurus must also show how it would fund a multibillion-real purchase while the target company restructures its own balance sheet. For minority shareholders, the board’s vote converts a two-year legal theory into a regulatory obligation, but the path from this week’s ruling to cash in hand still runs through several more chapters.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the CVM decide about the Oncoclínicas tender offer? The board voted 3-0 on Tuesday 25 August 2026 that Centaurus must carry out an Oncoclínicas tender offer for minority shares, reversing the regulator’s technical staff, which had concluded in June that no offer was required under the company’s bylaws. How much could the offer be worth? Market estimates point to around R$6.5 billion (about US$1.26 billion), assuming a price near R$16 per share, but the CVM has not fixed a value. The price, reference date and eligible shares remain open to further discussion. Does the ruling end the dispute over Oncoclínicas? No. Centaurus has filed an arbitration claim against Latache at B3’s Market Arbitration Chamber, and the Josephina III fund says that chamber has exclusive jurisdiction. The price and scope of the offer may still be contested.

World.title: Caputo to Unveil Economic Measures as Argentina Faces Arrears Crisis
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Argentina · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Announcement Caputo speaks at 10:00 on Wednesday 26 August 2026 at the Palacio de Hacienda

— Expected centerpiece a mortgage-credit scheme funded through the ANSES sustainability fund (FGS)

— Household stress 12.8% of family loans were in arrears in June; credit-card arrears hit 12.6%

— Debt test the Treasury faces 12.6 trillion pesos (about US$8.3 billion) in maturities at this week’s auction

— Congress first-round votes sought on the Central Bank charter reform and Fiscal Innocence II

A mortgage-credit gambit, a heavy debt test and two make-or-break bills: Caputo’s Wednesday is the economic team’s biggest day of the second half.

Argentina’s Economy Minister Luis Caputo holds a press conference at 10:00 on Wednesday 26 August 2026 at the Palacio de Hacienda in Buenos Aires to unveil the Caputo economic measures trailed in the local press, capping a week in which his team faces a record household arrears crisis, a heavy debt auction and a decisive congressional vote on two flagship bills.

The BCRA headquarters in Buenos Aires, whose charter reform faces a first-round vote in Congress on Wednesday.
