What the Caputo economic measures are expected to include

The announcement was confirmed after the government’s political-table meeting at the Casa Rosada, according to local media, and national outlets report that the centerpiece will be a new financing scheme to reactivate the mortgage-credit market. The plan would channel long-term liquidity to banks through the Fondo de Garantía de Sustentabilidad (FGS), the sovereign fund administered by the ANSES pensions agency that backstops the public pension system.

By putting the FGS into play as a leverage vehicle, the scheme aims to extend funding terms and cut the origination costs of housing loans, according to details leaked to the Argentine press. It would complement the recent easing of foreign-currency lending rules for companies that do not generate dollars, part of a broader push to get private credit moving again before the 2027 electoral cycle.

Caputo has form in using set-piece conferences to shift market expectations, and the Caputo economic measures announced today will be read as much for their political signal as for their technical content. Officials had not published the fine print at the time of writing.

The household arrears crisis behind the package

The urgency is visible in the Central Bank’s debtor registry. Some 12.8% of household loans were in arrears in June, with credit-card delinquency at 12.6%, according to BCRA data, a level unthinkable in late 2024, when the comparable ratio was 2.5%. Consultancy Focus Market calculates the irregular portfolio almost quadrupled in twelve months, from 2.7% in January 2025 to 10.6% in January 2026, with personal loans deteriorating fastest.

The monetary authority moved this week to contain the damage, capping the reference rate on financing from non-bank card issuers at 66.44% nominal annual for the September billing cycle. Retail data, meanwhile, show household consumption falling across categories, evidence of what analysts describe as a widening gap between the government’s celebrated macro aggregates and the reality of family budgets.

It is this social pressure that the Caputo economic measures must answer. Cheaper, longer mortgage credit would not cure arrears, but officials believe reviving formal credit is the only sustainable route to rebuilding household solvency without fiscal giveaways.

A decisive session in Congress

Hours after the Caputo economic measures are unveiled, the government will seek first-round approval in the Chamber of Deputies for two priority bills. The first is the reform of the Central Bank’s charter, a project steered by vice-minister José Luis Daza that would grant the institution technical independence and explicitly ban direct financing of the Treasury, provinces and municipalities.

The second, known as Fiscal Innocence II (Inocencia Fiscal II), aims to offer legal certainty to Argentines who bring part of the estimated US$170 billion held outside the formal financial system into the open. After committee debate, the draft now excludes public officials from the scheme’s benefits, a concession to critics who called the original a whitewash.

President Javier Milei received deputies and senators at the Casa Rosada on Tuesday to lock in votes, according to El Cronista, ahead of a session widely seen as a test of the government’s remaining congressional allies. Tax specialists caution that the take-up of any asset-declaration regime will depend on how much legal security investors believe Argentina can credibly offer.

A US$8.3 billion debt test, with no dollars on the menu

The week’s third front is financial. At this week’s auction the Treasury faces maturities of 12.6 trillion pesos (about US$8.3 billion at the wholesale rate of 1,511 per US$), down from an original 13.9 trillion after a bond swap with the Central Bank, according to brokerage Adcap. The Treasury holds deposits of roughly 8.3 trillion pesos (about US$5.5 billion) at the BCRA, giving it room to let part of the debt lapse and return liquidity to the system.

Significantly, the five-instrument menu, comprising three fixed-rate peso securities, one inflation-linked letter and one dollar-linked letter subscribed and settled in pesos, contains no US-dollar bond. The Treasury has therefore decided not to seek dollars from the local market this time, a shift after it had already cut takes on the dollar-denominated Bonar 2029 to US$50 million per round in mid-August, with US$774 million still available under the bond’s US$2,000 million cap.

The decision lands amid fresh currency pressure: the wholesale dollar broke through the 1,500 ceiling on Monday, jumping 0.7% to a record nominal 1,510, and edged up to 1,511.50 on Tuesday. Within the maturities sits a dollar-linked commitment equivalent to US$2,595 million whose repayment exchange rate is fixed on Wednesday, the brokerage PPI noted, making the day’s FX print doubly sensitive.

How investors read the government now

For all the domestic noise, foreign managers have not abandoned the Argentina story. Bank of America’s August survey of 30 Latin America fund managers running about US$90 billion found roughly 33% expect further improvement in Argentine assets over the next six months, against 23% neutral and a marginal negative share, making the country a relative exception in a region where risk appetite fell to its lowest since April 2025.

The government is also keen to show momentum beyond finance: on Monday it formally awarded eight highway concessions covering more than 3,900 kilometers under 20-year toll contracts, one of the largest infrastructure privatizations of the Milei era.

What happens next hinges on three verifiable outcomes: the detail of the Caputo economic measures at 10:00, the rollover rate at the debt auction, and the headcount in the Deputies’ vote. A clean sweep would strengthen the economic team’s hand into September; a stumble on any front would revive questions about the program’s political shelf life.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time is Luis Caputo’s press conference on 26 August 2026? Economy Minister Luis Caputo speaks at 10:00 on Wednesday 26 August 2026 at the Palacio de Hacienda in Buenos Aires. The announcement was confirmed after the government’s political-table meeting at the Casa Rosada, and Argentine media expect a mortgage-credit scheme to top the agenda. What do the Caputo economic measures include? The Caputo economic measures are expected to center on a mortgage-credit scheme funded through the FGS, the ANSES-administered sovereign fund, which would inject long-term liquidity into banks to extend loan terms and lower origination costs. Full details are due at the Wednesday press conference. What is Fiscal Innocence II and why does it matter? Fiscal Innocence II (Inocencia Fiscal II) is a bill offering legal certainty to Argentines who declare part of the estimated US$170 billion they hold outside the formal financial system. The government seeks first-round approval in the Chamber of Deputies on Wednesday; the current draft excludes public officials from its benefits.

World.title: Brazil Overtakes Mexico as Latin America’s Top FDI Destination in 2026
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Mexico · ECONOMY

Key Facts — New leader Brazil drew US$46.99 billion in FDI in January-June 2026, up about 33% year on year

— Overtaken Mexico posted a record US$34.97 billion, up 2.1%, but trails by about US$12 billion

— Recycled money 88.5% of Mexico’s FDI was reinvested profits; new investment was US$2.73 billion (7.8%)

— Slowdown fresh projects drew about US$1.02 billion in the second quarter, down from US$1.71 billion in the first

— Credit warning Mexico’s bonds pay yields above Guatemala’s and Panama’s despite investment-grade ratings

A US$12 billion half-year gap ends Mexico’s run as the region’s FDI leader, and exposes how little of its record haul is fresh money.

Brazil overtakes Mexico as Latin America’s leading destination for foreign direct investment in 2026, official figures compiled through Wednesday 26 August 2026 show. Brazil drew US$46.99 billion in the first six months of the year, about US$12 billion more than Mexico’s US$34.97 billion, a Mexican record confirmed by the Economy Ministry on Monday 24 August that nonetheless falls well short of its rival’s pace.

São Paulo, the financial capital of a Brazil that drew US$46.99 billion in first-half FDI.

How Brazil overtakes Mexico in the 2026 FDI race

The crossover is recent. Mexico closed the first quarter ahead, with a record US$23.59 billion, but Brazil’s inflows accelerated sharply between April and June, when US$9.08 billion arrived in June alone, flipping the regional ranking at the half-year mark. Brazil’s first-half total of US$46.99 billion is up about 33% on the same period of 2025, and its twelve-month accumulated intake has reached US$89.3 billion, equivalent to 3.58% of GDP, according to central bank data compiled by América Economía.

Mexico’s US$34.97 billion is still its highest ever for a first half, up 2.1% on the figure originally published for January-June 2025. But the growth rate is a fraction of Brazil’s, and behind the two giants the chasing pack is also moving: Chile drew US$9.16 billion (up 29%), Peru US$7.50 billion (up 26.7%) and the Dominican Republic US$3.28 billion (up 7.7%) in the same six months.

Concentration remains the region’s defining feature. Brazil and Mexico absorbed 62% of Latin America’s US$194.2 billion in FDI in 2025, according to ECLAC, and nothing in the 2026 data suggests that duopoly is loosening, only that the order inside it has changed.

A record headline built on recycled profits

The composition of Mexico’s record explains much of the story. Of the US$34.97 billion confirmed by the Economy Ministry, US$30.96 billion, or 88.5%, was reinvested profits of companies already operating in the country. New investment accounted for just US$2.73 billion, or 7.8%, with inter-company accounts making up the remaining US$1.29 billion (3.7%). Counting genuinely fresh money, meaning new projects plus inter-company flows, barely one dollar in eight entering Mexico was anything other than recycled earnings.

The flow of new investment is also decelerating. Quarterly figures imply fresh projects attracted about US$1.02 billion between April and June, down from US$1.71 billion in the first quarter, a drop of roughly 40% in three months at a moment when the government is marketing the Plan México investment drive.

As The Rio Times reported on Tuesday 25 August in its coverage of the record and the debt warning attached to it, the headline number flatters the underlying dynamism of new capital formation. The half-year comparison now shows what that composition costs in the regional race: the moment Brazil overtakes Mexico is also the moment the gap between recycling and expansion becomes visible in hard data.

Why Brazil is winning the capital race this year

Several forces explain why Brazil overtakes Mexico in 2026. Brazil offers scale, a deep domestic market and high real interest rates that keep carry-trade capital engaged, and its inflows are spread across agribusiness, energy, finance and industry rather than dependent on a single trade corridor. Mexico, by contrast, remains heavily tied to the United States, which supplied 48.2% of its first-half FDI (US$16.87 billion), followed by Spain with 14.2%.

Mexico’s manufacturing base is still attracting money: the sector took US$13.48 billion, 38.6% of the total, with electronics and computing equipment especially dynamic, and the Economy Ministry insists the record reaffirms the country’s appeal under Plan México. But the United Nations’ 2026 World Investment Report had already flagged the weakness: the value of greenfield projects announced in Mexico fell from about US$44 billion in 2024 to US$24 billion in 2025, a sign that companies prefer expanding what exists over building anew.

Debt markets are already pricing Mexico as a laggard

The credit dimension sharpens the Brazil overtakes Mexico story. In May, Moody’s cut Mexico to Baa3, one notch above junk, while Fitch already holds the sovereign at BBB-, the last rung of investment grade, and S&P carries a negative outlook on its BBB. Mexico has not lost its investment-grade status, but bond investors are not waiting for the agencies: Mexican sovereign debt pays yields above those of Guatemala and Panama, both rated below it.

GMO’s head of emerging-market debt, Tina Vandersteel, says Mexico’s standalone credit metrics now sit below Guatemala’s and Uzbekistan’s, both speculative-grade names. JPMorgan data show Mexico’s traditional yield advantage over regional peers has compressed to about half a percentage point from one and a half points in better times, as transfers to state oil company Pemex, more than US$130 billion across the López Obrador and Sheinbaum administrations against financial debt above US$70 billion, migrate the company’s losses onto the sovereign balance sheet.

For FDI, the message is uncomfortable: portfolio capital is charging Mexico junk-adjacent prices while direct investors mostly recycle old profits. Neither signal implies crisis, and even cautious fund managers rule out a payments accident like those of 1982 or 1994, but both point to stagnation rather than expansion.

What to watch in the second half of 2026

Whether Brazil overtakes Mexico for the full year will depend on the third quarter. Brazil must prove its second-quarter surge was not a one-off, while Mexico needs the new-investment line to recover if it is to close a US$12 billion gap. Third-quarter figures from both countries, due in November, are the next checkpoint.

Watch also the USMCA trade pact’s joint review and Washington’s tariff decisions, which hang over Mexico’s nearshoring pipeline, and Brazil’s October election, which polls suggest could unsettle the real. For now, the region’s investment map has a new leader, and the runner-up has a composition problem it can no longer disguise.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much FDI did Brazil and Mexico receive in the first half of 2026? Brazil received US$46.99 billion between January and June 2026, up about 33% year on year, according to central bank data. Mexico received US$34.97 billion, a record for a first half but up only 2.1%, leaving it about US$12 billion behind Brazil. Why is it significant that Brazil overtakes Mexico in FDI? That Brazil overtakes Mexico matters because Mexico had built its recent economic narrative on record investment inflows and nearshoring. Losing the regional lead, while 88.5% of its own record is reinvested profits rather than new projects, undercuts claims that fresh capital is flooding in. Is Mexico’s US$34.97 billion FDI record misleading? Not false, but incomplete. The Economy Ministry’s figure is a genuine first-half record, yet only 7.8% of it, US$2.73 billion, was new investment. Analysts say the composition shows confidence from established firms but weak attraction of brand-new projects, and bond markets already price Mexican debt near junk territory.

World.title: Oil Slides as Iran-Oman Talks Fuel Hopes of Strait of Hormuz Reopening
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Region · MARKETS

Key Facts — Price move Brent fell about 2% to US$86.80 early Wednesday after both benchmarks lost over 3% on Tuesday

— Diplomacy Iran and Oman discussed a temporary joint corridor and mine-clearing in the strait

— Reversal Monday’s Operation Economic Outcast sanctions gave way within 48 hours to talk of reopening

— LatAm FX the dollar closed 0.25% lower at R$5.1399 in São Paulo; Colombia’s TRM stood at 3,056.51

— Risk a tanker was struck near the strait’s entrance on Tuesday, underscoring fragile security

A fast reversal from Monday’s sanctions escalation puts Latin America’s crude exporters and their currencies back at the center of the Hormuz story.

Oil prices fell for a second straight session on Wednesday 26 August 2026 as Iran and Oman confirmed talks on a temporary joint shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, reviving expectations of a Strait of Hormuz reopening and, with it, the prospect of a broader settlement between Washington and Tehran. Brent crude slid about 2% to US$86.80 a barrel in early Asian trade, after both benchmarks lost more than 3% on Tuesday 25 August, while US West Texas Intermediate fell to US$80.87.

An oil tanker under US Coast Guard escort in the Gulf, as Hormuz reopening talks sink crude prices.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

From Monday’s sanctions package to Wednesday’s sell-off

The speed of the reversal has been striking. On Monday 24 August, Washington expanded sanctions aimed at cutting off Iran’s economic lifeline, a package the Treasury calls Operation Economic Outcast, blacklisting around 60 entities, individuals and vessels linked to Iranian shipping, aviation, gold, technology and digital assets, and warning that countries continuing to do business with Tehran could face penalties, though none were imposed immediately. Brent had settled on Monday near US$92 a barrel as traders weighed the risk of retaliation.

By Tuesday afternoon the narrative had flipped. Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi and his Omani counterpart Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi confirmed they had discussed a joint temporary navigational corridor through the strait and agreed in principle to clear it of mines. Al Busaidi described the talks as constructive and said he hoped a corridor and practical measures to restore navigation security would be announced soon. Brent settled 3.9% lower at US$88.58 a barrel; during the session the most-active contract traded down 3.6% at US$87.27 on the ICE exchange in London, after touching a low of US$86.81.

Selling resumed in Asia on Wednesday. The prospect of a Strait of Hormuz reopening has triggered profit-taking after weeks of war premium, said Mitsuru Muraishi, an analyst at Fujitomi Securities, though he noted that bargain hunting was limiting further losses and prices were likely to remain range-bound for now. Data from the American Petroleum Institute, showing a 4.2 million-barrel build in US crude stocks in the week to 21 August, added to the downward pressure.

What a Strait of Hormuz reopening means for Latin America’s oil exporters

For Latin America’s crude exporters, a Strait of Hormuz reopening is a double-edged sword. Brazil, whose pre-salt output makes it the region’s biggest producer, earns less per barrel when Brent falls, trimming export receipts and royalties that feed federal and state budgets. Colombia’s Ecopetrol, Ecuador and Venezuela face the same arithmetic, with Brent, which spiked to US$126 in April at the height of the war, now trading roughly a third below that peak.

Yet the peace dividend cuts the other way. The same diplomatic thaw that knocks US$5 off a barrel of crude also lowers the geopolitical risk premium across emerging markets, supporting the currencies, bonds and equities of the very countries whose oil revenue declines. For net importers such as Chile, Central America and the Caribbean, meanwhile, cheaper fuel is an unambiguous gain for inflation and trade balances.

Venezuela is the wildcard. Any lasting US-Iran détente could eventually reshape Washington’s sanctions posture toward other sanctioned producers, analysts say, though there is no sign so far that the Trump administration intends to ease pressure on Caracas as part of the Hormuz track.

Real firms in São Paulo, Colombian peso consolidates

Latin American markets leaned into the risk-on move on Tuesday 25 August. In São Paulo, the dollar closed 0.25% lower at R$5.1399 against the real, while the Ibovespa stock index jumped 1.55%, with local desks citing the Hormuz corridor news and easing US Treasury yields as the session’s drivers.

In Bogotá, the official TRM rate for Tuesday was set at 3,056.51 pesos per dollar, leaving the Colombian peso among the fastest-appreciating emerging-market currencies in August after the dollar fell more than 2.9% in the previous week. The peso has gained about 3.2% since President Abelardo de La Espriella took office on 7 August, although it gave back about 1% in Tuesday’s spot session, with the dollar rebounding to around 3,090 pesos as oil’s slide weighed on exporter sentiment.

Why the peace trade remains fragile

The physical reality in the strait lags the diplomacy. A tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles northeast of Oman’s Ash Shishah, at the entrance to the strait, on Tuesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported. No casualties were registered, but the incident was a reminder that a durable Strait of Hormuz reopening requires security guarantees that do not yet exist.

Traffic data tell the same story. Ship-tracking monitors counted just three transits on 23 August against a pre-crisis baseline of about 85 a day, with several hundred tankers and cargo vessels holding position away from berth and war-risk insurance premiums still elevated. The strait carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February.

There are also precedents for disappointment. A June memorandum of understanding that offered a formal path to reopening the waterway lapsed on 17 August after Washington declined to renew it, and Tehran insists publicly that the strait will not fully reopen until the United States lifts its naval blockade and oil sanctions. In a cautiously positive signal, the United States has begun sending personnel back to some Middle East diplomatic missions that were evacuated during the fighting, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters, and the US Navy says all mines in the strait have been cleared, according to Al-Monitor.

What traders watch next

The immediate catalyst is the formal announcement Iran and Oman have hinted at: the coordinates and conditions of the temporary corridor, and any US endorsement of it. The timing of any Strait of Hormuz reopening announcement will set the tone for Brent’s next US$5 move in either direction.

Beyond diplomacy, traders are watching US inventory data, tanker insurance rates and this week’s Federal Reserve signals for the dollar’s direction. For Latin America, the balance is clear: a confirmed corridor would entrench the risk-on mood lifting the real and regional equities, while another failed round of talks would put the war premium, and the pressure on the region’s currencies, straight back into the price of oil.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did oil prices fall on 25 and 26 August 2026? Oil fell because Iran and Oman confirmed talks on a temporary joint shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz, including mine clearance, reviving hopes of a wider US-Iran understanding. Brent lost more than 3% on Tuesday 25 August and about 2% more on Wednesday, sliding toward US$86.80 a barrel, as traders unwound the war premium built up since February. How does a Strait of Hormuz reopening affect Latin America? A Strait of Hormuz reopening would lower crude prices, trimming export revenue for producers such as Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela. But it also cuts the global risk premium, which supports Latin American currencies and stock markets, and it reduces fuel costs for net importers like Chile, Central America and the Caribbean. Could oil prices rebound if the Hormuz talks fail? Yes. A tanker was struck near the strait on Tuesday, traffic remains at a fraction of pre-war levels and a previous reopening deal collapsed in June. Analysts say those risks keep a floor under prices, with Brent likely to stay range-bound until a corridor is formally announced and insured.

World.title: Chile GDP Flat in Second Quarter, Joint-Weakest in the OECD
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Chile · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Q2 2026 GDP unchanged, 0 percent quarter-on-quarter, after a 0.3 percent fall in Q1

— OECD average The bloc grew 0.5 percent in the quarter and 2.3 percent year-on-year

— Bottom of table Chile tied Austria and Belgium for the weakest quarterly result

— Region Mexico grew 1.5 percent, Colombia 1.3 percent and Costa Rica 1.2 percent

— Response Kast launched a 12-member commission with 120 days to propose cutting ministries

Zero growth in the second quarter leaves Chile at the bottom of the OECD table and sharpens the case for President Kast’s plan to shrink the state.

Chile’s economy stagnated in the second quarter of 2026, with Chile GDP showing zero growth between April and June and a 0.3 percent year-on-year contraction, according to data the organization released on Monday 24 August, in the same week that President José Antonio Kast launched a commission to slim down and redesign the Chilean state.

Santiago’s financial district, as data showed Chile’s economy flat in the second quarter of 2026.

Chile GDP stalls while the OECD grows

The OECD reported that Chile’s economy showed no variation in the second quarter of 2026, after contracting 0.3 percent in the first three months of the year. The bloc as a whole grew 0.5 percent between April and June, accelerating slightly from 0.4 percent in the first quarter, according to the organization’s statement carried by El Mostrador.

Ireland recorded the strongest quarterly expansion in the club, at 3.9 percent, followed by Israel at 3.6 percent. At the other extreme, the OECD said, output was unchanged in Austria, Belgium and Chile, leaving Chile tied for the weakest quarterly performance among members.

The figures are more striking because they arrived in a difficult international environment: the OECD noted that the global economy absorbed the effects of the war in Iran, whose impact was felt from the start of hostilities in late February, yet most member economies still managed positive growth. El Mostrador said the numbers put the spotlight back on the low dynamism of the Chilean economy, noting that Chile was the only Latin American member whose economy shrank over the past year even as the bloc managed to accelerate its expansion in the quarter.

Lagging its Latin American peers

Among the Latin American members of the OECD, Chile posted the worst performance of the quarter. Mexico grew 1.5 percent, recovering from a 0.6 percent contraction in the first quarter, while Colombia expanded 1.3 percent and Costa Rica 1.2 percent, according to the organization’s data.

The annual comparison is starker still. Between the second quarter of 2025 and the same period of 2026, Chile GDP contracted 0.3 percent while the OECD as a whole grew 2.3 percent. Colombia led the region with a 3.4 percent annual expansion, ahead of Costa Rica at 2.2 percent and Mexico at 1.5 percent.

The major economies also slowed, but none stalled. The G7 grew 0.3 percent in the quarter, with the United States at 0.4 percent, Germany at 0.2 percent and Japan at 0.3 percent, while Spain accelerated to 0.7 percent, well above the euro zone average of 0.4 percent. Spain’s annual growth of 2.7 percent also outpaced the 1 percent recorded across the euro zone, underlining that the momentum seen elsewhere has passed Chile by.

A narrow escape from recession

A technical recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of contraction. Chile avoided that definition by a fraction: the 0.3 percent decline in the first quarter was followed by a flat second quarter, although the annual reading confirms that the economy is smaller than a year ago.

The stagnation sharpens scrutiny of the economic agenda of President Kast, whose administration argues that an oversized and duplicated state apparatus weighs on public finances and private investment. That diagnosis, summarized in official language as the need to eradicate duplicated functions and optimize the reallocation of public resources, is the premise behind the commission the president launched this week.

Opposition figures and business groups have instead pointed to uncertainty and weak investment as drags on activity, a debate that the next rounds of national accounts data will do little to settle quickly. What is not in dispute is the trajectory: the economy has gone six months without expansion, and output is now smaller than it was a year earlier.

Kast’s commission to redesign the state

The president gave the official start to the Comisión Nueva Arquitectura del Estado, a 12-member team of specialists that will have 120 days to evaluate a reduction in the number of ministries and to draft a comprehensive institutional modernization plan, according to El Desconcierto and El Observatodo. Chile has gone from 18 to 25 ministries in recent decades.

Its mandate is to propose a more rational ministerial structure, one that reduces portfolios, eliminates overlaps and reassigns resources, Kast said at the launch, adding that he wants a state filled by merit and not by political quotas. Any reduction of ministries will require bills negotiated with Congress.

The commission crosses party lines. It includes former ministers from the Bachelet, Piñera and Boric governments, among them Andrés Zaldívar, Gonzalo Blumel, Nicolás Monckeberg, Osvaldo Andrade and Adriana Delpiano, alongside Bettina Horst, Natalia González, Beatriz Hevia, Ernesto Silva, Natalia Piergentili, Zarko Luksic and labor lawyer Juan Antonio Urzúa. Beyond counting portfolios, the team is empowered to convene public sector workers’ groups and outside specialists, and to draw on studies and reports produced over the past three decades.

Political backdrop and what comes next

The commission and the weak growth data land at a delicate moment for the government, whose flagship security reform recently lost urgency in Congress, a setback covered previously by The Rio Times.

The commission’s 120-day mandate means its recommendations should arrive around the end of the year, after public hearings with state workers’ groups and specialists. The government says the goal is not an arbitrary number of ministries but a rigorous diagnosis to underpin the bills it will then send to the National Congress, where the measures will face amendment and negotiation.

For the economy, attention now turns to the third quarter. Another flat or negative reading would put the recession question back on the table and raise the stakes for the government’s state-redesign and growth agenda heading into 2027. The government is betting that a credible plan to rationalize public spending can improve confidence and unlock investment while external demand remains hostage to the conflict in the Middle East. Whether that argument convinces markets, and a Congress where the administration lacks majorities, will become clearer as the commission begins its hearings in the coming weeks.

Frequently Asked Questions

How did Chile GDP perform in the second quarter of 2026? Chile GDP showed zero growth quarter-on-quarter between April and June 2026, after a 0.3 percent contraction in the first quarter. Year-on-year, output fell 0.3 percent while the bloc as a whole grew 2.3 percent, the only annual contraction among the OECD’s Latin American members, according to the organization. What is the Kast commission on the state? The Comisión Nueva Arquitectura del Estado is a 12-member body of former ministers and specialists from across the political spectrum. It has 120 days to propose a leaner ministerial structure, eliminate duplicated functions and reassign public resources. Any cuts to ministries would then require legislation in Congress. Is Chile in a recession? Not by the usual technical definition, which requires two consecutive quarters of contraction. Chile’s economy shrank 0.3 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and was flat in the second. However, output is 0.3 percent smaller than a year earlier, the only annual contraction reported among the Latin American members of the OECD.

World.title: Is Costa Rica’s 98% Literacy Rate Really Accurate?
World.content:
Costa Rica has long promoted itself as the most literate country in Central America, and by the numbers it is. Government statistics put the literacy rate among people 15 and older at roughly 98 percent, a figure repeated in tourism brochures, investment pitches and international rankings for decades. But a closer look at how that number is produced, and who it leaves out, suggests the real picture of who can and cannot read and write in this country is considerably worse than official statistics admit.

The core problem is that Costa Rica’s literacy figure comes from self reported survey answers, not from any actual reading test. When a census worker or household survey interviewer asks someone whether they can read and write, the person answers for themselves, and there is no verification.

Illiteracy carries deep social stigma, particularly among older adults and in rural communities, so people frequently say yes even when they can do little more than sign their name. This pattern of self reported literacy running well ahead of tested literacy has been documented across Latin America and the developing world for years, and there is no reason to think Costa Rica is an exception.

For some unknown reason, Costa Rica has also never participated in the OECD’s Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies, known as PIAAC, the only rigorous international test that measures actual functional reading and math skills among working age adults. Chile is currently the only Latin American country that has taken part.

Without that data, nobody, not INEC, not the Ministry of Education, actually knows how many adults in Costa Rica can functionally read a lease, a prescription label or a job application. The government’s own household survey data hints at how large that gap might be. The 2023

Encuesta Nacional de Hogares found that while more than 95 percent of children between 5 and 18 attend school, only 43 percent of adults 24 and older have completed secondary school or higher. Again, it is self reported information. Even that still leaves a majority of Costa Rican adults with, at most, a primary education, a population in which functional literacy gaps are common even among people who would most likely answer yes to a census worker’s verbal question.

Then there is the migrant population, which the national statistics were never designed to capture well. Costa Rica is home to an estimated 400,000 to 500,000 Nicaraguan born residents, many without legal documentation, along with smaller communities from Panama, Colombia and Venezuela.

Household surveys sample dwellings, and undocumented families are far less likely to be reached, or to fully disclose who lives in the home, which means this group is structurally underrepresented in the literacy statistics altogether. Nicaragua’s own illiteracy rate runs well above Costa Rica’s, so a large undercounted population from a higher illiteracy country almost certainly pulls the real number up.

Rural and indigenous territories carry a similar blind spot. Decades old census data already showed rural illiteracy running more than three times the urban rate, and there is little evidence that gap has closed. A national average near 2 percent can mask rates several times higher in specific rural cantons and indigenous territories, places that get folded into a countrywide figure dominated by San José’s educated, urban population.

There is also a personal dimension to this that statistics alone cannot capture. I have at least one member of my own family and one employee who cannot read or write, and I suspect there are others in my life who have simply never told me. What I have learned over the years is that people carry this quietly, and they only reveal it once they trust that you will not judge them.

That trust takes time to build, and most surveys, census takers and government forms never get anywhere near it. It is one of the reasons I have made a habit of leaving voice messages rather than sending text messages to certain people in Costa Rica. A written message assumes a level of comfort with reading that is not universal, and a voice note sidesteps that quietly, without ever making the moment about literacy at all.

I suspect this same dynamic explains why certain phone apps, video content and voice based advertising perform so much better here than text heavy websites or written promotions. A population with a meaningful hidden pocket of nonreaders is going to gravitate toward whatever does not require reading, and that shows up in behavior long before it shows up in any government survey.

Conservative estimates are that at least somewhere between 150,000 and 300,000 people currently living in Costa Rica, citizens and migrants combined, cannot read and write at a functional level, several times the roughly 90,000 suggested by the official illiteracy rate.

Until Costa Rica actually tests adult literacy rather than asking people to self report it, the true scale of the problem will remain a matter of estimation rather than record.

World.title: Rain Returns to Costa Rica Tonight on Ground That Cannot Take Much More
World.content:
More rain is coming tonight, and where it lands matters more than how much falls. Tropical Wave (a stretch of unsettled air that moves west across the tropics) 36 reaches Costa Rica overnight and will push rainfall up while it passes. Because of that, here is how the day shapes up before it gets here. The Caribbean and northern regions stay cloudy, with on-and-off rain and showers. The heavier spells come early in the morning and again at night. Afternoon rain scatters and thins, though it may push into the northern and eastern edges of the Central Valley.

The Pacific side gets the better end of it, with skies from partly to mostly clear. Expect afternoon showers and thunderstorms in the Central and South Pacific and across parts of the Nicoya Peninsula. Then the wave arrives after dark and the rain picks up again. On its own, that is an ordinary forecast for late August. The problem is what it is falling on.

The ground across the Caribbean and northern regions has barely stopped absorbing water since July 20. Eight tropical waves have crossed the country since then. Between August 16 and 17, parts of the southern Caribbean and Turrialba took 360 millimetres of rain, about 14 inches, in 48 hours.

Soil that saturated stops soaking anything up and new rain runs straight off into rivers and creeks instead, which is why streams there rise faster now than the rainfall totals alone would suggest. It is also why slopes slide. Nine areas remain under a national emergency declaration because of that rainfall — Guatuso, Turrialba, Sarapiquí, and Limón, Pococí, Siquirres, Talamanca, Matina and Guácimo. Tonight’s rain lands on all of them.

There is a second reason to be careful this week, and it has nothing to do with weather. Yesterday’s earthquakes near Coronado shook loose material along the mountain route between San José and the Caribbean. Rock and soil came down on Route 32 around the 30-kilometre mark, near mile 19, closing the road for part of the morning. Roughly 80 aftershocks followed through the day.

Slopes that held through the last storm are weaker than they were a month ago. Rain on freshly disturbed ground is the combination that puts material on the road. So, if you are driving to or from the Caribbean coast this week, check conditions before you leave rather than after you are already in the mountains. Route 32 has closed repeatedly this month, sometimes with only minutes of notice, and it can reopen and close again the same day.

When it does close, there are other ways across. Route 10 runs between Siquirres and Turrialba. The Bajos de Chilamate–Vuelta de Kooper road offers a northern alternative. Vara Blanca is passable but has been restricted to light vehicles during past closures. All three take longer, and all three are subject to the same weather.

If you meet water across the road, turn around. This is the advice that gets ignored most and causes the most trouble. Moving water hides how deep it is and how fast it is going, and flooding regularly scours away the roadbed underneath, so a surface that looks intact may not be there at all.

The same applies on foot near swollen rivers and creeks, which can rise sharply with little warning when the ground upstream is already full. Costa Rica’s weather service updates its bulletins through the day, and the emergency commission publishes alert levels by region. Both are worth a look before you commit to a drive this week rather than after.

The wave will move on. The saturated ground it leaves behind will take considerably longer.

World.title: Scientists Name the Fault Behind Costa Rica’s Coronado Earthquakes
World.content:
Costa Rica’s seismologists now have a name for what shook the Central Valley awake yesterday, and it comes with a history. The National Seismological Network at the University of Costa Rica has linked yesterday’s earthquakes near Coronado to the Río Sucio fault system. The network calls the connection preliminary, but it rests on two pieces of evidence pointing the same way — the quakes and their aftershocks cluster tightly along where the fault runs, and the direction the ground moved matches how this fault is known to behave.

A fault is a fracture in the earth’s crust where two blocks of rock grind past one another. When they lock, strain builds. When they slip, the ground shakes. This one is not a surprise to scientists. Researchers at the university’s Central American School of Geology identified it back in the 1990s using satellite imagery, fieldwork and records of past quakes in the area. The system runs about 30 kilometers, roughly 19 miles, and the rock on either side slides sideways past itself rather than one block dropping below the other.

That sideways motion explains something thousands of people noticed. Security cameras across the valley captured buildings, lamps and hanging signs swaying side to side rather than jolting straight up. That is what this kind of fault does. The track record is the part worth paying attention to.

The network ties three earlier earthquakes to the same system. The most serious was the Patillos earthquake of December 30, 1952, a magnitude 5.9 that killed 21 people according to historical records. More recently there was Capellades on November 30, 2016, a magnitude 5.5. And in August 2023, a magnitude 4.4 struck with several smaller quakes just north of where Monday’s sequence unfolded.

Seismologist Lepolt Linkimer of the university network has said assessments of the fault put its potential at above magnitude 6. The National University’s Volcanological and Seismological Observatory is not ready to name a single culprit. Its position is that the area sits inside a broader zone containing several faults, and that more than one may have been involved.

“It is a series of faults, not just the seismic zone as such,” said observatory seismologist José María Sequeira. Work continues, he said, to establish which structure was directly involved, and whether one fault moved or several. Sequeira named Alto Grande, Río Patria, Lara, Río Sucio and La Hondura among the faults in that zone, most of them taking their names from the rivers running above them.

The zone stretches across the ground between the Turrialba and Barva volcanoes, passing Irazú, and belongs to a wider band of fractured crust reaching from the Limón lowlands to the Pacific side. Finding exactly where these faults run is harder than it sounds. Most are buried under soil with no visible crack at the surface, so geologists read the landscape for clues. The Río Sucio is one of the clearer cases — the river cuts an unusually straight line, and the small quakes cluster along it.

Mapping each aftershock sharpens that picture, showing where the movement concentrates both across the surface and at depth. The aftershocks kept coming all day. The National University’s observatory counted 80 between 1:39 a.m. and 6 p.m. Monday, an average of one roughly every 12 minutes. The university network logged 23 in a narrower window, counting only those at magnitude 2.2 or above — the same kind of methodological gap that produced the differing magnitude figures reported on Monday.

The university network recorded shaking intensity across the central region at levels five to six on a twelve-point scale, meaning it was felt clearly indoors, rattled objects and, at the upper end, moved furniture. Damage stayed limited to a garden wall in Coronado, a downed power pole in Moravia and rockfall that briefly closed Route 32.

No deaths or injuries were reported and both institutions expect the aftershocks to continue for hours and days yet, tapering off in frequency as sequences like this normally do. The university network says it will keep watching and update as new data arrives. None of this is unusual ground for Costa Rica as it sits where tectonic plates collide offshore and is threaded with active faults inland, which is why permanent monitoring exists at all. What changed this week is that one of those faults stopped being an abstraction on a map.

World.title: 19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black
World.content:
19-year-old man remanded for allegedly stabbing brother in the eye; come to court with his eye black

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 19-year-old Belize City man has been remanded to the Belize Central Prison after being accused of attacking his older brother with a knife during a family dispute.

Brenton Conrad Archer, a construction worker of Iguana Street, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his 22-year-old brother.

Archer pleaded not guilty.

Police allege that Archer and his brother became involved in an altercation at a residence on Iguana Street on Friday, August 21. The confrontation reportedly escalated into a fight during which Archer’s brother was stabbed several times.

Police later visited the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where the brother was observed with lacerations to both sides of his mouth as well as stab wounds to his left eye and cheek.

The prosecution did not object to bail for Archer; however, the Magistrate expressed concern that the brothers may live at the same residence or in close proximity to each other.

Archer told the court that his brother does not live in the same yard, but the Magistrate opted to temporarily withhold bail while the prosecution verifies their living arrangements.

The court said the precaution was necessary to avoid another confrontation between the siblings once Archer is released.

Archer, who also appeared in court with visible injuries to his eye and a bandaged right hand, was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on September 2, 2026, when the issue of bail is expected to be revisited.

World.title: Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup
World.content:
Sheffan Hemmans, Alberto Arreaza remanded over alleged armed burglary and theft of $46,000 pickup

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A member of the Belize Coast Guard and a salesman/manager were remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Tuesday after being charged with aggravated burglary in connection with an alleged armed home invasion in Hattieville.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sheffan Devan Hemmans, a member of the Belize Coast Guard, and 46-year-old Alberto Arreaza, a salesman, manager and farmer from Teakettle Village, appeared before a Magistrate in Court #5, where they were jointly charged with aggravated burglary.

Police allege that on Thursday, August 20, the men, while armed with a firearm, entered a home in the Mile 17 area of Hattieville and stole a pickup truck.

The vehicle is valued at $46,000.

Both men pleaded not guilty to the charge.

The Magistrate informed Arreaza and Hemmans that, because the alleged offence involved a firearm, the lower court could not grant them bail at this stage. They were advised that they may apply to the High Court for bail through an attorney if they wish to secure their release before becoming eligible for bail consideration in the Magistrate’s Court.

Both men were subsequently remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Arreaza and Hemmans are due back in court on October 20, 2026, when they are expected to receive disclosure in the case.

World.title: Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea
World.content:
Man accused of stealing cousin’s bicycle remanded after court rejects guilty plea

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 27-year-old Belize City construction worker accused of stealing his cousin’s bicycle was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after telling the court he was considering pleading guilty simply because he had no one to bail him.

Israel Anthony Usher appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft.

Police allege that on August 13, 2026, Usher stole a 24-inch Hurricane Beach Cruiser bicycle valued at $500 from a female relative at a Benbow Street address.

Before entering a plea, Usher told the Magistrate that if he pleaded not guilty he had no one to secure bail for him, and asked whether pleading guilty would result in a fine instead.

The Magistrate told Usher that a guilty plea could only be accepted if he was actually admitting that he stole the bicycle.

Usher then denied stealing it, telling the court that the owner is his cousin and had allowed him to borrow the bicycle. According to Usher, police later stopped him while he was riding the bicycle against the flow of traffic and confiscated it after he was unable to produce proof of ownership.

He claimed his cousin later believed he had stolen or disposed of the bicycle and made a theft complaint against him.

After hearing his explanation, the Magistrate refused to accept a guilty plea merely for convenience and entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf.

Usher was offered bail in the sum of $500 plus one surety of the same amount, but was unable to secure bail by the end of the day and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

He is due back in court on October 6, 2026, when the theft matter will continue.

World.title: Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him
World.content:
Belize City man ordered to stay 100 yards from brother after allegedly pulling knife on him

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City businessman accused of assaulting his brother, including allegedly threatening him with a knife, is out on bail but has been ordered by the court to stay at least 100 yards away from his sibling while the case remains active.

Thirty-two-year-old Alexander Elvis Jones, a resident of the Conch Shell Bay area, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with common assault and aggravated assault with a dangerous instrument upon his brother.

The charges stem from an alleged dispute on August 5, 2026.

Jones pleaded not guilty to both counts.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $1,000 plus one surety of the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Jones must have no contact with his brother or any other prosecution witnesses and must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant. He is also required to attend all court dates or risk having his bail revoked.

Jones met bail and is due back in court on October 5, 2026, for disclosure.

World.title: Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside
World.content:
Woman granted $800 bail after allegedly threatening to burn down her sister’s home with sister and children inside

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 38-year-old Belize City woman has been granted bail after being charged with threat to damage property following an alleged family dispute in which she is accused of threatening to burn down her sister’s home.

Shantae Robateau, a customer care representative, appeared in court unrepresented and pleaded not guilty to the charge. Police allege that during an incident on July 31, 2026, Robateau threatened her sister, saying she would burn down the house while she and her children were inside.

According to the police report, the sister told investigators that she was at her Ebony Street home at around 9:15 p.m. when Robateau allegedly arrived outside the residence carrying a piece of 2-by-4 wood, shouting and demanding that Jones come outside.

The complainant reportedly contacted their older brother, who lives nearby, and asked him to intervene. Police say that as efforts were made to remove Robateau from the property, she allegedly threatened to physically harm her sister and later threatened to burn the house down with her sister and her children inside.

The woman subsequently made a report to police, prompting an investigation. Robateau later turned herself in to police and was charged.

At her arraignment, the prosecution did not object to bail but requested that conditions be imposed. The Magistrate granted Robateau bail in the sum of $800 with one surety of the same amount.

As part of her bail conditions, she must report to the Raccoon Street Police Station every Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. and attend all scheduled court appearances.

The case was adjourned until October 13, 2026.

World.title: Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case
World.content:
Justin Goff rejects 1 year sentence for guilty plea in ammunition case

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Justin Stephen Goff, 38, has decided to maintain his not guilty plea and proceed toward trial on a charge of keeping unlicensed ammunition, two days after asking the Belize City Magistrate’s Court for an indication of the sentence he could receive if he pleaded guilty.

Goff appeared in court Friday morning and told the Magistrate that, after considering the matter, he would not plead guilty.

On Wednesday, August 19, Goff had requested a sentence indication as he considered changing his plea. He was reportedly informed that, after consideration of an early guilty plea and other mitigating and aggravating factors, he could face a sentence of approximately one year and four months’ imprisonment.

Goff, however, rejected that option on Friday and will instead contest the charge.

His case was adjourned until September 4, 2026, when he is expected to receive disclosure from the prosecution.

Goff was first arraigned on April 7, 2026, after police alleged that he was found three days earlier in possession of three live rounds of ammunition — two S&B rounds and one Aguila round — without a licence.

At his arraignment, Goff pleaded not guilty and alleged that the ammunition had been planted on him by a police officer. He told the court that he had been asleep beneath a shed when officers approached and questioned him about a firearm.

Goff claimed that an officer later produced three rounds of ammunition and falsely attributed them to him.

He remains on remand while the case proceeds.

World.title: Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases
World.content:
Protecting Belize’s Children: UNHCR and UNICEF train social workers to handle high-risk cases

By Zoila Palma: UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, and UNICEF are working to strengthen Belize’s child protection system by training social workers and child protection professionals to better respond to vulnerable children, including those affected by displacement, abuse, neglect and family separation.

The Best Interest Procedure Training brings together frontline professionals from across the country to develop practical skills for making decisions that prioritize the safety, rights and well-being of children.

Participants are taking part in case studies, interactive discussions and practical exercises focused on assessing risks and developing appropriate protection responses.

The training is especially important for cases involving violence, exploitation, neglect, abuse, displacement and family separation, where decisions can have lasting consequences for children.

The Best Interest Procedure provides a structured, child-centered approach to help social workers determine what course of action is most appropriate for each individual child.

The initiative forms part of continued collaboration between UNHCR, UNICEF and the Department of Human Services within the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs.

UNHCR Officer-in-Charge in Belize Mariya Voloshkevich said strengthening the capacity of social workers is an important investment in Belize’s child protection system, while UNICEF Representative Sajid Ali emphasized that every child has the right to protection, care and support.

Department of Human Services Director Shawn Vargas stressed that family separation must be approached with particular care. He noted that children have a fundamental right to family life and, whenever it is safe and appropriate, should remain with or maintain meaningful contact with their families. He emphasized that separation should not be treated as an easy or automatic solution, and that any decision to separate a child from their family must be lawful, necessary and proportionate, while considering both the immediate and long-term impact on the child.

UNHCR and UNICEF say they will continue working with Belizean officials and partners to strengthen child protection services and safeguard the rights and well-being of children across the country.

World.title: Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October
World.content:
Imari Young keeps bail after missing court date, trial set for October

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Fresh Pond resident Imari Young, who is before the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on a burglary charge, was allowed to remain on bail Friday after being brought before the court on a bench warrant for failing to attend a previous court date.

Young appeared unrepresented before Magistrate Neeshad Rohammad, who asked him to explain why his bail should not be revoked after he failed to appear in court on July 22.

Young told the court that he had been sick at the time. He also said his mother is hospitalized and that his father recently died. Young claimed that he had obtained a doctor’s document explaining his absence, although the court reportedly had no record of receiving it.

Despite the missed appearance, the Magistrate did not revoke Young’s bail and allowed him to remain free while his case continues.

Young is charged with burglary and is now scheduled to return to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on October 14, 2026, when his trial is expected to begin.

World.title: Unhealthy trend: Student obesity surges to 15.3%
World.content:
The Global School-based Health Survey confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight. (Photo: Adobe stock)

MORE than three in every 10 students captured in a recent survey by the National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) were overweight while 15.3 per cent of them were obese.

The Global School-based Health Survey (GSHS), which was conducted between January and March this year, had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools.

It confirmed fears that there has been an increase in the number of Jamaican students getting obese and overweight, while underweight remains a concern.

According to the survey, obesity moved from six per cent in 2010 to 15.3 per cent in 2026, while the number of overweight students jumped from 21.7 per cent in 2010 to 31.7 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, there was an uptick in underweight students, from 2.1 per cent in 2010 to 3.4 per cent in 2026.

The survey also found a dip in physical activity from 23.2 per cent in 2017 to 19.6 per cent in 2026, while 70.2 per cent reported less than eight hours of sleep, which can be attributed to the long hours students spend on the Internet as sedentary behaviour — sitting down for more than three hours per day increased from 56.4 per cent in 2017 to 68 per cent in 2026.

“Students [who are] less active, more sedentary, and many not getting enough sleep means that there is an increased risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems,” said the NCDA.

It called for more physical activity, greater promotion of recreation and sports, and encouragement for students to adopt healthy sleep habits.

The NCDA blamed unhealthy eating patterns for the rise in obesity among students, and recommended the promotion of healthy school food environment, expansion of nutrition education, and promotion of balanced diets.

But despite the increase in obesity and overweight, the survey found that in the 30 days before it was conducted there was a drop in consumption of one or more sodas per day by students.

In 2010 the NCDA found that 72.5 per cent on the respondents had consumed one or more sodas in the 30 days before the survey, while this year only 49.7 per cent of the respondents said they had done so in the past seven days.

The survey said underweight was highest among grade nine boys, 6.4 per cent, and grade 11 girls, 4.8 per cent.

Meanwhile, the highest rate of obesity was among grade seven girls, 43.2 per cent, and grade seven boys, 40.5 per cent.

The Global School-based Health Survey, noted the NCDA, provides high-quality data to inform decision-making and action for school and youth health.

In his reaction to the survey findings, Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton urged parents and guardians to ensure their children eat healthy foods at home and school.

He said it is always a better choice to take a meal from home to school if the school does not have facilities for the preparation of hot meals.

Tufton also urged parents and guardians to encourage their children to participate in more physical activities if they want to ensure that they do not fall victim to diabetes, heart disease, and other non-communicable diseases.

“Parents and guardians must insist that their children become more health conscious. Fast food and sugary beverages are not healthy, and I want to remind you parents that, should these young ones get diagnosed with a non-communicable disease, it will follow them into adulthood and put more stress on your resources as well as the health system,” said Tufton.

The NCDA said the survey has shown that healthy eating, regular physical activities, and adequate sleep are essential for the well-being, learning, and long-term health of Jamaica’s children and adolescents.

It added that the lack of physical activity increases the risk of obesity, chronic diseases, poor academic performance, and mental health problems.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID); and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: A different route for boys
World.content:
In this video grab Seargeant Kevin Wallace, dean of discipline and drill instructor at the Jamaica Constabulary Force Cadet Academy, inspects trainees during muster.Video: Jamaica Constabulary Force

As Jamaica continues to grapple with the persistent underperformance of boys in school, the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) is offering an alternative path that combines academics, discipline, and mentorship to help young men find their footing.

The JCF Cadet Academy, established in September 2021, was born out of the police force’s experience working with young people through its Safe Schools Programme and other youth initiatives where cops observed particular challenges among boys, including truancy.

Speaking on the JCF’s Force4Good podcast, principal of the academy Deputy Superintendent of Police Tanecia Johnson said the force recognised the need for a setting where it could provide more focused support to young men.

“When those reports come in, it’s always about the boys outnumbering the girls in terms of truancy and so on, and so as a force… we decided that something must be done in terms of having a better structure to have these boys in an area where we can have that direct concentration,” she said.

The academy now combines traditional schooling with a highly structured boarding environment, with police, trained teachers, guidance counsellors, and other staff working closely with the students.

Johnson said the academy’s approach is based on more than discipline, with staff seeking to understand the circumstances affecting each student and build relationships that encourage them to open up.

“Oftentimes in the schools the students will tell us as the police, as their mentors, as their motivators, things that they will not tell a school principal, things that they will not tell their parents,” she revealed.

Those conversations, Johnson said, allow the academy to address issues such as anger, identity, purpose, attitude and a student’s plans for the future.

The approach is producing encouraging academic results.

This year’s Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate (CSEC) performance included a 100 per cent pass rate in information technology and physical education and sports, while human and social biology recorded 98 per cent, English A 92 per cent, and office administration 90 per cent. Mathematics recorded a 75 per cent pass rate.

At the Caribbean Advanced Proficiency Examination (CAPE) level, communication studies recorded an 88 per cent pass rate, information technology 93 per cent, law – unit one 84 per cent, and law – unit two 75 per cent. Johnson said the results represent the academy’s best academic performance since it was established.

For Johnson, however, the results are only part of what the academy is trying to achieve.

She recalled the experience of a 17-year-old student who arrived after struggling to gain CSEC passes. When staff spoke with him about his experience they discovered that his academic difficulties did not necessarily reflect his ability.

“Sometimes all it takes is a change of environment for these youngsters, and at the Cadet Academy we’re thriving because, first and foremost, we have educators, we have our teachers, but love is central to what we do,” she said.

Johnson said that philosophy extends to how students are treated when they make mistakes. Rather than focusing on punishment, staff speak of corrective measures and ensure students have immediate access to adults when problems arise.

According to Johnson, the academy normally takes about 80 students in an intake and has approximately 10 resident facilitators and 15 external teachers, in addition to administrators, guidance counsellors, and access to the JCF’s medical services. It currently offers seven CSEC and four CAPE subjects.

The academy also serves as a potential pathway into the JCF, although Johnson stressed that becoming a cop is not compulsory and admission to the academy does not guarantee recruitment.

Students who want to join the force must still meet the requirements, sit the JCF entrance examination, and undergo further background checks.

Of the 35 students who graduated on June 25 this year, 34 were awaiting the next intake to join the JCF, while one planned to attend university first.

Johnson said that, overall, 99.9 per cent of students who choose to pursue policing after completing the programme progress towards the JCF, with more than 175 former cadets now serving in the organisation.

But the academy’s purpose is not simply to produce police personnel.

Johnson said students are encouraged to pursue tertiary education or other careers if that is the path they choose, while the JCF hopes the education and personal development they receive will prepare them for life beyond the academy.

The academy’s model comes against a separate national conversation about the performance of boys in Jamaica’s education system, where they continue to face challenges in areas such as engagement, attendance, and academic achievement.

That wider concern provides an important backdrop to the academy’s results, but Johnson said the programme itself grew from the JCF’s direct experience with young people and its decision to create a more concentrated intervention.

World.title: ‘Baddies build furniture too’
World.content:
Carpenter Sydonie Miller at her shop in DunKirk, Kingston (Photo: Garfield Robinson).

With work hard to find and financial constraints mounting during the coronavirus pandemic, one Jamaican woman discovered a hidden talent that opened an unexpected livelihood for her in a labour-intensive trade not often pursued by local females – carpentry.

Twenty-nine-year-old Sydonie Miller had been finding it difficult to secure a job in 2020, during the heights of COVID-19, despite having a bachelor’s degree in business management and secretarial skills.

Miller, who was a new mother at the time, said her husband, a taxi operator, was the only one working and she was determined to find a way to contribute to her family.

Her journey to carpentry began with a desire to own a padded bedhead and being quoted what she considered an exorbitant price to have one made.

“At the time, it was padded bed did run the place. When I go to ask the price, them a give me an arm and a leg for it. Me say me nah pay that,” Miller told Observer Online.

So, she decided to build it herself.

Seeking the guidance of a carpenter friend on Charles Street and gathering the necessary materials, Miller went on to make her first bedhead.

After completing the project, Miller’s curiosity and determination pushed her to learn more. She eventually made her way to Oxford Street, where veteran carpenters such as Chucky, Paul, Max, Abi Doll and Warren took her under their wings and taught her how to build a wider range of furniture, including dressers, chests of drawers and beds.

But for Miller, learning the trade was not difficult because she has always been a practical learner. She quickly grasped the skills being taught to her.

“If you’re going to do something, I see what you’re doing. If you show me one time, you don’t have to show me again. Just the one time, I know what to do,” she explained.

But the mother of three said her entry into carpentry was about more than simply learning how to build furniture. She believes the skill was placed in her path for a reason.

“At the time, I was at work and I can’t forget the day. The almighty say I give you a skill, go and use it. I have business management, secretarial skills. I thought it was that skill but I never knew it was this skill. So when him say I give you a skill, go and use it, me just say alright me ago just go deal with the bed head. Me see say me can build dresser and me just a build. Me go under the wings of the veterans,” she said.

Miller, who now owns her very own furniture business, Luxurious Furnitures by Syd, said her client base now ranges from individual customers to stores in the downtown Kingston area.

When Observer Online visited her shop on Banana Street in the McIntyre Villa community of East Kingston, Miller was seen working on a bedhead and bed bottom for one of her customers.

While her skills have helped her build a business, Miller said being a woman in a male-dominated trade has presented its own challenges.

“Some of them, when them see a woman come and say you know say me build this, them don’t believe it” she explained.

Miller said some customers only become convinced that she builds the furniture herself after seeing a male carpenter deliver one of her pieces.

Despite the doubters, Miller said she has also encountered customers who appreciate the fact that she is a woman in the trade and are willing to give her the time needed to complete their furniture.

“To be honest, it’s a bittersweet moment, but at the end of the day there are some people that really love me, who are really happy that I’m a woman and I do this. You have some patient ones, big up on unu self. Them say alright then, I’ll give you time,” she added.

The carpenter said each piece of furniture requires patience and attention to detail, with the process involving several stages before a finished product is ready.

“For me its patience, to really put in the work, because remember, furniture building takes time. It has different layers, different processes to build. So to build a bed head like this, it takes time. I have a lot of different grades of sanding to do,” she said.

She further explained: “I have to start the sanding from, like, 80, and I go down to 180. Then I go down to 200. Then I go down to 220. It’s patience. And you have to get all the nooks and crannies. You can’t just sand off just the bigger parts. You have to sand from the corners, from underneath, behind, everything. So it’s just patience.”

Of all the furniture she has made since entering the trade, Miller said one particular piece remains her favourite, a king-size mahogany bed set. She said the piece holds special significance because it challenged her skills when she was still new to furniture building.

Miller is now encouraging other women not to allow traditional perceptions about certain professions to prevent them from pursuing their interests.

“Don’t follow the stigma say a man work. Woman can do it, too. Once you see something that you want to do just do it. Learn the skill, do it, because at the end of the day, it’s not who do it. It’s really how you set your mind to do it or if you have the determination to do it,” Miller said. “So don’t follow them a man work. Baddies build furniture too. Baddies build furniture too.”
