World.title: Fewer students drunk or high
World.content:
(Photo: Adobe stock)

THE National Council on Drug Abuse (NCDA) is reporting that fewer teenagers are using illegal drugs or drinking alcohol across Jamaica, but the numbers remain concerning.

According to the NCDA, its recent Global School-Based Health Survey (GSHS) conducted January to March 2026 — which had 3,058 respondents from 32 schools, with 76 per cent participation among students and 100 per cent from schools — showed that the consumption of alcohol by students in grades seven to 11 dropped from 52.5 per cent in 2010 to 38.8 per cent in 2026.

At the same time, the number of children who started consumption of alcohol before age 14 has decreased from 80.2 per cent in 2010 to 71.5 per cent this year. Also, teenagers who get drunk after the consumption of alcoholic beverages dropped from 35.5 per cent in 2010 to 21.5 per cent in 2026.

But 10.3 per cent of adolescents still attend school under the influence of alcohol, and 10.6 per cent are exposed to s about alcohol.

The NCDA — an agency of the Ministry of Health and Wellness — believes the overall message for positive trends has been working; however, it says continued action is needed to strengthen early prevention programmes, enforce underage drinking laws, reduce youth exposure to alcohol marketing, and increase parent and school engagements.

The survey also found that the use of ganja among adolescents declined from 21.5 per cent in 2017 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, a trend welcomed by the NCDA.

However, the organisation says it is concerned that 24.3 per cent of adolescents have easy access to the weed, while it noticed an emergence in the use of ecstasy, also known as molly.

Ecstasy is a synthetic psychoactive drug with both stimulant and psychedelic effects. Teens use it at parties and other gatherings, but it can cause dangerous spikes in body temperature, dehydration, high blood pressure, and heart failure.

With some students still attending school under the influence of substances because of the easy access to ganja and ecstasy, the NCDA says it will be expanding its substance-use prevention programme, aimed at strengthening prevention, delaying initiation, reducing access, and providing timely support for young people.

It also plans to improve the monitoring of emerging drugs.

In the meantime, the GSHS found that physical fights among students declined from 50.1 per cent in 2010 to 27 per cent in 2026, while injuries from fights dropped from 59.6 per cent in 2010 to 49 per cent in 2026.

In addition, the survey says bullying dropped from 40.2 per cent in 2016 to 27 per cent in 2026.

However, the survey found that 15 per cent of teenagers faced cyber bullying in the past year but there was no comparative figure with 2010. Another 16.9 per cent experienced bullying off school compounds.

The NCDA said despite a drop in physical fights among students, it will be strengthening its violence-prevention programme as it seeks to maintain safe school policies.

“Safe environments are essential for academic success and healthy development,” said the NCDA.

“Violence and injuries impact students’ physical and mental health, learning and well-being. Bullying and cyberbullying can lead to anxiety, depression, low self-esteem, and social isolation,” the NCDA added.

The GSHS is an international gold-standard survey developed by World Health Organization, in collaboration with United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF); United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

It measures health behaviours and protective factors among students 13 to 17 years of age and is used in 110 countries.

World.title: More vacancies than advertised
World.content:
Numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts.

With the new academic year just days away numerous schools are scrambling to fill permanent and temporary teaching posts. But Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) President Anniona Jones says the influx of s across various media do not reflect the full picture of the staffing needs.

According to Jones, while some vacancies have been caused by teachers embarking on well-earned vacation breaks, others are the result of educators leaving the system, some without proper notice.

“Some of these resignations do not reach the regional office, and sometimes we fill [vacancies] based on old resumes and not necessarily place all of it in an ad because not every school has the fiscal position to even run an ad. So what you’re seeing in the paper is the tip of the iceberg of the actual gaps in schools because many of us do not place in the national papers the s for teachers. We use a lot of social media, word of mouth, our teachers’ groups, Jamaica Teachers’ Association groups, and so on. That’s what’s happening. So we really don’t have a good picture nationally on what is really happening on the ground,” Jones told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The educator, who was responding to queries by the Observer about what accounts for the almost perennial influx of s yearly during the summer break, explained that the system itself is partly accountable.

“The education system asks all members of the academic staff to apply for their leave by November of the first term, for the following academic year. So leave applications are made almost a year in advance. Usually, by June we would get notification from the Ministry of Education indicating which teachers’ leave application is approved. This year it came a little later in July, and we see where a priority was placed on approving leave applications, certainly in Region One, which is Kingston and St Andrew, for persons who would have applied for eight months,” Jones outlined.

She said while the leave amounts might seem staggering, a little known fact is that “it takes a regular classroom teacher or vice-principal five years of service in order to qualify for four months of leave”.

“So, unlike many people’s workplace where they will get two weeks’ vacation leave, we don’t do that in education, and there are a lot of reasons for that. However, that’s how the system is set up. So teachers will get leave of four months or eight months. They’d apply for study leave, and they would know at that period of time,” she said.

Jones noted that because of the late approvals, principals were not made aware, until July, of how much their staffing levels would be affected for September.

“Usually that’s when many principals know how many of the teachers who have applied for leave have had their leave approved, and whether or not it is for four months, eight months, a year study leave, two years, or so on. So that means that July and August of every year, obviously, you’re going to see a large number of applications in the media, and we will have to fill these positions for smooth start of school for September,” Jones said.

She noted that teacher migration and not just vacation entitlements have also influenced the s of vacancies.

“There are several factors causing teacher migration. It’s not a national problem only, it’s not a regional problem only, it’s an international problem; and if you look at many of the international bodies, such as Education International, some projections go as high as 40 million teachers may be needed within the next decade globally. There are lots of reasons why teachers are leaving the education system: terms and conditions of service, salary, moving on to other interests, and so many other reasons. But we do have a significant shortage in some areas, the industrial arts [for example]. Obviously, persons can earn far more money in the private sector than in teaching,” she told the Observer while noting that Jamaican educators are in high demand by other territories.

The recruitment, she said, is also driven by the fact that there are “shortages in some areas that are undersubscribed like history, geography, the foreign languages like French, Spanish” in addition to the fact that some schools are located in remote areas, or in communities where Zones of Special Operations are in force, or areas that experience high levels of crime or violence, therefore “not many people may want to work in some of those areas”.

According to Jones, the discontinuation of a special hazard allowance — a grant that made to teachers who worked in very remote or rural situations, or in high-risk areas — as an incentive is also a contributor to some schools finding it difficult to fill vacancies.

“So there are many factors that would influence how fluid the system is. And then, of course, if we only have four months available, and that teacher gets a position that is potentially permanent, a teacher may go in that regard. So the short-term vacancies may also be difficult to fill,” the JAPSS president stated.

She said it is difficult to provide a total number of all schools with unfilled vacancies.

“If you look in the papers you will find that even schools that would have advertised before, they may have conducted interviews and even made an offer to a teacher. A teacher may rescind that offer from one school and move to another school where they did interviews because teachers are applying for multiple jobs, they’re doing many interviews, and then they’re picking once they’re offered. So, because of how fluid the system is, you may also find that you may think that you have filled a vacancy, and a teacher calls back to say, ‘I am so sorry. Instead of working at your school for four months or eight months, I’ve just been offered a position for a year, or a clear vacancy at another school, and so I’m going to take that offer instead’. So even though you may think that you filled the vacancy, it now becomes available again because the teacher is moving in the direction of what is best for them and their families,” Jones said.

Asked to say whether this meant the association still has no clear picture as to readiness for the new school year Jones said, “We have filled most of the vacancies… but many schools will have at least one or two positions that they’re hoping to fill this week, with some schools having as many as six or eight positions that are yet to be filled”.

Jones, in the meantime, had this message for parents, guardians, and students: “Every Jamaican child deserves high-quality education, and conditions of work for the teacher are conditions of learning for the children. So if it is that we want the best for our children, then it means we should want the best for the teachers. So, please help us to advocate for the conditions that will be required for us to be able to attract the best and the brightest, retain the most experienced teachers, so that our children can ultimately benefit.”

Added Jones, “Let’s celebrate those who have gone on their well-earned leave; [working] five years to get four months is a lot [and working] 10 years to get eight months is a lot. So let’s celebrate with those who are taking well-deserved breaks. But let us work together to advocate for a better education system.”

World.title: Celene Hall takes Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 crown
World.content:
Celene Hall makes her first walk as Miss Universe Jamaica 2026.

Despite winning five sectional prizes, the newly crowned Miss Universe Jamaica 2026 titleholder, Portland native Celene Hall said she had no idea that she would have emerged the winner.

Hall competed with 32 other ladies for the coveted title and to represent Jamaica at the Miss Universe finals in Puerto Rico in November.

he coronation show took place on Sunday night inside a jam-packed ballroom at AC Hotel Kingston.

“I know I received a lot of sectional awards, but honestly, it wasn’t until the crown was placed on my head that I really knew that I was Miss Universe Jamaica 2026,” Hall told the

Jamaica Observer shortly after she was crowned.

This marked the start of a new journey and the end of countless days and nights of practice, rehearsals, and training.

Hall first entered the Miss Universe Jamaica Portland pageant, which she won a few months ago.

According to Parish Director Shanique Rogers, Hall was transformed during the process.

“From the beginning, she listened, she understood what the crown represented, and, most importantly, she was willing to learn… She is not the same woman who entered the competition in Portland. The Miss Universe Jamaica Portland platform challenged her, developed her, and helped shape her into the queen she is today,” Rogers, a former Miss Universe Jamaica finalist, told the Observer.

She added: “Seeing Celene win makes me incredibly proud, because I know the amount of hard work, dedication, and behind-the-scenes effort that went into preparing her for this moment. To see that hard work pay off is truly rewarding.”

Hall concurred that the pageant challenged her.

“I knew the space would challenge me more to grow into the absolute best version of myself, and that is the reason why I entered in the first place,” she shared.

From Passley Gardens in Port Antonio, she attended Titchfield High School.

Her beaming parents, three sisters and two brothers were on hand to witness her success.

“She started modeling from primary school and she just kept going, and we have been supportive of her,” said her mother, Sonia Hall.

Father Victor said, “Celene has been a queen from ever since. I told her mother from the beginning that Celene had what it takes.”

The coronation show started more than an hour late, and once it got going there was no turning back. The 33 contestants opened the show but they were quickly reduced to a top 20.

The ladies then moved into swimwear before the top 14 were announced.

The evening gown competition resulted in the final six spots being filled.

After being interviewed, the final three were revealed to be Kadejah Anderson, Celene Hall, and Tianna McDaniel.

Hall won the Essence of Style Award, Best in Swimwear, Best in Evening Gown, Most Aware, and the Altruism Award.

Tianna McDaniel was adjudged Most Photogenic; Andrea Hill – Most Congenial; Marcie Lee Smith – Best Personality; Alanda Newman – Runway Star Award; and Marsha Roberts, Alanda Newman and Channon Smith made a three-way tie for Spirit of the Pageant award.

At the end of the night second runner-up was determined to be Anderson, while McDaniel, a medical practitioner, finished in the first runner-up position, as Hall snagged first place.

World.title: ‘Cricket isn’t dead!’
World.content:
Jamaica Kingsmen opener Kirk McKenzie hits the ball during the Caribbean Premier League T20 match against Trinbago Knight Riders at Sabina Park in Kingston on August 15, 2026.

JAMAICA Cricket Association President Dr Donovan Bennett believes the Jamaica Kingsmen have already made a strong impression on the island is optimistic they can play a key role in developing grassroots cricket locally.

The Caribbean Premier League (CPL) returned to Sabina Park for the first time since 2019 as the new Jamaica franchise hosted four games which concluded last Tuesday.

Tens of thousands of Jamaicans turned out for the four matches against the Barbados Tridents, Trinbago Knight Riders, Guyana Amazon Warriors and St Kitts and Nevis Patriots with some of the Caribbean’s top players on display including the Kingsmen’s own Rovman Powell and Andre Russell as well as regional stars Nicholas Pooran, Shimron Hetmeyer and Sunil Narine.

It continued the trend of growing crowd interest shown by local fans following last summer’s series between the West Indies and Australia, as well as Sri Lanka’s visit in June.

Bennett believes the Kingsmen’s home leg is a good reflection of the state of cricket in Jamaica.

“I have heard many persons who are or were cricket fans saying that cricket is dead in Jamaica but what both the Sri Lanka tour and the CPL that followed have clearly said is that cricket is not dead in Jamaica,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

“In fact, cricket is still one of the most popular sports in the country and that as long as the people are fed the right diet, they get what they want to see, they will come out and support us and it was clear to everybody from the crowds. It was a fantastic atmosphere, not just the numbers, but the participation because the crowds were a behind the team with almost every ball that was bowled. It was really something electric and really a pleasure to sit and observe.”

Although pleased with action on the pitch, Bennett says he was impressed by the Kingsmen’s early investment in youth cricket.

The team’s ownership sponsored the All-Grace Shield and All-Headley Cup exhibitions tournament in July, which saw some of the best high school cricketers from the urban and rural areas go head to head in a 50 over match and a T20 match over two days. The

Observer understands the Kingsmen handed over $3.1 million to the JCA to execute the matches.

“As I made a presentation to them, it was a yes and I can tell you, the amount that was literally given to us for the two games is a significant amount of money which comfortably put both games on,” Bennett said. “I think it is something that should encourage the schools to participate on a wider basis and for players to have something substantive to look forward to at the end of the season. It should be the responsibility of ISSA but in a situation where ISSA does not have an interest, then I think the JCA has got to take up the responsibility and get those games on a yearly basis.”

While happy with the progress the Kingsmen have made, Bennett wants them to do more to help develop the next generation of Jamaican cricketers.

“As soon as the CPL is concluded, hopefully we can sit down with the Kingsmen to discuss other development programmes because I am not one of those who sees development from above downwards. I think that is one of the problems with West Indies Cricket over the years is that a lot of money has been spent at the top and very little at the bottom,” he said.

“We have had initial discussions, we haven’t had any decisions as yet. But certainly things like our under-13 programme has got to be put on the table because we really want to do an extended, comprehensive under-13 programme. Every year, we need to have an Under-13 Jamaica team and then from that, we need to extract the best players out of that group every year and put them into a specialised, continuous programme so that in a couple of years’ time, we can have a large cadre of players who, from an early age, have been taught the right things, the right attitudes and also the seriousness at which they should take the cricket, both representing Jamaica and the West Indies.”

The Kingsmen, who have four games remaining in the league stage, are currently just outside the play-off spot in fifth on four points. They return to action on Thursday against the Patriots at Warner Park in St Kitts.

World.title: Before You Book: Questions You Should Ask Your Hotel Wedding Venue
World.content:
Finding a beautiful hotel venue is exciting. You can already picture the décor, the guests arriving, the food being served and everything coming together perfectly.

But before you sign the contract or pay that deposit, there are a few important conversations you need to have.

When planning a wedding at a hotel, what you don’t ask can sometimes cost you just as much as what you do. A venue may look perfect during a walkthrough, but the details behind the scenes — from additional fees and set-up times to catering restrictions and technology — can have a major impact on your event.

Here are some things you should know before saying yes to a hotel venue.

What Exactly Is Included in the Venue Cost?

Never assume that everything you see during your tour is included in the quoted price. You should also ask about taxes, service charges, overtime charges and any additional fees that may appear on the final bill. The goal isn’t simply to know the rental price; it’s to understand the true cost of hosting your event there.

Will the Space Really Work for Your Wedding?

Capacity is about more than the maximum number of people allowed in a room. A ballroom might accommodate 300 people theatre-style but significantly fewer once you add banquet tables, a stage, dance floor, buffet stations, décor and audiovisual equipment.

Explain exactly what you’re planning and ask the hotel how many guests the space can comfortably accommodate with your preferred layout.

Think Beyond the Start and End Time

Your invitation might say 6:00 pm, but your event begins long before the first guest arrives. Decorators, florists, entertainers, photographers and production teams may need several hours to prepare. Ask when vendors can access the venue, where they can load and unload, and how much time is allowed for breakdown afterward. If additional set-up or breakdown time comes at an extra cost, that’s something you want to know well in advance.

Understand the Food and Beverage Details



If the hotel provides catering, don’t stop at choosing a menu. Ask about food-and-beverage minimums, service styles, what’s included in the per-person price and how dietary requirements and allergies are handled. If you’re hoping to bring a special cake, outside caterer or another food or beverage item, confirm whether it’s permitted and whether additional fees apply.

These small details can have a surprisingly big impact on both your plans and your budget.

Ask About Vendors, Technology and Entertainment

If you already have a favourite decorator, DJ, photographer or production company, confirm that they’re allowed to work at the hotel. Some properties have preferred or exclusive vendors, while others may require outside suppliers to provide insurance or meet specific requirements.

Technology deserves the same attention. Ask what’s available for microphones, speakers, screens, projectors, lighting, electrical connections and Wi-Fi. And before planning candles, elaborate installations, confetti, hanging décor or late-night entertainment, ask about the hotel’s restrictions. There may be rules around open flames, wall or ceiling installations, amplified music and the time entertainment must end.

Consider the Guest Experience

Walk through the experience from your guests’ point of view. Where will they park? How easy is it to find the event space once they enter the hotel? Accessibility matters too. Ask about ramps, elevators, accessible restrooms and step-free access for guests who may need them.

A beautiful venue means very little if getting into it — or moving around it — is difficult for your guests.

What Happens When Plans Change?

Guest counts rarely remain exactly the same from the day you book until the day of your wedding. Find out when the final guaranteed number is due and what happens if attendance increases or decreases.

If your wedding booking includes overnight accommodation, discuss room blocks, booking deadlines and any commitments attached to those rooms.

You should also understand the hotel’s cancellation and rescheduling policies. Are there cancellation charges? And what happens if circumstances outside your control affect the event?

Is there a back-up location secured for you if you are outdoor and it rains?

These aren’t the most exciting questions to ask, but they’re some of the most important ones to have answered in writing.

Know Who Will Be Looking After You



The person who shows you the ballroom and prepares your proposal may not be the person managing your event on the day. Ask who your main contact will be throughout the planning process and who will be responsible for your function once event day arrives. Knowing exactly whom to call when you need an answer or something changes can make the planning process considerably easier.

And Finally, Ask the Question People Often Forget



After you’ve gone through everything on your list, ask your hotel representative: “Based on the type of event I’m planning, is there anything else you think I should know before I book?”

It’s a simple question, but an experienced event professional may immediately identify something you haven’t considered.

Before You Sign



Choosing a hotel event venue isn’t only about finding the prettiest ballroom or the most attractive package. You’re choosing a partner that will play a significant role in your guests’ experience.

The right venue shouldn’t just look good in photographs. It should have the space, team, policies and resources to help your event run smoothly — from the first vendor arriving for set-up to the final guest heading home.

Because when it comes to wedding planning, the questions you ask before you book can save you from the surprises you don’t want later.

World.title: France and Germany collide over Europe’s industrial future
World.content:
France and Germany are clashing over how far the EU should go to protect European industry — with Paris pushing stronger “Made in Europe” rules and Berlin warning against provoking new trade fights.

Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart look at what that battle says about Europe’s struggle to go green, stay competitive and keep its markets open at the same time.

Then, Brussels is rattled by another wave of shootings. We look at the drug trade behind much of the violence, the Antwerp connection, and the political fight over whether the capital has enough police resources — or whether Belgium’s fragmented system is part of the problem.

And on a much lighter note: Eurostar may finally get some serious competition. New operators are lining up to run through the Channel Tunnel, raising the prospect of more trains — and maybe cheaper tickets — between Brussels and London.

Have you witnessed any of the recent shootings in Brussels? Or has the rise in gun violence changed how you feel about the city? We’d like to hear from you.

World.title: Kemi Badenoch’s Conservatives wish they could be as popular as she is
World.content:
“Kemi is popular. We are trying to promote the rest of the shadow Cabinet to make sure that popularity rubs off on the rest of the party,” said one Badenoch staffer, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record.

So far, it hasn’t worked.

“Badenoch’s success has still failed to translate into any meaningful movement in the polls for her party,” said Scarlett Maguire, founder of independent polling firm Merlin Strategy. “The Conservatives’ mediocre polling numbers, still worse than when they lost the 2024 election, shows the extent to which they have lost trust in their brand.”

New look conference

The party’s first big set piece moment this autumn will come when the Conservative Party meets for its annual conference in Birmingham at the beginning of October.

Badenoch’s performance at last year’s gathering marked the beginning of her transformation as party leader, and her team is hoping to repeat the trick by making this year’s conference more Badenoch-focused.

There will be less policy this year, according to one shadow minister familiar with the plans and also granted anonymity to speak freely.

World.title: Comment “le mur de fer” promis contre l’immigration clandestine à Mayotte s’est enlisé
World.content:
Un plan opérationnel “avant fin 2029, voire 2030”

Un appel d’offres, publié par le ministère de l’Intérieur le 12 août et repéré par POLITICO, dévoile l’ampleur du retard pris par le programme “mur de fer”. Celui-ci vise à recruter un prestataire extérieur, dont le rôle sera justement d’accompagner l’administration dans la mise en place globale du dispositif. Selon le phasage détaillé dans le règlement de consultation de l’appel d’offres, le plan “Uhura wa shaba”, dans toutes ses composantes, pourrait ne pas être pleinement opérationnel avant fin 2029, voire 2030.

En effet, une fois le prestataire sélectionné — fin 2026, au plus tôt, d’après les délais fixés dans ce document — celui-ci devra s’engager dans la préparation, puis l’organisation d’un “dialogue compétitif” pour choisir les industriels susceptibles de fournir les équipements et technologies nécessaires, pour une période de 33 mois au total. S’en suivra la phase “d’exécution” de ce chantier, pendant 51 mois.

“Si l’on fait les comptes, cela renvoie la mise en place du rideau de fer à 2030-2034, ce n’est pas acceptable”, s’agace Saïd Omar Oili. “J’y vois le signe que le gouvernement veut sous-traiter au privé la réflexion globale de la lutte contre l’immigration à Mayotte, un sujet de souveraineté, fustige Estelle Youssouffa. Lancer un tel chantier maintenant, c’est aussi un constat d’échec sur ce qui a été fait ces dernières années”.

Les radars actuels moins performants que les précédents

Dans l’appel d’offres, le ministère reconnaît lui-même que la “couverture des radars installés au début des années 2000 est significativement incomplète”. Celle-ci s’est retrouvée d’autant plus fragilisée par la tempête Chido qui a détruit une large partie des moyens de surveillance et d’interception.

“Des mesures de rattrapage ont été déployées : quatre radars légers et des caméras longue portée ont été achetés”, affirme le ministère de l’Intérieur, sollicité par POLITICO. Mais “ces radars ne disposent toutefois pas d’une portée de détection équivalente à celle des anciens radars”, pointe un rapport sénatorial publié en avril 2026 sur Mayotte et la Réunion. Le programme “rideau de fer […] n’a pas tenu ses promesses”, conclut ce document.

Selon les projections inscrites dans le marché public, le rideau de fer devait rendre “atteignable” l’interpellation de 20 000 étrangers en situation irrégulière en mer par an, contre 4 584 en 2025, d’après le bilan de la préfecture de Mayotte. Cette année-là, un total de 23 421 personnes ont fait l’objet d’un éloignement du territoire.

World.title: Belgium awards scholarships to Palestinian students — but gives them no way to leave Gaza
World.content:
The obstacles facing them are partly procedural, mostly political. POLITICO spoke to four of the scholarship recipients, who were told visas could only be obtained in person at a Belgian diplomatic post, such as the one in Jerusalem. Two of them have been able to successfully obtain visas with the help of lawyers in Belgium, suggesting solutions can be found even in Belgium’s rigid immigration system.

But visas on their own are of little help. None of the students and researchers offered funded places in Belgium currently have any way to actually get there.

In a written statement, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories said it facilitates and encourages the evacuation of students and researchers from Gaza at the request of a third country.

Anneleen Van Bossuyt speaks during a plenary session at the Belgian Federal Parliament in Brussels on June 5, 2025. | Nicolas Maeterlinck/BELGA MAG/AFP via Getty Images

But a spokesperson for Belgium’s foreign ministry, led by Prévot of the centrist Les Engagés party, said there was currently no decision in the coalition government to organize any more evacuations. The department said it was “actively investigating” what could be done to help the students but that any decision on new evacuations would be the “responsibility of the government as a whole.”

Two Belgian government officials, granted anonymity to speak candidly, said that the coalition was divided on just about everything related to Palestine. While Prévot’s foreign ministry says it is looking for solutions, the French-speaking centrist Reformist Movement party (MR), whose leader Georges-Louis Bouchez is known for his pro-Israeli positions , and De Wever’s New Flemish Alliance (N-VA) are said to be against further evacuations.

“It’s common knowledge that if something gets stuck [on this issue], it’s going to be those two parties that are against it,” one of the officials said. MR and De Wever’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

World.title: Andy Burnham has to shape the UK’s social media ban. Australia and France could show him how.
World.content:
MPs return to Parliament next week after the summer break, and Burnham’s government will need to decide how the ban — which is supposed to come into effect in spring — will work.

Australia

Australia was the first country in the world to introduce a social media ban for kids in December last year. Last month, the Australian government published its first wave of findings on the experiences of more than 4,000 children and families since the ban took effect.

The numbers do not show a huge drop in kids accessing social media. The proportion of under-16s holding at least one social media account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.3 percent at the three-month follow-up. Meanwhile, the proportion who reported using a social media platform (with or without an account) fell even less, from 85.9 percent to 81.5 percent.

Australia only requires age-restricted platforms to take “reasonable steps” to prevent under-16s from creating or keeping accounts. Access via logged-out experiences, for example, is permissible.

The rationale is that account-based access — and the data harvesting that comes with it — increases the likelihood of exposure to potentially harmful design features, such as algorithmic suggestions or infinite scroll.

But the U.K. could go further than Australia by casting a wider net to cover both account ownership and access. That could implicate not just the social media platforms, but internet service providers too. The previous Starmer government has already laid the groundwork by handing itself powers, via the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act, to force ISPs to keep kids out.

World.title: Nigel Farage wants to scrap GDPR for the UK
World.content:
“[T]he GDPR has strangled small businesses and tech firms alike in a web of unnecessary regulation ... Ten years after the Brexit referendum we should not still be following ridiculous EU privacy laws that hurt British businesses,” Reform UK MP Robert Jenrick said in a statement.

The EU GDPR provides for a wider set of individual rights around personal data (including the “right to be forgotten”) than New Zealand's Privacy Act does.

However, Reform UK stressed in its press release that following the New Zealand model would preserve the U.K.'s EU data adequacy status, meaning personal data would still be allowed to flow freely between the U.K. and EU.

The European Commission only grants adequacy to countries that provide an essentially equivalent level of data protection to that of the EU.

The U.K. has already diverged from Brussels on privacy laws with the passage of the Data (Use and Access) Act last year, which relaxed some aspects of the U.K. GDPR in a bid to boost economic growth.

World.title: Haze from El Niño-fuelled wildfires threatens health of millions in Indonesia, ministry warns
World.content:
Millions of Indonesians risk health complications from exposure to thick haze covering several cities and towns, officials said on Wednesday, as El Niño-fuelled wildfires wreak havoc on Borneo and Sumatra islands.

 

Indonesia, a vast archipelago, has battled wildfires for weeks that have led to school closures and thousands of people requiring medical treatment, with smoke also reaching neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore.

The health ministry said 3.4 million people living in seven provinces on Borneo and Sumatra were at risk of respiratory infections due to exposure.

In Pekanbaru, the capital of Sumatra's Riau province, thick smog forced the government to shutter dozens of schools as it urged residents to stay indoors.

"The smog gets thicker at night, making Pekanbaru almost like a dead city. A lot of people don't dare go out. And if they do, they wear masks," Abdullah, a 38-year-old entrepreneur, told the AFP news agency.

"My eyes sting so badly. When I go outside, it really feels like breathing in the smoke from freshly burned trash," added the Pekanbaru resident who, like many Indonesians, has one name.

A man stands among houses as haze from wildfires blankets the city of Palembang, 25 August, 2026 AP Photo

In Jambi, also on Sumatra, 31-year-old homemaker Farida said the haze had already affected her family's health.

"My four-year-old child and I have begun coughing so much, especially when we stay outdoors too long," she told AFP. "I have trouble breathing."

The Jambi local government has ordered home schooling for children in kindergarten and elementary school for the remainder of the week.

The health ministry said it had distributed more than 260,000 face masks to residents of the hardest-hit areas.

On Tuesday, President Prabowo Subianto said the government had deployed dozens of helicopters, aircraft, water pumps and thousands of personnel to battle the blazes.

"Now I think it has begun to be brought under control, mitigated. In several places, I believe, and I hope that within the next one to two weeks everything can be resolved," Prabowo said.

Most wildfires are blamed on slash-and-burn practices to clear land for farming.

Police said over the weekend they had arrested 72 people on suspicion of starting fires.

Fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares of land, an area three times the size of the capital Jakarta, the government said last week.

That is already larger than during previous El Niño seasons in 2019 and 2023.

A helicopter conducts a water bombing to extinguish wildfire burning through a peatland field in Danau Lamo, 24 August, 2026 AP Photo

The El Niño weather pattern triggers worldwide changes in winds, atmospheric pressure and rainfall.

Malaysia said it stood ready to help put out fires.

Poor air quality in Malaysia's Sarawak state, on Borneo island which it shares with Indonesia and Brunei, led to nearly 600 schools being closed last week.

At one point on Wednesday morning, tracker IQ Air ranked the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur second-most polluted city globally.

World.title: More than 50 kidnapped as violent gang attack in Haiti leaves at least 47 dead
World.content:
At least 47 people were killed and more than 50 kidnapped after armed men attacked a community near Haiti’s capital earlier this week, the United Nations (UN) said on Tuesday.

 

The assault is believed to be one of Haiti’s largest mass kidnappings in recent years.

Kenscoff resident Marc Paul, 42, said his brother, stepmother, stepfather and two cousins were among those kidnapped. His 16-year-old niece was also abducted and raped before managing to escape and reunite with him.

“I had to run over bodies,” Paul said, recalling his escape from the attack. “I can’t sleep knowing all these people died." Paul and his family had already lost their home to a previous gang attack in January 2025.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack, saying 22 of the victims were reportedly executed in a church compound where they had sought shelter.

“The relentless gang attacks on communities and the loss of lives underscore the alarming security conditions in Haiti,” he said.

Men transport an empty coffin on a motorcycle in the Kenscoff neighborhood of Port-au-Prince., Haiti, Tuesday, 25 Aug, 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All right reserved

Haitians demand greater police protection

The attack has raised fresh concerns over security in Haiti, shattering hopes that conditions in the Caribbean country were improving.

Some survivors accused the government of not providing enough protection prior to the attack, with Haiti’s National Police rejecting those accusations.

“This is a message to the government and the police that their claims of protection do not match reality,” said the head of the Haiti Observatory at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, Romain Le Cour.

“The gangs are saying: when we choose to attack, we can, and we will succeed.”

Le Cour added that if police and armoured vehicles were indeed stationed in Kenscoff prior to the attack, then the assertion is concerning: “You let the gangs come in even if you had everything in place?”

Haiti’s National Police said on Tuesday that an investigation had been ordered into the attack to determine whether there had been “complicity or negligence.”

Additional specialised units were also deployed to the area, with police saying they had an “obligation to protect the civilian population.”

A long-running gang violence crisis

The first major attack on Kenscoff occurred in January 2025 and since then, there have been sporadic attacks in the mountains surrounding the town centre. Sunday’s assault was the largest to date.

Armed groups control an estimated 70% of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, as well as large areas of the country’s central region and beyond.

Gang violence has displaced a record 1.5 million people across Haiti, while more than 3,050 people were killed between January and June, according to UN figures released on Tuesday.

Nearly 800 cases of rape were reported between April and June, 87% of which were gang rapes. At least 81 people were also kidnapped during the same period, the UN said.

The number of kidnappings reported from April to June represents a more than 40% increase compared with the previous quarter.

World.title: Anthropic IPO: Five things to know before its Wall Street debut
World.content:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, is expected to go public within weeksin a listing that could eclipse the record set by SpaceX’s Wall Street debut in June.

 

Here are five things to know about the company:

Built by former OpenAI executives

Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives who believed that the potential risks posed by artificial intelligence were not being taken seriously enough.

The company — whose name means, somewhat paradoxically, “relating to human beings” — is led by chief executive and co-founder Dario Amodei, a San Francisco native with a doctorate in biophysics from Princeton University, an unusual background among leading technology executives, many of whom studied computer science.

His sister, Daniela, is also a co-founder and the company’s president. Anthropic has 5,000 employees, according to PitchBook.

From upstart to leading contender

Until this year, Anthropic was widely seen as trailing OpenAI, which burst onto the scene with ChatGPT in November 2022, transforming the technology industry and triggering an AI arms race.

But while OpenAI expanded into areas ranging from video generation to web browsers, Anthropic pursued a narrower strategy, focusing on artificial intelligence tools for software developers and businesses.

That strategy has paid off spectacularly: coding is one of the relatively few artificial intelligence services for which customers have proved willing to pay substantial sums.

Claude Code, its assistant for developers, has become one of the company’s most popular products, helping to push Anthropic’s annual revenue rate above $65bn (€55.6bn).

Only a small proportion of ChatGPT users, meanwhile, pay a subscription fee, while OpenAI has reportedly scaled back work on video generation and other projects.

Trump administration clashes with Anthropic

The momentum comes despite severe political headwinds, with Anthropic at loggerheads with the Trump administration — a dispute that could give investors pause.

In March, the government terminated its contracts with Anthropic and designated the company a supply-chain risk after it refused to give the military unfettered access to its artificial intelligence models.

Anthropic described the move as unconstitutional retaliation and launched legal action against the US government. The dispute could take years to resolve.

The White House has also objected to Amodei’s repeated warnings about the dangers of artificial intelligence — including its potential impact on jobs — and his calls to regulate the technology in a similar way to airlines or banks.

Amodei is also linked to effective altruism, a philosophy of targeted charitable giving scorned by conservatives in Silicon Valley and Washington.

Huge sums still needed

Like OpenAI, Anthropic requires vast amounts of computing power and infrastructure to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence models and remain ahead of its competitors, amid concerns that China could catch up.

Both companies have raised money at unprecedented levels, with Anthropic valued at $965bn (€829bn) after raising $65bn (€55.8bn) in May.

As the sums involved grow beyond the capacity of many venture-capital investors and sovereign wealth funds, a public listing would give Anthropic access to a much larger pool of capital. But it would also expose the company to greater scrutiny over whether its vision for the artificial intelligence revolution can produce a sustainable business.

OpenAI, after initially considering a listing this year, is now reportedly considering waiting until 2027.

Investors must stomach heavy losses

According to Bloomberg, Anthropic aims to raise more than the $75bn (€64.3bn) secured by SpaceX in its record June IPO, excluding the over-allotment option exercised later.

SpaceX, which absorbed Musk’s artificial intelligence start-up xAI before going public, made its listing a partial bet on artificial intelligence as well as space technology. Its shares skyrocketed initially before coming back down to earth, and now sit at about their $135 offering price.

Anthropic's investors will likewise have to stomach huge losses for the foreseeable future.

The company lost almost $42bn (€36bn) in 2025, according to US media reports, and is likely to continue burning through cash for years.

To attract investors, Anthropic is expected to argue that it is targeting a total addressable market worth more than $30tn (€25.7tn), according to the Wall Street Journal. This refers to its estimate of the potential market available to the company, not its own expected revenue.

World.title: Row over weight of half a loaf leaves German baker with €15,000 bill
World.content:
A baker in Bavaria who says he had to spend €15,000 on new scales after a row with a customer over half a loaf of bread has made headlines across Germany.

 

The dispute took place in Pfaffenhofen an der Ilm, a town north of Munich, where baker Matthias Breitner has for decades sold half loaves to customers who do not want to buy a whole one.

The dispute started by email

As first reported by Bild and RTL, the row began when a customer emailed to complain after weighing a half loaf at home and discovering it was 10 grams lighter than half the stated weight of a full loaf.

“Sometimes you win, sometimes you lose. Next time it will surely be ten grams more,” Breitner replied.

The customer subsequently contacted the authorities, and the local weights and measures office told Breitner he could no longer sell half loaves without weighing them individually.

An unhappy customer picks a fight over 10 grams of bread Symbolbild - AP Photo

The rules stem from Germany's Pre-packaging Ordinance (Fertigpackungsverordnung), which implements EU requirements as well as additional national provisions.

Breitner says he does not want to sell pre-packaged half loaves, meaning portions cut for customers must instead be weighed at the point of sale.

As a result, he says he had to install new scales across his bakeries at a total cost of around €15,000.

Breitner said some other bakeries had stopped selling half loaves because they feared similar complaints and problems with weights and measures authorities.

German courts report rise in cases

Separately, German courts have reported a sharp increase in cases, with some officials suggesting that artificial intelligence is making it easier for people to prepare lengthy legal submissions.

According to reports by Tagesschau and the Süddeutsche Zeitung, more than 16,000 cases had been filed with the Berlin Labour Court by August — roughly as many as it would normally receive in an entire year.

Officials have cited the growing use of AI tools, including ChatGPT and Gemini, as one possible factor behind the increase, because they allow users to produce lengthy legal documents quickly.

However, there is no evidence that AI played any role in the complaint against Breitner's bakery.

World.title: The world’s 10 best cities for nightlife have been revealed – and only three are in Europe
World.content:
Bangkok has just been named the world’s best city for nightlife in 2026.

 

The Thai capital topped the ranking from Time Out following a survey of more than 24,000 local residents across 150 cities worldwide.

City dwellers were asked about things like how affordable night outs are, and if a city feels lively, diverse and safe after dark.

A solid 73% of Bangkok residents rated their city’s nightlife as good or amazing, while Time Out’s experts praised its variety, with everything from rooftop spots and dive bars.

Topping the list on the continent with second place overall is Berlin, which should come as no surprise to anyone that has experienced the clubbing scene there.

The magazine praised the city for “continuing to set the benchmark for nightlife”, with a further 78% of locals rating it highly.

Picking up third place, New York City was praised for its ever-evolving scene that keeps things exciting, whether you’re after a casual glass of wine or a late-night warehouse rave.

The top five was rounded out by Melbourne in Australia, and São Paulo in Brazil.

How Europe fared in the nightlife ranking

Aside from Berlin, two other European cities made it into the top 10 – Brighton in eighth, and Amsterdam in 10th.

UK seaside resort Brighton received the highest community score, with 84% of locals saying it’s easy to meet people and feel part of the city's community, and tied second with New York as the cities most likely to be described as both “lively” and “diverse and inclusive”. The city was also praised for its LGBTQ+ scene.

Amsterdam earned its place thanks to its bustling nightlife scene in the city centre and beyond, with Time Out highlighting WorldPride 2026 as helping to cement the Dutch capital’s reputation as “one of Europe's most welcoming and inclusive places to go out”.

“A good night out is no longer defined by one type of venue; in 2026, street parties and rooftop raves are bigger than ever, while locals are no longer flocking to one or two big-name venues, instead heading to nightlife districts where bar-hopping is the name of the game,” Grace Beard, travel editor at Time Out, said.

“What makes the cities on this list so special is their ability to adapt to our changing nightlife habits. From over-30s parties to speakeasies and listening bars, every city offers unforgettable experiences for every kind of night out and every kind of person. That's exactly what great city life should look like.”

World.title: Epstein accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell loses 'frivolous' bid to overturn US conviction
World.content:
A US federal judge has rejected a bid by Ghislaine Maxwell, a key accomplice of notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, to throw out her conviction on sex trafficking charges.

 

Maxwell, 64, has been sentenced to 20 years in prison and is the only person convicted of a crime in connection with Epstein, who died in a New York jail cell in 2019 while awaiting his own trial.

In his ruling, Judge Paul Engelmayer said that Maxwell's claims that her constitutional rights at trial and sentencing were violated "are all meritless and all or almost all are frivolous."

"Nearly all its claims are procedurally barred; the overwhelming testimonial and documentary evidence adduced at trial conclusively established her guilt; and her petition's claims are demonstrably meritless, and generally based on speculation, distortions, and/or outright falsehoods," Engelmayer wrote.

Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of supplying underage girls to Epstein, whose ties to powerful business executives, politicians, celebrities and academics have fuelled years of scrutiny and conspiracy theories.

Audrey Strauss, acting US attorney for the Southern District of New York, points to a photo of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell in New York, 2 July, 2020 AP Photo

Under a new law passed last year, President Donald Trump's administration released vast troves of investigative files relating to Epstein, drawing huge public attention to the case.

High-profile figures including Britain's former Prince Andrew have been publicly disgraced for their associations with Epstein.

In February, Maxwell was subpoenaed by the House Oversight Committee to discuss her relations with Epstein but refused to answer any questions. Her lawyer stated she would only speak if Trump granted her clemency.

Last October, the US Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal by Maxwell of her sex trafficking conviction.

Trump, who also had a years-long relationship with Epstein, initially opposed releasing the so-called Epstein files, prompting accusations of a cover-up that dogged his first year back in office.

The Republican has denied any link to Epstein's crimes.

World.title: Higher education: Renting a room in Lisbon costs over €500 as demand outstrips supply
World.content:
September marks the start of the new academic year, bringing new challenges for thousands of Portuguese students. For those entering higher education, one of the toughest begins straight away: trying to find somewhere to live.

 

According to data from the Directorate-General for Higher Education (DGES), 49,991 students were placed in the first phase of the National Access Competition for Higher Education, 6,092 more than in the previous year, corresponding to an increase of 13.9%.

Within this group, thousands are forced to leave their parents' home to continue their studies at a university in another city. The figures appear to confirm this trend: according to Idealista, the property sales and lettings portal, demand for rooms rose by 27% in the second quarter of 2026.

According to the platform, Beja was the market with the sharpest surge in demand, recording "an increase of 160% year on year". Next came Coimbra (120%) and Porto (104%), "two of the country's largest markets, where demand more than doubled in a year". The portal also identifies Évora, Viseu and Bragança as having "very significant increases".

The Portuguese capital, Lisbon, recorded a rise of 17 per cent in demand for rooms to rent.

Setúbal, Vila Real, Faro, Braga, Castelo Branco and Portalegre were the only cities where demand fell compared with the previous year.

Demand increased but supply did not keep up: according to Idealista, the number of rooms on the market fell by 11%.

"Porto (-43%) and Coimbra (-48%) saw the largest contractions in supply — precisely two of the markets where demand more than doubled, which is increasing the pressure on prices in these cities," the platform said in a statement.

Évora, Lisbon and Leiria also saw supply decline.

Demand rises but prices remain relatively stable

According to the platform, "room rents increased in 13 of the 20 municipalities analysed", with the biggest rises recorded in Funchal and Vila Real.

For those coming to Lisbon to study, the challenge goes even further than simply finding a room: the Portuguese capital remains the country's most expensive city for room rentals, "with median prices of around 550 euros a month".

Next come Funchal, at 500 euros per month, Porto, at 450 euros, Ponta Delgada, at 430 euros, and Faro rounding out the top five with a median price of 420 euros.

Rooms costing up to 300 euros can only be found in Leiria, Vila Real, Beja, Viseu, Castelo Branco and Portalegre. Guarda and Bragança are the most affordable cities, at 210 and 220 euros respectively.

By way of comparison, the August report published last year by the Student Housing Observatory (source in Portuguese) indicated that renting a room in Lisbon had an average price of 500 euros, with the highest price found at 722 euros. The same report showed that, over the same period, renting a room anywhere in the country cost an average of 416 euros.

Students are not the only ones renting rooms

Although university students are one of the main drivers of the rental market, the country's current reality means they are not the only ones looking for rooms.

At a time when rents are rising and it is becoming increasingly difficult to buy a home, this tough equation is also pushing up demand for rooms among the wider population, particularly young people of working age.

"The data published in this analysis show that the rental of rooms is not a housing option only for students, but is also becoming the option chosen by young people in their first years in the labour market and in some cases even later," the statement reads.

"The current reality of the Portuguese rental market in major cities means that it is difficult for many single or divorced people to bear the cost of a home, making the rental of a room the most advantageous option" - and, very often, the only one.

Student residences cannot keep up with demand

Renting a room on the private market is one option for those starting their studies, but there are also public and private student residences, although these are too few to meet demand.

The latest data from the Purpose Built Student Accommodation (PBSA) report by property consultancy CBRE showed that there are 27,700 beds in public and private student residences. Last academic year there were 147,000 Portuguese students living away from home, plus 80,000 foreign students, with the figures pointing to a shortfall of more than 100,000 beds in student residences.

In June 2026, the National Plan for Accommodation in Higher Education (PNAES) estimated the supply of accommodation for higher education students at 17,974 beds (source in Portuguese) in residences belonging to public higher education institutions.

To help young people now starting their search for a room, DECO Proteste has launched a platform (source in Portuguese) that allows students to find the accommodation offered by higher education institutions and to see which municipalities in the country provide student accommodation or support programmes for students living away from home.

World.title: NYC: Mamdani opposes rally with Hindu nationalist leader
World.content:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani voiced opposition to an upcoming event featuring RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, calling the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" while acknowledging the city can't block a private event.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it.

Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK.

What did Mamdani say?

When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event."

Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from."

His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India."

"It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision."

Who is organizing the event?

The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity.

Bhagwat is visiting several countries in a bid to reform the RSS's global perception [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled.

"Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity."

What is the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh and how is it related to PM Modi?

The RSS is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.

The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.

In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.

100 years of the Hindu nationalist RSS movement To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Rights organizations decry rise in abuses against religious minorities

However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."

United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.

India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities.

The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.

World.title: Pakistan: Islamabad hospital fire kills at least 14 infants
World.content:
A fire broke out in the third floor of a maternity ward in Islamabad. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has called for an immediate investigation into the tragedy.

A least 14 infants were killed after a fire broke out at the maternity ward of a hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Wednesday.

"A fire broke out on the third floor of the MCH Ward at PIMS Hospital," the district office of Islamabad said, referring to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences.

The blaze broke out at around 6:45 a.m. (0145 UTC) when an air conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery, rescuers said.

Distraught parents gathered outside the hospital Image: Aamir Qureshi/AFP

Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time, adding that one was rescued.

Outside the hospital, a nurse read out the names of babies who had perished as their families gathered around.

"I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," one father told the AFP news agency.

"My wife was in the ward. They took everyone out. We were sitting on the road waiting for help."

Investigation underway

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

"A tragedy involving children is an irreparable loss," he said in a statement.

"Those ​responsible should be identified, and ​the strictest action should be taken."

The incident is one of the deadliest hospital fires in recent memory in Pakistan, where healthcare is subsidized but public hospitals are often are under-resourced and overburdened.

World.title: Despite international bans, landmines are back in force
World.content:
It was considered a major achievement when most countries in the world agreed to ban anti-personnel mines in the 1990s. But given the Russia-Ukraine war, the situation in Europe is changing.

Raheela Bibi was outside playing with her siblings when a landmine exploded. It was August 2020 and she was 12, living in Pakistan. Both her hands were amputated after the incident. Her sister suffered a serious leg injury, while her brother's eye was hurt. Bibi told DW in 2023 that though it was extremely difficult for her to do her homework, she was determined to continue with her education.

In 2025, more than 5,000 people, mainly civilians, were killed or injured by landmines or unexploded ordnance according to a preliminary analysis by the NGO Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor. In South Sudan, 90% of the victims last year were children.

Landmines are actually designed to injure adults not kill them. This is because an injured soldier is more of a strain on an enemy country's resources than a dead soldier. But in peacetime, landmines continue to pose a deadly threat not only to soldiers but to civilians and particularly children, who often die.

Decades after the brutal conflicts from 1991 to 2001 that were Yugoslav wars, people continue to be killed and injured by landmines in former Yugoslavia, particularly Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Landmines are not designed to kill adults but to maim them Image: Mast Irham/dpa/picture alliance

Ottawa Treaty in force since 1999

In 1999, there were approximately 25,000 landmine casualties per year. This prompted pressure to ban the use of anti-personnel landmines. In 1997, representatives from more than 120 countries signed the Ottawa Treaty, which became legally binding in 1999. In total, 166 countries ratified the treaty, but not China, India, Russia or the US.

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty. Ukraine has also withdrawn though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.

"This is a dangerous precedent that European states, of all countries, have set," Simone Wisotzki from the Frankfurt-based Leibniz Peace Research Institute (PRIF) told DW. "Other parties to the Ottawa Treaty, which could also face equally extreme situations in times of conflict, could take the same step. We would then have to deal with more withdrawals, which would, of course, undermine the legitimacy of the entire treaty."

Last year, Ukraine withdrew from the treaty and justified the move citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines in Ukrainian territory. "We cannot remain bound under conditions when the enemy has no restrictions," said Roman Kostenko, the secretary of the Ukrainian parliament's committee on national security, defense and intelligence.

If a country isn't at war, its withdrawal from the Ottawa Treaty is supposed to take effect six months after its announcement. If it is at war, however, withdrawal should take effect only after a peace treaty has been signed. Despite the legal uncertainty, Ukraine is reportedly already using mines, albeit on a much smaller scale than Russia.

A quarter of Ukraine affected by landmines

According the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS), as of mid-2025 approximately 25% of Ukraine was affected by landmines and explosive ordnance. This applied not only to Ukrainian-controlled territories but also to Russian-occupied areas in the east and southeast of the country.

"Since February 2022, over 1,150 civilians have been killed or injured by landmines and explosive remnants of war (ERW)," UNMAS writes on its website, pointing out that the cost of full demining is estimated at just under $35 billion (approx. €30 billion) over 10 years.

Poland, Finland (which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine), Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, which have all suffered from Russian aggression and occupation in the past, also decided to withdraw from the Ottawa Treaty last year.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has stated on several occasions that his country wants to be able to mine its eastern borders with Russia very quickly if need be. The state-owned Polish defense company Belma has been contracted to produce anti-personnel mines in large quantities. Lithuania has also announced that it will resume the manufacture and purchase of landmines.

The Finnish military has said that if mines are necessary, they should be laid responsibly, accurate maps of their position must be created and there should be precise plans for demining.

Wisotzki from PRIF said that this is progress compared to the past but that modern anti-personnel mines often have integrated sensors and smart technologies that make it difficult to remove and destroy the mines.

"That's why I'm very critical of this and say that even new technologies present problems that, in turn, make mine clearance more difficult. In practice, mines are always laid in areas that are also used by civilians. They then remain in those territories and then injure civilians disproportionately."

In its reports, the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor has pointed out that while mines that were laid during past conflicts continued to be cleared, mines continue to be laid in Ukraine or in other countries such as Myanmar.

Decades after conflicts people continue to demine territories, such as here in Cambodia Image: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP

Less arms control in the world

This comes at a time when there is increasingly less arms control. In the past few years, three major agreements between the United States and Russia have expired or been terminated: the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty that banned all nuclear and conventional ground-launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and missile launchers with intermediate range; the New Start Treaty which is a nuclear arms reduction treaty; and the Treaty on Open Skies, which set out the framework for a regime of observation flights over the territory of participating states.

In 2023, Russia's withdrawal also effectively put an end to the CFE treaty that aimed to create a secure and stable balance of conventional armed forces in Europe and to remove the capability to launch surprise attacks or large-scale offensives

"Humanitarian arms control — which includes the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention — was in effect the only area that could still be said to be working," Wisotzki said. "And that is no longer the case."

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: US military kills 4 in Caribbean boat strike
World.content:
The US military killed four people in a strike on a suspected drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean, the latest in a campaign that has killed more than 200 people and drawn condemnation from rights groups.

The US military struck a boat in the Caribbean Sea on Tuesday, killing four people, US Southern Command said.

It's the latest action in a nearly yearlong controversial campaign by President Donald Trump's administration targeting alleged drug traffickers in Latin America.

What do we know about the latest US strike in the Caribbean?

"Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southern Command said in a post on X, accompanied by a video showing what appeared to be a boat in motion, followed by a flash.

The command did not identify those killed or give a precise location, saying only that the boat was operating along established smuggling routes in the Caribbean.

No evidence was released showing the vessel carried drugs.

Fishers in Colombia worry as US strikes alleged drug boats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to a count by AP news agency, the strike brings the death toll to at least 227 people across 68 strikes since the campaign began about a year ago. Reuters news agency, tracking Caribbean and Eastern Pacific strikes together, put the total above 210.

Tuesday's strike followed another one in the Eastern Pacific over the weekend that killed two people. The weekend strike was the first by the US military in more than two months.

Rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and independent United Nations investigators, say the strikes violate international law and amount to extrajudicial killings.

Why is the US conducting these strikes?

Trump says the United States is engaged in an "armed conflict" with drug cartels operating in the region and has framed the strikes as necessary to clamp down on the drug trade and its toll on American lives. But his administration has not made public the evidence behind its claims that those killed were trafficking narcotics.

The campaign is also expanding, with Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth saying this month that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to allow joint US military operations against criminal groups within their borders. Guatemala has disputed that any such agreement was reached.

Ecuador began similar joint operations with the US in March.

World.title: China: Dissident artist jailed for satirical Mao sculptures
World.content:
Sculptor Gao Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs." His supporters have called for his immediate release.

A court in China has reportedly sentenced a dissident artist to three years in jail for sculptures which satirized former Chinese revolutionary leader Mao Zedong.

Sculptor Gao Zhen, 70, became famous in the 2000s for addressing sensitive topics in China such as the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution or the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre through artworks he produced with his younger brother Gao Qiang.

Zhen, who is based in New York, was arrested during a visit to Beijing in August 2024. He was tried this year ⁠in a ⁠one-day behind-closed-doors trial and found guilty of "infringing upon the reputation of heroes."

"We feel outraged," Gao's wife Zhao Yaliang told the Reuters news agency. "Ever since I learned of the ​verdict, I haven't been able to recover from it. It's devastating."

Zhao also said she and her son, who is a US citizen, had been barred from leaving China since Zhen's detention two years ago.

Which Mao sculptures were deemed illegal?

Zhen was charged under China's "Law on the Protection ⁠of Heroes ​and Martyrs," legislation which came into effect in 2018 and was strengthened in ​2021.

The artworks found to have broken the law, however, date to 2005 and 2009, according to Shane Yi, a researcher at Chinese Human Rights Defenders who has been advocating for Gao's case.

"The court has now sentenced him to three years ... for artwork he made as far back as 2005, some 16 years before the law he was charged under even existed," Yi told Reuters, calling the punishment "a very clear case of a violation of a person's freedom of expression."

The artworks in question are reported to be "Mao's Guilt," a 2009 bronze statue of the former leader kneeling remorsefully, and the "Miss Mao" series of caricatures which depict Mao with breasts and a Pinocchio-like nose.

Calls for Zhen to be released

"No artist should face criminal punishment for creating work that challenges official narratives or encourages critical reflection on history," Amnesty's China Director Sarah Brooks told the Associated Press.

"The lengthy pre-trial detention and, ultimately, decision to convict Gao Zhen and sentence him to the maximum three-year prison term under this offense illustrate the authorities' determination to deter others from engaging in independent artistic expression."

Researcher Yi said: "The only outcome that respects Gao Zhen's rights is his immediate, unconditional release."

There has as yet been no official statement from the court.
