World.title: Baku Stock Exchange nearing completion of integration with Tabadul platform
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Baku Stock Exchange (BSE) is continuing technical integration and testing for the Tabadul platform to expand access to regional markets.

BSE Board Chairman Ruslan Khalilov told Trend’s correspondent this in response to a question.

He said the project involves testing a mechanism that would allow local Azerbaijani brokerage companies to connect directly to the stock markets of partner countries through Tabadul.

According to the BSE representative, the project’s basic testing is expected to be fully completed by the end of the year.

“The first official trading operation (‘Go Live’) is targeted for early next year. At the same time, the relevant adjustments to the legislative framework are planned to enable the project to operate at full capacity and facilitate remote brokerage mechanisms,” he said.

World.title: BSE chairman highlights importance of new functionality for secondary bond market
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 26. Baku Stock Exchange (BSE) continues work to automate trading operations in the secondary bond market, with the launch of the new functionality planned by the end of the year.

BSE Board Chairman Ruslan Khalilov told Trend’s correspondent, in response to a question, that the new functionality will allow investors to buy and sell bonds on the secondary market automatically through their brokers.

“Until now, in both the primary and secondary bond markets, each investor has had to approach a brokerage company and place an order. The brokerage company then buys or sells the required amount of bonds based on that order. What we are talking about is simply automating the same operation. The new functionality in the exchange trading system will allow each investor to automatically buy and sell bonds traded on the secondary market through a broker,” Khalilov said.

According to him, the rules for calculating the “clean price” and “dirty price” of bonds under the new system have also been agreed with market participants.

“We discussed these issues with members of the Azerbaijan Capital Market Association and brokerage companies. The negotiations have now been completed. Based on the common rules agreed upon by market participants, we have commissioned a vendor company to develop the functionality. Its development, full testing and delivery will take about three months. We plan to have it delivered by the end of the year,” the BSE chairman said.

Khalilov also said that trading volumes of shares on the secondary market are at a satisfactory level.

“Trading is taking place on the secondary market. In the ‘Market Watch’ section, you can see the secondary-market volumes for both PASHA Bank and International Bank of Azerbaijan. Currently, the turnover ratio of the secondary market relative to free-float shares is by no means low. It is quite good. Market-making organizations are also supporting this,” he said.

The BSE chairman also noted growing interest from foreign companies in Azerbaijan’s capital market.

“Recently, investor demand relative to placement volumes has increased significantly compared with previous years. For example, if you compare bond issuances by other banks with Ziraat Bank’s issuances in previous years, in earlier periods only 10-15 investors, mostly institutional ones, showed interest in such volumes. The measures being implemented in automation, digitalization and financial literacy are beginning to produce results. There is considerable interest,” Khalilov said.

According to him, this interest is also beginning to be reflected on the issuer side.

“Foreign companies are showing interest in the Azerbaijani market and are contacting us. For now, this is at the information exchange and preparation stage. However, there are no companies that have submitted a specific application yet,” the BSE chairman said.

World.title: Video shows antisemitic road rage abuse in Adelaide's CBD
World.content:
The Anti Defamation Commission says a Jewish woman visiting Adelaide was subjected to antisemitic abuse on her first day in the city.

In a video released by the commission, people in a car driving on Hutt St in the city appear to be yelled at by someone in another car.

"Come and face me you f***ing gutless c***. You're a Jew aren't you? You're a f***ing Jew aren't you?" the man can be heard yelling in the video.

The car then speeds away, using the right turn lane to cut in front of traffic heading north.

While only a short clip of the interaction has been made public, Anti Defamation Commission chairman Dvir Abramovich said the abuse came "out of the blue".

"One theory is something enraged him about the car or about traffic," Dr Abramovich said.

"He saw those two individuals and he exploded into rage using that word Jew but there was no context, there was no interaction, there was no engagement between the Jewish passengers in that car and that individual."

The video captured an incident on Hutt Street, in Adelaide's CBD. (Supplied: Anti-Defamation Commission )

Dr Abramovich said the woman lives in Melbourne and was visiting another Jewish person in Adelaide, who was also in the car, to see if the city would be a good place to relocate as she feared what he said was rising antisemitism in Melbourne.

"The irony here is unbelievable. Here you have an Israeli-Jewish woman who wants to relocate from Melbourne," he said.

"She arrives in Adelaide, on her first day she's exposed to Jew hatred of the worst level."

Dr Abramovich said the pair were considering reporting the man to police, and had recorded his number plate.

SA Police said it had so far not received any formal report relating to the footage.

"SAPOL encourage the owner of the footage to contact police by attending at their nearest police station and providing their details and a copy of the footage," a spokesperson said.

"We also encourage those involved to report the matter to police."

World.title: Bus company fined $650k over deadly Greta crash
World.content:
Families and survivors of a bus crash which claimed 10 lives have described the lasting impacts of the tragedy as the bus company was fined $650,000 for employing a drug-impaired driver.

Brett Andrew Button, 61, is serving a maximum of 32 years in jail for the Greta bus crash in 2023.

Separately, Linq Buslines and its directors Christopher Fogg and Anthony Royle have pleaded guilty to charges brought by the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator.

They admitted to failing in their duty of care in relation to risks linked to overspeeding, fatigue and the employment of drug-impaired drivers.

Christopher Fogg pleaded guilty to breaching heavy vehicle law. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

Sentencing proceedings have been held in Gosford Local Court this week.

Judge Kirralee Perry today said "no amount would take away the pain" of families affected.

She agreed with prosecutor Georgia Lewer that Linq Buslines recruited a man who put the community at risk.

"The offender [Linq Buslines] recruited a man [Brett Button] who had been stood down from a previous employer with an opioid dependency and posed a significant risk," Judge Perry said.

The court heard the only reference check was by text message, with a former boss calling Button a "good bloke".

Linq Buslines has ceased operating. (ABC Newcastle: Romy Stephens)

The text message exchange also described bus drivers as "steering wheel attendants", a term that drew the ire of Judge Perry.

"It is flippant at best and it is wholly inappropriate in terms as being used as a way to provide a reference check for somebody who is going to be put in charge of driving a heavy vehicle," she said.

She fined Linq Buslines a total of $650,000.

Directors Mr Fogg and Mr Royle faced a maximum fine of $59,000 for their offence related to overspeeding.

Judge Perry said the offending related to seven drivers who oversped on 12 occasions.

"The company and directors fell short in ensuring they complied with their duty," she said.

The judge fined Mr Royle and Mr Royle $12,000 each and said the offending was at the "lower end" of the range.

She declined a request not to record a conviction for both men.

Anthony Royle pleaded guilty to breaching heavy vehicle law. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

She said Mr Royle was "in shock and overwhelmed with sorrow and so gutted by the incident".

The judge said Mr Fogg had also shown remorse.

"He has had a strong stress response to the crash and subsequently over the past three years he has been preoccupied by the sheer scale of the loss of life," she said.

Judge Perry expressed her sympathies to families affected by the "devastating crash" throughout proceedings.

Linq Buslines is no longer trading after bus contracts were not renewed and accreditation was terminated in March.

Victims speak

Families and survivors of the crash delivered emotional victim impact statements in court today.

Sharyn Junkeer suffered horrific injuries in the crash and travelled to Gosford from Melbourne to deliver her statement.

"It looks like a shark has taken a bite out of my thigh and hip, leaving me with a hideous disfigurement," she said.

Ms Junkeer choked back tears describing the impact of the crash in which she had previously said she thought she would die.

Jason and Sharyn Junkeer choked back tears describing the moment their lives changed. (ABC News)

"Every day I have to live with the knowledge that I survived this tragedy while so many others did not," Ms Junkeer said.

Her husband Jason Junkeer also gave a statement and paused at times while delivering it.

"It's been three years now and I have not got better," he said.

"I still live with chronic pain, a brain injury, PTSD and depression."

Matt and Leanne Mullen gave victim impact statements. (ABC News)

Family travel to deliver statements

Matt and Leanne Mullen travelled to Gosford Courthouse from Singleton to deliver their addresses, both describing crippling grief.

Their daughter Rebecca, a young doctor, died that night at Greta, along with nine others.

"The impact on the family is that has broken me," Mr Mullen said.

" I can still see the bus on its side. I wake up to it often at night. "

He told the court he was glad Mr and Mrs Junkeer, who he previously did not know, survived the crash.

Mrs Mullen spoke of the daily impact losing a daughter has had on her life.

"That night has changed my daily interactions with my community," she said.

"Life is no longer simple or carefree in the community that I love."

World.title: Melbourne attack accused tells court 'at least they're both still breathing'
World.content:
The man charged over an apparently random attack on a woman and her son in Melbourne's CBD has told a court his humanity remained intact because the pair survived the incident.

A 10-year-old child was allegedly punched by a stranger outside the police station on Spencer Street on Tuesday.

The same man then allegedly repeatedly stabbed the boy's mother with a pair of scissors.

Bystanders restrained a 27-year-old man until police arrived.

The woman and her son were both taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Police talk to a woman and her son after the alleged random attack on Spencer Street in Melbourne. (Supplied)

Jerry Sowood was charged with several offences including intentionally causing injury and conduct endangering life.

The Sunshine West man fronted the Melbourne Magistrates Court via video link on Wednesday afternoon, appearing to describe details of the incident when the magistrate began asking about health issues that might affect his time in custody.

"There's no need to hide it," he said.

"At least they're both still breathing, so I kept my humanity intact."

He appeared to refuse an offer of a nurse visit and, when asked if he took any regular medications, said: "I was in a mental state of mind."

The court heard it was the man's first time in custody.

A lawyer told the court he was not given bail instructions when he visited Mr Sowood.

No application was made.

Mr Sowood will return to court in November.

World.title: Woman ordered to pay $27k after kittens found in freezer
World.content:
A Tasmanian woman has been ordered to pay the RSPCA almost $30,000, after almost 70 cats were found living in "squalid" conditions and a dozen kittens were found dead in her freezer.

WARNING: This story contains details and images depicting the mistreatment of animals which may cause distress

Karen Maree Blake, 67, pleaded guilty to one count of management of animals, and 21 counts of cruelty to animals, in March.

In the Hobart Magistrates Court on Wednesday, prosecutor Robert Fisher told the court that RSPCA inspectors attended Blake's Midway Point home in December 2024 due to a complaint about overbreeding and the living conditions of her cats.

"Inspectors were met with a powerful smell of urine, faeces and ammonia," Mx Fisher said.

" The property was in a state of squalor, rubbish and faeces on every surface. "

Karen Blake was sentenced to six months imprisonment, wholly suspended for four years — meaning she will not serve time unless she commits another offence. (Supplied: RSPCA Tasmania)

Twelve kittens were found dead in her freezer, and several kittens were found decomposing around the house.

In total, 69 cats and two dogs were surrendered or seized from her property by the RSPCA following that inspection.

Years of complaints

Mx Fisher told the court that the RSPCA had attended Blake's property several times between 2017 and 2024 due to complaints by the public, prompted by the smells and noises coming from her property.

Blake was a registered cat breeder at the time, but Ms Blake's defence lawyer, Hope Cooper, told the court she had not sold cats for "quite some time".

Karen Blake was a registered cat breeder, though her defence lawyer said she hadn't sold any for "quite some time". (Supplied: RSPCA Tasmania)

Ms Cooper said her client had suffered from several mental health issues, including anxiety, depression and agoraphobia, and has a physical illness which causes her pain, fatigue and sensory issues.

"She became overwhelmed in her life in 2017 due to the passing of her father and caring for her mother," she said.

Ms Cooper said Blake had cooperated with authorities and was glad that someone reported her situation.

" She was frozen in her own situation and wasn't able to reach out for help. "

The RSPCA says veterinary examinations of the cats identified a range of welfare conditions. (Supplied: RSPCA Tasmania)

Magistrate Chris Webster told the court this was a "very serious" example of cruelty to animals.

"There was a long history where you were told you weren't looking after them properly; you should have done something about it," he said.

"The number of cats that had died would have been a warning sign to anyone."

He sentenced her to six months' imprisonment, wholly suspended for four years — meaning she will not serve time unless she commits another offence.

He made an order to disqualify her from ever owning a cat again in her life and disqualified her from owning any dog — other than her current dog — for five years.

Blake was also ordered to pay the RSPCA $27,000 for the veterinary and boarding costs of the animals they seized.

RSPCA Tasmania leading inspector Ally Hoyle and inspector J Harlow. (ABC News: Scout Wallen)

Speaking outside court, Ally Hoyle, leading inspector with RSPCA Tasmania, welcomed the sentence.

"We are happy with today's sentence. It is a good outcome for us, and the animals involved.

" We hope that it is definitely a deterrent in the future for any reoffending. "

The RSPCA said that while a large number of the cats had to be euthanased, some were able to be rehomed with help from a local cat management facility.

World.title: Rabbi's moving tribute to son-in-law as antisemitism royal commission ends
World.content:
An historic probe into the prevalence of antisemitism in Australia has ended with an impassioned call to confront the hatred that had for years preceded the Bondi Beach terror attack.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion came to an emotional close on Wednesday, bringing to an end more than 60 days of public hearings.

Chabad of Bondi director Rabbi Yehoram Ulman was the last of more than 340 witnesses to take the stand, dedicating much of his statement to his son-in-law and Bondi Beach terror attack victim Rabbi Eli Schlanger.

Rabbi Eli Schlanger was killed in the Bondi Beach terror attack. (Supplied: Facebook)

His was the first of 10 victims' funerals that Rabbi Ulman would preside over after the attack at a Hanukkah celebration on December 14, 2025.

"I looked at the coffin of the man who had married my daughter, who had become my son, who had worked beside me for years," Rabbi Ulman said.

"The mourners overflowed into the street."

Addressing Commissioner Virginia Bell SC, Rabbi Ulman said he was grateful for the work of the inquiry.

"Over these past months you have carried a solemn burden, listening to the pain of a community, examining the health of our society, and helping chart a path forward," he said.

Rabbi Yehoram Ulman told the inquiry Australia was at a "crossroads". (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Rabbi Ulman said the responsibility for addressing Jew hatred would now fall to government, institutions and communities.

"The events that brought us before this royal commission are for us not simply a statistic or headline," he said.

"For us, it is an empty seat at a Shabbat table, it is a child asking a parent whether it is safe to wear something identifying them as Jewish.

"You have heard confronting evidence. People came forward and relived painful experiences because they believe it is important for the truth to be heard and for Australia to learn from it.

"We must have the tools and the courage to confront hatred and radicalisation whenever and wherever it emerges."

'In moments of darkness, we still have a choice'

He said Australia was at a "crossroads" and must decide "what it is prepared to tolerate, what it is prepared to defend, and what values it is prepared to stand up for".

"A society in which hatred and extremism are allowed to grow is ultimately a threat to the character of the country itself," he said.

"In moments of darkness, we still have a choice. Anger and division, or another path," he said.

Hundreds of floral tributes were left outside Bondi Pavilion in memory of the 15 people killed. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Rabbi Ulman at times became emotional when telling the commission about Rabbi Schlanger's then-two-month old son, who was also injured during the attack.

"My prayer is that when my grandson is old enough to understand what happened to his father, he will also be able to understand what Australia chose to do about it and that he would be proud of the choice we made," he said.

The royal commission has now adjourned.

Ms Bell has requested that her final report and recommendations be delivered by December 18, 2026 instead of the initial December 14 due date.

The commissioner said this was to avoid distracting from the "solemn occasion" of the first anniversary of the attack.

More than 20,000 submissions have been made to the commission, with 550,000 documents received in response to notices to produce.

World.title: Man convicted for $15k spend on stolen credit cards 'likely' from dark web
World.content:
A man in South Australia's Riverland has been convicted and jailed after purchasing almost $16,000 worth of Bunnings gift cards and merchandise, using stolen credit cards "likely" obtained from the dark web.

Aijaypal Tim Sanghera, 38, appeared via video link at the Berri Magistrates Court and pleaded guilty to 12 counts of dishonest dealing with property, one count of possession of a prohibited weapon and one count of possession of a prescription drug.

The court heard Sanghera used stolen credit card information to make 11 click and collect orders at several Bunnings stores for 98 items.

Police prosecutors told the court the orders, placed over a five-week period between April and May 2026, were purchased from stores in Berri, Parafield Gardens and Edwardstown.

Of the 98 items purchased, 20 were $500 Bunnings gift cards, which were all linked to Sanghera's Bunnings PowerPass account.

"As a result, it's not the individual card holders that are at a loss because those credit card companies have reversed the transaction," police prosecutors told the court.

"The total loss to Bunnings on those 11 transactions [was] $15,899.65."

The court heard Sanghera had endured a difficult upbringing and may suffer from borderline personality disorder. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

The court heard the police investigation suggested Sanghera had obtained "a bulk of personal data likely from the dark web of stolen credit cards".

Police prosecutors said some of the items purchased with the cards were found during a search of Sanghera's residence in Bookpurnong on June 10 this year, making the total uncompensated loss for Bunnings $14,592.

They told the court less than a gram of methamphetamine, three ice pipes and a dagger were also found.

Defence lawyer Craig Caldicott told the court Sanghera had a difficult upbringing, witnessing his father's suicide by poisoning and was the victim of sexual abuse as a teenager, which had fuelled a drug addiction.

Mr Caldicott also told the court a lengthy prison sentence would not be beneficial, arguing it did not address the root of the problem.

"The problem with incarceration, it doesn't address the issues of drug addiction," he said.

Senghara was sentenced to four months prison and a two month good behaviour bond for his offending.

'Protecting the community is paramount'

Magistrate Jay Pandya described Sanghera's offending as "deliberate and relentless", and "fuelled and motivated to raise funds to continue to be able to obtain drugs and use drugs".

She said sentencing had to reflect the seriousness of the offending.

"The most important part of sentencing is protection of the community," Magistrate Pandya told the court.

"These are ordinary people in the community, who are impacted by people like yourself, who are fuelled and motivated to commit crimes for their own advantage and to fund illegal habits.

" Your offending was not simple — it involved a number of steps. "

Magistrate Pandya accepted Sanghera's guilty plea.

"You have been clear about taking responsibility and you have been clear about your remorse," she said.

World.title: 'Clearly wrong': Division erupts as NT government politicians clash over VAD
World.content:
Division within the Northern Territory government has erupted in parliament, with politicians clashing during debate over long-awaited voluntary assisted dying (VAD) legislation.

The Country Liberal Party's (CLP) VAD bill was being debated into the night on Tuesday, when NT government backbencher Tanzil Rahman accused his colleagues of being inauthentic and of deliberately mischaracterising the VAD debate.

Dr Rahman said the claimed behaviour "genuinely upsets me", describing the bill put forward by the CLP as "a very narrow VAD act, that will take us 10 years back in standard".

The first-term MLA, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into VAD, singled out NT Attorney-General Marie-Clare Boothby, who introduced the bill.

Marie-Clare Boothby introduced the VAD bill. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Ms Boothby has strongly defended the bill's "safeguards", which include a clause that will restrict VAD access to people with 12 months or less to live.

A controversial so-called doctor gag clause is also included, meaning medical professionals will not be able to initiate VAD discussions with terminally ill patients.

Dr Rahman has flagged that on Thursday he will move amendments to remove both clauses, which go against the recommendations made by the inquiry he chaired.

Another proposed amendment from Dr Rahman would prevent care facilities from refusing to provide information about VAD in residential settings.

Last night, he told NT parliament an individual's "terminality" — how sick they are, and therefore how likely they are to qualify for the 12-month window — was not always clear.

Tanzil Rahman plans to move amendments to the NT government's VAD bill. (Supplied: Department of Legislative Assembly)

"Today, the attorney-general said, 'I make no apologies for the safeguards I put in place and similarly, the 12-month prognosis period … is so important. Without it, terminality is subjective and we just can't have that'," Dr Rahman said.

"Respectfully, I also can't make any apologies for the fact that I have to challenge that.

" Because the fact is, terminality is completely subjective and everybody knows it. "

Deputy Chief Minister Gerard Maley immediately criticised Dr Rahman's contribution to the debate, backing in the 12-month timeframe.

CLP fielding VAD amendments A week out from a conscience vote on voluntary assisted dying in the NT, several CLP backbenchers have proposed amendments to the bill.

"I think [Dr Rahman] unfairly attacked the attorney-general, saying that he couldn't support [the 12-month timeframe], because I think his words were it was 'subjective', '12 months'," he said.

"He put a proposal in his amendments, which I'll just read one of the lines: 'The person is approaching the end of the person's life' — that's subjective!

"So he's replacing, in his view, a 'subjective' sentence with another subjective [sentence].

" So it really shoots his own argument in the foot. "

Mr Maley said Dr Rahman's "approach has gone all wrong".

"I wasn't going to speak about his amendments because I'm not going to support them, but I think his argument was just clearly wrong," he said.

"And having a go at the attorney-general using that word' subjective' and he's replaced it with three times that."

During his speech, Mr Maley criticised MLAs who had spoken to media publicly on the topic, saying the VAD issues were "above media hits".

Member for Fannie Bay, Laurie Zio, is among the NT politicians who have spoken to the media about VAD. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

It came after Dr Rahman and fellow government backbencher Laurie Zio — who is supportive of the amendments — both did interviews about VAD before the bill returned to parliament for debate.

"I know some people in the parliament have gone out in the media and done all sorts of things about it, but my view is above that," Mr Maley said.

"This is about a very delicate subject that needs to be treated with dignity.

"This is not about personal profiles or legacies … this is about getting things right for Territorians."

Debate on VAD has played out inside NT Parliament House this week. (ABC News: Michael Parfitt)

The amendments are unlikely to pass when a conscience vote is held on Thursday, with just six MLAs in the 25-seat parliament saying on Tuesday they would definitely support changes to the bill.

Opposition Leader Selena Uibo is also planning to move similar amendments to Dr Rahman, but it is currently unclear how many Labor MLAs will support them.

The NT was the first Australian jurisdiction to legalise voluntary assisted dying in 1995, but the laws were overturned by the Commonwealth in 1997.

The Territory did not regain the power to legislate its own VAD laws until 2022.

World.title: Potential insolvent trading probe after modular builder's closure
World.content:
The WA Consumer Protection Commissioner is calling on clients of a modular home building company which abruptly closed last week to lodge formal complaints so it can investigate further.

Bella Modular, a Perth-based manufacturer of transportable granny flats and home office buildings, wrote to all its customers on August 19 to say it would not be able to complete their outstanding projects.

In an email sent to clients last week, the company said, "Due to unforeseen and significant financial difficulties, Bella Modular is unable to complete your project directly."

The letter said a new manufacturer had agreed to take over existing contracts and complete the projects but did not provide the new firm's details.

Bella Modular has already closed its premises in Hopeland on Perth's southern fringe.

Builder's sudden closure A Perth modular home manufacturer has blindsided its customers by announcing its sudden closure and takeover by a new firm.

WA Consumer Protection Commissioner Trish Blake told 102.5 ABC Perth she wanted anyone affected to lodge a formal complaint with the department.

"I will be asking the team to investigate further and to look into it," she said.

"I'm also keen to link in with ASIC, because my concern is there may have been some trading whilst insolvent, questions that need to be answered."

Consumer rights apply

Dozens of customers have paid deposits, some more than $100,000, but have not received their buildings which are months, and in some cases, years overdue.

"Often with these companies, particularly if you've got a letter that says 'we're in financial hardship, we can't deliver your product', that tells me that something very wrong potentially has gone on in the background, which is why I want to refer things to ASIC as well," Ms Blake said.

Trish Blake says she has asked her team to investigate the company. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Because the homes are manufactured off-site and clients independently arrange for them to be transported and place on sites, the contracts are not covered under building indemnity insurance which covers losses when a building company goes out of business.

However, Ms Blake said customers still had rights under Australian Consumer Law.

"There is an offence for wrongly accepting payment and not delivering," she said.

"Particularly … taking payment when they know they don't really have a reasonable chance of delivering.

" We want to look into all of this, which is why we need as many complaints as we can get, so that we can get across the entire fact scenario of this one and see what action we can take. "

At this stage, Ms Blake said it was unclear whether the agency would be able to get customers' deposits refunded.

A Credit Watch report shows the company has a debt to the Australian Taxation Office of $576,614.68.

It is also facing three court actions for other payments totalling just over $170,000.

Customers in limbo

Peter Elliot, who ordered a granny flat intended for his parents in May 2025, and which is now months overdue, said he was shocked to receive the letter.

Mr Elliot paid a $90,000 deposit, which was 50 per cent of the cost of building, to guarantee a three-month completion time and had been hoping to have his parents living in his backyard by Christmas 2025.

"This was a disability-ready home for them to move into as they progress further in their lives," Mr Elliot said.

He said he was uncertain how another company would complete the build.

"I can't envisage another company taking on, effectively, the 50 per cent debt against the buildings that are either underway or promised to be underway," he said.

Fellow concerned customer Steve Evans has paid almost $160,000 towards a customised home from Bella Modular.

He initially paid a deposit of $28,000, then was contacted by the company four weeks ago to ask for a further $130,000, which he paid.

"I feel like a bit of a patsy … and I've got a horrible pit in my stomach that I've lost the money," Mr Evans said.

World.title: The financial trend raising the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financePrivate credit The financial trend raising the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney Kishor Napier-Raman August 26, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of home buyers across Sydney’s suburban fringes have been left hanging after this week’s $3 billion collapse of property developer Bathla Group. But looming over the crushed dreams of would-be apartment owners is a bigger story which has raised the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney: the rapid rise of the private credit market – essentially loans made to businesses from financial institutions outside the traditional banking system. A Bathla construction site at the corner of Cosmos Way and Hynds Road in Box Hill in Sydney’s outer north-west. Janie Barrett For businesses in sectors like construction, real estate and hospitality that are more exposed to the boom and bust of the business cycle, private credit, or shadow banking, has been a vital source of finance. In the post-global financial crisis era, banks became more reluctant to lend to such risky borrowers. The regulatory shackles were also tightened in Australia after the conclusion of the banking royal commission in 2019. “About 10 to 15 years ago, the banks would’ve been up to their eyeballs in this lending, and their bad debts would’ve been climbing,” said Hugh Dive, chief investment officer at Atlas Funds Management.



As banks retreated, private credit funds stepped into the void. Related Article Pubs From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis “It’s [private credit] been an important escape valve for the major banks because they have a watch list of concerns. Private credit has helped them manage those watch lists,” Jarden analyst Matthew Wilson said. To account for the risky nature of those loans, funds typically charge higher interest rates to borrowers than those offered by banks. Buoyed by the possibility of higher returns, investors poured money into private credit funds, and the sector’s growth has turbocharged in the post-pandemic era into a $US3 trillion ($4.19 trillion) global market. “For investors, it’s higher risk and higher reward,” said Nathan Zaia, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.



In Australia, where the private credit sector is worth about $200 billion (a 500 per cent increase since 2015), lenders have convinced a growing class of investors including superannuation funds that those rewards are too big to ignore “We’ve been hearing in presentations for a couple of years about the huge growth potential, how ‘we’re much more nimble than the slow and boring banks’,” Dive said. Now, thanks to a changing economic climate, those risks are starting to become too big to ignore. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has been ringing alarm bells about the sector for some time now. “When done well, private credit provides an important source of funding and supports economic growth and innovation,” the corporate watchdog said in a recent note. “But weaknesses in governance, disclosure, valuation practices and conflicts management become more pronounced as conditions tighten.”



What makes private credit attractive to an investor – like high interest rates and relatively loose regulations and lending standards – are precisely what can cause risk to build up. “In an environment where you’ve had rates going up, inflation, the costs rising, and delays to your project as well, if the price of the asset falls, that’s what catches these construction firms,” Zaia from Morningstar said. Related Article Superannuation Warning to DIY super funds over booming $200 billion sector On Tuesday, Bhart Bhushan, the former taxi driver who co-founded Bathla in 1997 with his brother Rajinder Mohan, blamed the company’s collapse on a “perfect storm” of factors – weakening demand, rising construction costs and the impacts of the Albanese government’s tax changes unveiled in the May budget. But the dark clouds are gathering above the entire private credit sector. This month, Centuria Capital, an ASX-listed fund, paused redemptions (in other words, stopped investors getting some of their money out) over concerns about exposure to Bathla. On Tuesday, MA Financial, the firm co-founded by Sydney Swans chair Andrew Pridham, limited redemptions on its $2.3 billion fund, citing changes to the property market and “press speculation” about other private credit managers.



The firm does not have any exposure to Bathla, and has rejected proposals to lend to the company in the past. Private credit is the golden thread that links Bathla’s collapse to so many of the biggest business stories of the past month. Failed pub baron Jon Adgemis, who declared bankruptcy owing $1.8 billion to creditors last year and whose business interests are being picked over in the Federal Court, had attempted to build a hospitality empire fuelled by private credit loans. Freight giant ACFS Port Logistics, which is owned by the billionaire Tzaneros family, was tipped into administration by private credit lender ScotPac, and owes nearly $300 million to various creditors. Fears about private credit surged into the foreground in the United States last year, thanks to the collapse of car parts manufacturer First Brands and subprime auto lender Tricolor. “When you see one cockroach, there are probably more,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon warned, in a now viral soundbite which has come to symbolise Wall Street’s fears about the underlying health of the shadow banking sector, and the global economy at large. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon has warned about the risks of private credit Bloomberg



Fears that the private credit sector could, like the subprime loan market in 2007, build up dependence on high-risk debt that spirals into a full-blown financial crisis are likely overblown. “It’s not that systemic, it largely involves sophisticated investors’ money, so it’s a different dynamic,” Jarden’s Matthew Wilson said of the sector. Even so, Dive warns that there could be more unpleasant defaults like the Bathla story during the years to come. “This is not the same as the GFC. It will be very unpleasant for the people investing, but it doesn’t damage the pipes of the financial system,” he said. Dive also warned that, unlike during the 2000s crash, and the COVID-19 pandemic, the government was unlikely to provide the sector with a sweeping compensation package.



“Private credit funds are shit out of luck,” he said. So too are the punters, who bought off-the-plan properties from the Bathla Group. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:01pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital on Tuesday night, two days after she was found unresponsive in a suburban northern beaches home. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger Emergency services responding to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights home about 5.45pm on Sunday and found the girl unresponsive. She was flown to Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical condition, where she died on Tuesday night.



Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex. Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young peoples’ understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in early last year that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely. The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence and a 700 per cent increased risk of homicide, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

World.title: Australia news as it happened: National Cabinet agrees only Australian citizens to be allowed guns; MP Luke Gosling steps aside as special envoy; Tributes flow for Dolly Parton
World.content:
Meta Platforms Inc and US state attorneys-general have discussed a possible mid-trial settlement of a blockbuster case accusing the company of deliberately designing Facebook and Instagram to addict teens, people familiar with the matter said.

The trial, now in its second week in federal court in Oakland, California, poses an enormous risk for Meta, as the top legal officers of 29 states are seeking both massive financial penalties on behalf of the public and mandatory changes to how the platforms operate.

Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram at Meta Platforms Inc, left, arrives at the California court on Tuesday. Bloomberg

The people familiar with settlement talks asked not to be identified due to their sensitivity.

A spokesperson for Meta had no immediate comment. A representative of the attorney-general’s office in California declined to comment. Representatives of the other three states leading the case – Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey – didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

World.title: Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesConsulting Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract Colin Kruger Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:46pm ,first published 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG has been dumped as the incoming auditor of Macquarie Group, costing the firm a contract that was expected to be worth $700 million over the next decade and marking the biggest single financial blow yet from its whistleblower scandal. Macquarie told the ASX on Wednesday afternoon that it had determined to “no longer recommend” the appointment of KPMG as auditor” at next year’s shareholder meeting, meaning it will instead

retain rival firm PwC. Macquarie chairman Glenn Steven (right) told a parliamentary committee into the KPMG scandal that it was “conceivable” Macquarie could tear up its audit contract. Alex Ellinghausen The announcement comes the same week that KPMG cut 380 employees and partners in what is expected to be just the first wave of job losses following the whistleblower scandal. Those cuts were concentrated in its consulting division, but with major contract losses, the audit section will require fewer staff. In a statement, Macquarie’s spokesman said the decision followed the scrutiny of KPMG Australia’s audit practice, including by a parliamentary committee investigation.



“It also follows Macquarie’s formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia,” the Macquarie spokesman said. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The firm has been in turmoil since a whistleblower revealed that some of its most senior partners had accessed confidential client data to win new business, a serious breach of trust. Auditors require unfettered access to customer information to do their work, which is essential to the integrity of financial markets. Macquarie said its directors also hold concerns about KPMG’s capacity to deliver the audit given several key members of the proposed KPMG Australia audit team have departed; “and culture, including a culture that transparently discloses issues.” Macquarie’s audit contract is the country’s largest because of the complexity of the banking, investment and trading giant’s business.



KPMG said that while it was disappointed by the outcome, it respected the decision taken by Macquarie. “Today’s announcement by Macquarie is a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real,” said KPMG chief executive John Sams. “Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time.” Related Article Consulting Former RBA governor dragged into KPMG scandal Sams said Macquarie’s decision showed why KPMG had to change, and cited work underway including major leadership changes and cooperation with the parliamentary investigation. The Macquarie contract loss may be the trigger for the next round of redundancies in an echo of what PwC went through during its tax leaks scandal in 2023, when its staff shared confidential information about an upcoming government policy with clients.



PwC announced plans to cut hundreds of staff the same day Westpac ended a 20-year relationship with the audit firm. That had generated more than $70 million in fees over the previous two years alone. KPMG won the Macquarie contract in circumstances that have been extensively examined in the whistleblower public hearings. World.title: He’s finally stood aside, but Gosling is still a headache for the PM
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalCourts He’s finally stood aside, but Gosling is still a headache for the PM James Massola Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:40pm ,first published 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Luke Gosling is the distraction Anthony Albanese neither needed nor wanted. And his decision to “temporarily” step down on Wednesday from his role as special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia has come not a moment too soon. With an increasingly cranky business community still hounding the prime minister about tax changes and workplace laws, states bickering over how to power the AI revolution and cost of living still Australians’ top concern, the government has enough on its plate without a possible byelection in Gosling’s Northern Territory seat of Solomon, which the MP held by a slender 1500 votes in 2025. Luke Gosling (left) with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at an RAAF base in July. The prospect of a byelection in Solomon is real, and that would be a nightmare for the Albanese government. A loss would be read as a virtual referendum on the government and its most recent budget.



To recap: Gosling, the federal member for Solomon and former soldier, has been accused of an alleged assault on David Con­nolly, the administrator of the Northern Territory (a position equivalent to that of state governor), at a Thai cultural festival in Darwin on July 18. He denies the charges, has vowed to fight them and had his bail conditions varied on July 31 so he could attend the same public events as Connolly, as long as he gave 48 hours’ notice and stayed at least 15 metres away from Connolly. Now the Solomon MP has been accused by NT police of breaching his bail conditions by attending the second day of the Australia versus Bangladesh Test in Darwin and providing Connolly’s office with less than an hour’s notice. Gosling has vigorously denied all charges and protests his innocence. But if he is found guilty and sentenced to an offence punishable by at least a year’s imprisonment, he could be expelled from parliament under section 44 of the Constitution, with a byelection to follow. In political terms, it doesn’t get much more serious than that – Albanese will not want to fight a midterm byelection. Governments often lose these contests to the opposition (Labor’s 2023 win in the Aston byelection was the first time a government had won a seat from the opposition in 102 years, for example).



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor leapt on the fresh charges yesterday of breaching bail and renewed his call for Gosling to be stood aside from the envoy role, which offers no additional salary and few additional responsibilities. That’s exactly what Albanese, when opposition leader, would have done. “These allegations are matters for the courts, but Anthony Albanese has a decision to make about who serves in his government. He should stand Mr Gosling down today,” Taylor said on Tuesday evening. Related Article ALP Labor MP steps aside from envoy role after alleged assault, bail charges Albanese is a pick-and-stick guy who loathes giving a centimetre of ground to his political enemies. But cutting Gosling loose while the matter was before the courts was a no-brainer and should have happened sooner. It’s not an admission that Gosling is guilty. It’s a sensible precaution.



The position of special envoy for this or that issue is a relatively new phenomenon in politics. Sometimes it’s consequential, such as when former Labor senator Patrick Dodson was special envoy for reconciliation and implementation of the Uluru Statement or the appointments of the twin special envoys for combating antisemitism and Islamophobia, respectively Jillian Segal and Aftab Malik. But sometimes the position of special envoy is little more than a political bauble, used to placate MPs who miss out on a position in the ranks of the ministry. When Barnaby Joyce was cooling his heels on the backbench in 2018-19, Scott Morrison appointed him special envoy for drought. Joyce thought so highly of the role that he didn’t write a report: instead, he provided Morrison with updates via text message. This is not to suggest that Gosling has taken a similarly laid-back approach to his role and, of course, the three areas of focus – defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia – are all consequential.



If Gosling is acquitted, he can return to his role. But that’s a big if. Until then, Albanese’s strategists will watch and wait. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Shock job cuts at Austrac despite expanding role battling financial crime
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesRegulation Shock job cuts at Austrac despite expanding role battling financial crime Colin Kruger August 26, 2026 — 5:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s highest-profile money-laundering regulator is preparing for significant cuts to its workforce barely a month after its financial crime fighting role was expanded to oversee tens of thousands of new businesses. Austrac is seen as the country’s most feared financial regulator and has previously taken legal action that led to massive fines for breaches of anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws, raising billions in government revenue. Austrac CEO Brendan Thomas will oversee significant cuts at the financial crime regulator. Max Mason-Hubers The watchdog also monitors financial transactions through banks, casinos and an array of other businesses for potential criminal activity including money-laundering, child exploitations, terrorism financing and fraud of government programs. On Wednesday, it signalled it was preparing to cut jobs after growth in its workforce including among staff employed on projects coming to an end.



“Consultation is under way on a number of potential organisational and workforce changes, and no final decisions have been made on structures, positions or individual outcomes,” Austrac chief executive Brendan Thomas said. The agency did not comment on information provided to this masthead by Austrac staff that the regulator will be reducing its workforce by as much as 8 per cent to less than 800 people. Thomas said Austrac had grown significantly in recent years to support major anti-money-laundering reforms and regulate a much larger number of businesses. “Since 2024, our workforce has increased by more than 300 people as we built the capability needed to deliver those reforms,” he said. “Austrac employed a range of staff on temporary projects and many of those are coming to an end. As work moves into its next phase, we are considering how we best organise our people and resources to meet our future priorities.”



Insiders not authorised to speak about the cuts due to the sensitivity of the matter have attributed the cull to a government mandate to reduce government spending, as well as the wind-back of resourcing due to the completion a transformation project. In November last year Finance Minister Katy Gallagher confirmed the government was looking at federal public service cuts to avoid a budget blowout. Government departments and agencies were expected to save as much as 5 per cent of their costs in a move that sparked warnings of further public service job losses. An edict from Finance Minister Katy Gallagher to cut public service costs was one of the drivers of the Austrac cuts. Dominic Lorrimer Department of Home Affairs, the federal agency that oversees Austrac, declined to comment on the matter. Austrac is responsible for combating criminals who launder an estimated $60 billion in illicit profits in the Australian economy each year which is used to fuel further criminal activity.



Last month, the watchdog’s coverage was expanded to include real estate agents, lawyers, conveyancers, accountants and dealers in precious metals and stones. “Bringing these sectors into the regime is about closing those gaps – putting more scrutiny on high-risk transactions and stopping dirty money at the point it enters the system,” Thomas said at the time. “This means more eyes on the ground where we know criminal exploitation occurs, helping us detect suspicious behaviour earlier and disrupt it at scale.” Late last year, Austrac’s anti-child abuse experts joined with eight banks to combine data and tools to identify suspected purchases of child abuse material and identified multiple suspicious payments to “vulnerable minors”. Austrac has been one of the most high-profile government regulators with a track record of extracting record fines and settlements with some of Australia’s biggest corporations.



Related Article Opinion

Casinos The $400 million sting that could snuff out Star for good Elizabeth Knight Business columnist This includes Westpac’s $1.3 billion fine in 2020 for systemic anti-money-laundering breaches – the largest civil penalty in Australian corporate history. The watchdog eight years ago also hit the Commonwealth Bank with a $700 million penalty for breaking anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws, and in 2023 secured a $450 million fine for Crown Resorts for systemic money-laundering breaches. The Federal Court is still determining an appropriate fine for casino operator Star Entertainment, which could top $400 million and could put its financially struggling business in jeopardy. Last month, Thomas gave a speech outlining the massive challenges Austrac is facing with the volume of illicit money in the Australian economy rising sharply due to drugs and illicit tobacco.



“The challenge is not simply the scale of illicit money, but the speed at which it now moves and the creativity with which it is disguised,” he said. “We are now seeing AI tools capable of generating entire identity ecosystems – passports, payslips, bank statements and employment histories – within minutes.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. World.title: ‘She’s a mythological figure’: America mourns the one person everybody loved
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaVale ‘She’s a mythological figure’: America mourns the one person everybody loved Michael Koziol August 26, 2026 — 5:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nashville: Ernie Samora left home in Denver just a month ago and moved to the capital of country music. Little did he know that Tennessee was about to lose its undisputed queen. “Dolly was a bright light of kindness and generosity and empathy and understanding,” the 24-year-old says as he surveys the neon lights of Nashville’s Broadway. Ernie Samora on the main street of Nashville on Tuesday night. Michael Koziol “She made amazing music on top of that. I thought I knew a lot about Dolly, and I’ve learnt so much more about her today after her passing. People are just talking about all the good things she did. “She’s like a mythological figure at this point. I fully believe she will go down with the likes of Elvis and Michael Jackson.”



We are standing in the shadow of Dolly Parton’s SongTeller Hotel, a new addition to downtown Nashville which includes a museum of all things Dolly, and is due to welcome its first guests next month. Only a few days ago, Parton told People magazine how proud she was of the project. She acknowledged a few lingering health issues. On Tuesday, just a few blocks away at the Vanderbilt hospital, she died. She was 80. Fans of country music icon Dolly Parton pay tribute to her on the Music City Walk of Fame. Getty Images Nashville’s famous country music strip was bursting with spontaneous Dolly joy on Tuesday night, with bands plucking a song or two from her bulging songbook, or taking requests from eager crowds. Parton’s passing has brought a rare moment of national reflection. AP Photo/George Walker IV



At Doc Holliday’s Saloon, Jonny and Matt performed Jolene. Somewhere in the din, somebody was doing a karaoke version of I Will Always Love You. At Miranda Lambert’s Casa Rosa, a young woman named Ashley Christensen sang 9 to 5. “I heard that was part of a movie. Steel Magnolias, right?” she said afterwards. The crowd cried out: “No!” While Parton was ill with cancer, her death still came as a shock. Tuesday night’s tributes were improvised; outside the historic Tootsies Orchid Lounge, someone had pinned a cardboard sign to the purple brick wall. “We will always [heart] Dolly,” it said. “It’s hard to be a diamond in a rhinestone world.” “I think she is pretty much the only one left that universally everybody just loves”: Nashville singer and bartender Amanda Taylor. Michael Koziol Across the road at AJ’s Good Time Bar, bartender Amanda Taylor jumped on stage to perform Islands in the Stream. Further away at the iconic Grand Ole Opry, bluegrass singer-songwriter Rhonda Vincent threw out the script and opened the evening with Coat of Many Colours, plus more of Parton’s songs later in the night.



“Really, she’s more than a legend, she’s an icon,” Taylor told this masthead after her song. “And I think she is pretty much the only one left that universally everybody just loves. Nobody has a bad word, nobody’s divisive about it – everybody just loves her.” Related Article Vale Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80 From Nashville to Washington, Americans feel as though they have lost one of the last pieces of the national fabric that bound everybody together. To say that Dolly Parton was universally beloved is no understatement – and in present-day America, that’s a rare thing. She was mourned by Donald Trump and the Democratic Socialists of America alike. Nathan McDermott, a New York-based journalist, posted their tributes side by side on X and said: “We probably won’t ever see anything like this for the rest of our lives.” Flags at the White House were lowered to half-mast in honour of Dolly Parton. Donald Trump said her like would not be seen again. AP Photo/Alex Brandon



A movement swirled to rename Nashville International Airport after Parton. Local Democrat Christopher Hale said if such a bill were introduced at the Tennessee legislature, “it would pass unanimously”. Gallery Gallery icon 12 images Vale Dolly Parton in Australia American flags outside the Nashville Metropolitan Courthouse were at half-mast, as they were around the country, following a directive from the White House. “There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump said on social media. Just off Broadway in Nashville’s Music Garden – a small park that contains the Music City Walk of Fame – well-wishers had surrounded Parton’s star with flowers and candles. “I’m devastated, like everyone else,” said Heidi Ludwig, 56, who was visiting from Hermosa Beach, California. “She was just a light in this world. I feel like everything’s gone dark without Dolly here. It’s pretty sad.”



Heidi Ludwig (right) with her friends Lauren and Kimberly Hartog at Dolly Parton’s star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Michael Koziol Men and women, black and white, singles and couples – they all stopped to pay their respects. “It’s special to be here today,” said James Toone of Las Vegas. “The feeling here in the city, it’s full of love – and a lot of sorrow.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Woolworths doesn’t need Ooshies effect to beat Coles, says CEO
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesSupermarkets Woolworths doesn’t need Ooshies effect to beat Coles, says CEO Jessica Yun Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:20pm ,first published August 26, 2026 — 8:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Woolworths chief Amanda Bardwell has celebrated the success of its Ooshies collectables campaign but says the supermarket giant’s rebound started before the introduction of the promotion. Australia’s biggest grocery chain posted its full-year results on Tuesday. Net profit lifted by 18.1 per cent to $1.14 billion, and revenue grew 3.6 per cent to $71.5 billion across the whole Woolworths group. While collectables campaigns can act as a sales “amplification”, Woolworths will not increase their frequency, chief executive Amanda Bardwell said. Louie Douvis Food sales at the grocery chain increased 4.6 per cent to $53.9 billion in the 2026 financial year, ahead of rival Coles, which on Tuesday reported supermarket sales rose 3.7 per cent to $41.5 billion for the full year. Woolworths’ sales growth has picked up even more pace since it launched its wildly popular collaboration with Disney in mid-July, which became a craze among young children and drove parents to shop in the company’s stores. In the first two months of the new financial year (July and August), food sales grew 7.6 per cent, with the supermarket estimating 1.5 per cent to 2 per cent of it was down to the promotional campaign.



“What I know is that the Ooshies collectables have been very successful for us,” Bardwell said. “What’s critical is to have the underlying retail foundations right first: the great experience, great value, and then you can amplify with things like [collectables]. But getting those basics right is the most important thing first.” Related Article Supermarkets Why Coles won’t copy Woolies’ Ooshies sugar hit Collectables campaigns, which are typically tied to a spending level, are a major driver of foot traffic: experts from Citi estimate Ooshies may have boosted sales by as much as $100 million. “We see some customers who certainly might decide to add a few more items to their basket while they’re shopping with us, so they qualify for the extra Ooshie. And then we do have some customers who might not shop with us very frequently who choose to switch to Woolies during that period,” said Bardwell.



Woolworths will not increase the promotion’s frequency, Bardwell said. Her Coles counterpart, Leah Weckert, said on Tuesday that children’s collectables delivered shorter sales hits compared with those targeted at adults, such as cookware and glass containers. Bardwell said shoppers’ value-seeking habits were here to stay. “For three years now we’ve been talking about the pressure on household budgets,” she said. “We’ve moved beyond a temporary phase into a new reality of entrenched value-seeking. The Ooshies campaign has been a big winner for Woolworths. “Customers have developed money-saving habits to stretch their weekly shopping as far as possible.”



In the colder months, Australians turned to slow-cooking meats, with chuck, osso bucco and brisket selling twice as quickly as other beef cuts. Over the 2026 financial year, Woolworths launched 445 new private-label products, including in Mexican, Asian and Italian cuisine ranges. Online sales across the broader corporate group jumped 15.9 per cent to $10.6 billion as customers shifted from next-day delivery to same-day delivery. One-hour deliveries grew 65 per cent for Milkrun, which Woolworths acquired in 2023, and DoorDash. Discount department chain Big W, which has been a drag on the broader Woolworths company, bounced back to profitability with earnings of $64 million after booking losses of $33 million the year before. While local supermarket sales rose 4.6 per cent, this figure came off the back of a period affected by industrial action and supply chain disruption from Christmas 2024. Excluding those impacts, sales grew 4.1 per cent.



Investors welcomed Woolworths’ results, sending its share price 3 per cent higher to $40.02 in the afternoon. The company declared a fully franked final dividend of 52¢ per share, a 15.6 per increase on last year’s dividend. Woolworths’ share price has recovered by more than 20 per cent over the past 12 months. Related Article Opinion

Supermarket wars Pushy about Ooshies: Kids are pumping up Woolies’ sales Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Josh Gilbert, an analyst at share trading platform eToro, said the grocery chain, which was subject to sustained political and public scrutiny for years over food prices, had managed to get customers back in the door. “Woolworths cut prices this year and still managed to make more money, which is a rare feat in supermarkets with margins so wafer-thin,” he said. “Amanda Bardwell inherited a business with plenty to fix when she took the reins, but her rebuild is showing up where it counts.” Woolworths had shifted shopping behaviour during the Ooshies campaign, Gilbert added, but cautioned that a great promotion shouldn’t be mistaken for permanent gains in market share.



“This is what a supermarket recovery looks like. The challenge is keeping those shoppers now that the toys have left the checkout. “Woolworths has shown it can get shoppers back this year. [The 2027 financial year] will be about proving they will stay.” The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: The financial trend raising the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financePrivate credit The financial trend raising the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney Kishor Napier-Raman August 26, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hundreds of home buyers across Sydney’s suburban fringes have been left hanging after this week’s $3 billion collapse of property developer Bathla Group. But looming over the crushed dreams of would-be apartment owners is a bigger story which has raised the alarm from Wall Street to western Sydney: the rapid rise of the private credit market – essentially loans made to businesses from financial institutions outside the traditional banking system. A Bathla construction site at the corner of Cosmos Way and Hynds Road in Box Hill in Sydney’s outer north-west. Janie Barrett For businesses in sectors like construction, real estate and hospitality that are more exposed to the boom and bust of the business cycle, private credit, or shadow banking, has been a vital source of finance. In the post-global financial crisis era, banks became more reluctant to lend to such risky borrowers. The regulatory shackles were also tightened in Australia after the conclusion of the banking royal commission in 2019. “About 10 to 15 years ago, the banks would’ve been up to their eyeballs in this lending, and their bad debts would’ve been climbing,” said Hugh Dive, chief investment officer at Atlas Funds Management.



As banks retreated, private credit funds stepped into the void. Related Article Pubs From playboy to bankrupt. The $1.8b rise and fall of Jon Adgemis “It’s [private credit] been an important escape valve for the major banks because they have a watch list of concerns. Private credit has helped them manage those watch lists,” Jarden analyst Matthew Wilson said. To account for the risky nature of those loans, funds typically charge higher interest rates to borrowers than those offered by banks. Buoyed by the possibility of higher returns, investors poured money into private credit funds, and the sector’s growth has turbocharged in the post-pandemic era into a $US3 trillion ($4.19 trillion) global market. “For investors, it’s higher risk and higher reward,” said Nathan Zaia, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.



In Australia, where the private credit sector is worth about $200 billion (a 500 per cent increase since 2015), lenders have convinced a growing class of investors including superannuation funds that those rewards are too big to ignore “We’ve been hearing in presentations for a couple of years about the huge growth potential, how ‘we’re much more nimble than the slow and boring banks’,” Dive said. Now, thanks to a changing economic climate, those risks are starting to become too big to ignore. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission has been ringing alarm bells about the sector for some time now. “When done well, private credit provides an important source of funding and supports economic growth and innovation,” the corporate watchdog said in a recent note. “But weaknesses in governance, disclosure, valuation practices and conflicts management become more pronounced as conditions tighten.”



What makes private credit attractive to an investor – like high interest rates and relatively loose regulations and lending standards – are precisely what can cause risk to build up. “In an environment where you’ve had rates going up, inflation, the costs rising, and delays to your project as well, if the price of the asset falls, that’s what catches these construction firms,” Zaia from Morningstar said. Related Article Superannuation Warning to DIY super funds over booming $200 billion sector On Tuesday, Bhart Bhushan, the former taxi driver who co-founded Bathla in 1997 with his brother Rajinder Mohan, blamed the company’s collapse on a “perfect storm” of factors – weakening demand, rising construction costs and the impacts of the Albanese government’s tax changes unveiled in the May budget. But the dark clouds are gathering above the entire private credit sector. This month, Centuria Capital, an ASX-listed fund, paused redemptions (in other words, stopped investors getting some of their money out) over concerns about exposure to Bathla. On Tuesday, MA Financial, the firm co-founded by Sydney Swans chair Andrew Pridham, limited redemptions on its $2.3 billion fund, citing changes to the property market and “press speculation” about other private credit managers.



The firm does not have any exposure to Bathla, and has rejected proposals to lend to the company in the past. Private credit is the golden thread that links Bathla’s collapse to so many of the biggest business stories of the past month. Failed pub baron Jon Adgemis, who declared bankruptcy owing $1.8 billion to creditors last year and whose business interests are being picked over in the Federal Court, had attempted to build a hospitality empire fuelled by private credit loans. Freight giant ACFS Port Logistics, which is owned by the billionaire Tzaneros family, was tipped into administration by private credit lender ScotPac, and owes nearly $300 million to various creditors. Fears about private credit surged into the foreground in the United States last year, thanks to the collapse of car parts manufacturer First Brands and subprime auto lender Tricolor. “When you see one cockroach, there are probably more,” JP Morgan chief executive Jamie Dimon warned, in a now viral soundbite which has come to symbolise Wall Street’s fears about the underlying health of the shadow banking sector, and the global economy at large. JPMorgan boss Jamie Dimon has warned about the risks of private credit Bloomberg



Fears that the private credit sector could, like the subprime loan market in 2007, build up dependence on high-risk debt that spirals into a full-blown financial crisis are likely overblown. “It’s not that systemic, it largely involves sophisticated investors’ money, so it’s a different dynamic,” Jarden’s Matthew Wilson said of the sector. Even so, Dive warns that there could be more unpleasant defaults like the Bathla story during the years to come. “This is not the same as the GFC. It will be very unpleasant for the people investing, but it doesn’t damage the pipes of the financial system,” he said. Dive also warned that, unlike during the 2000s crash, and the COVID-19 pandemic, the government was unlikely to provide the sector with a sweeping compensation package.



“Private credit funds are shit out of luck,” he said. So too are the punters, who bought off-the-plan properties from the Bathla Group. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:01pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital on Tuesday night, two days after she was found unresponsive in a suburban northern beaches home. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger Emergency services responding to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights home about 5.45pm on Sunday and found the girl unresponsive. She was flown to Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical condition, where she died on Tuesday night.



Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex. Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young peoples’ understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in early last year that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely. The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence and a 700 per cent increased risk of homicide, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732).

World.title: Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract
World.content:
Breaking BusinessCompaniesConsulting Macquarie dumps KPMG from the nation’s biggest audit contract Colin Kruger Updated August 26, 2026 — 5:46pm ,first published 5:32pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

KPMG has been dumped as the incoming auditor of Macquarie Group, costing the firm a contract that was expected to be worth $700 million over the next decade and marking the biggest single financial blow yet from its whistleblower scandal. Macquarie told the ASX on Wednesday afternoon that it had determined to “no longer recommend” the appointment of KPMG as auditor” at next year’s shareholder meeting, meaning it will instead

retain rival firm PwC. Macquarie chairman Glenn Steven (right) told a parliamentary committee into the KPMG scandal that it was “conceivable” Macquarie could tear up its audit contract. Alex Ellinghausen The announcement comes the same week that KPMG cut 380 employees and partners in what is expected to be just the first wave of job losses following the whistleblower scandal. Those cuts were concentrated in its consulting division, but with major contract losses, the audit section will require fewer staff. In a statement, Macquarie’s spokesman said the decision followed the scrutiny of KPMG Australia’s audit practice, including by a parliamentary committee investigation.



“It also follows Macquarie’s formal enquiries of KPMG to consider its capacity to deliver the audit, as well as the nature and impact of ongoing issues at KPMG Australia,” the Macquarie spokesman said. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The firm has been in turmoil since a whistleblower revealed that some of its most senior partners had accessed confidential client data to win new business, a serious breach of trust. Auditors require unfettered access to customer information to do their work, which is essential to the integrity of financial markets. Macquarie said its directors also hold concerns about KPMG’s capacity to deliver the audit given several key members of the proposed KPMG Australia audit team have departed; “and culture, including a culture that transparently discloses issues.” Macquarie’s audit contract is the country’s largest because of the complexity of the banking, investment and trading giant’s business.



KPMG said that while it was disappointed by the outcome, it respected the decision taken by Macquarie. “Today’s announcement by Macquarie is a clear reminder that the consequences of our past failings are real,” said KPMG chief executive John Sams. “Rebuilding trust will require sustained action, transparency and time.” Related Article Consulting Former RBA governor dragged into KPMG scandal Sams said Macquarie’s decision showed why KPMG had to change, and cited work underway including major leadership changes and cooperation with the parliamentary investigation. The Macquarie contract loss may be the trigger for the next round of redundancies in an echo of what PwC went through during its tax leaks scandal in 2023, when its staff shared confidential information about an upcoming government policy with clients.



PwC announced plans to cut hundreds of staff the same day Westpac ended a 20-year relationship with the audit firm. That had generated more than $70 million in fees over the previous two years alone. KPMG won the Macquarie contract in circumstances that have been extensively examined in the whistleblower public hearings.
